News.title: 'Apocalyptic' Cairngorms wildfire leaves residents 'angry' after evacuations
News.content:
'Apocalyptic' Cairngorms wildfire leaves residents 'angry' after evacuations

Residents in the remote village of Nethy Bridge, in the Scottish Highlands, are furious following wildfire evacuation orders and 'apocalyptic' plumes of smoke from a nearby blaze

View 5 Images Residents are 'upset, angry and frustrated' (Image: RSPB Scotland/PA Wire)

Residents have spoken of their anger after being told to flee an "apocalyptic" wildfire in Scotland - with some ordered to leave their pets behind as huge plumes of smoke engulf the area.

‌



The wildfire has been raging through the Cairngorms National Park this week, with residents in the Highlands village of Nethy Bridge describing seeing enormous clouds of smoke before they were evacuated.

‌



More than 500 firefighters have been battling the blaze for the past 10 days, forcing the evacuation of homes in the remote region.

‌



Sandy McCook, chairman of the Nethy Bridge and Vicinity Community Council, said residents of the Cairngorms village have been left "upset, angry and frustrated" after seeing large plumes of smoke from the wildfire on Friday before they were evacuated. "Apocalyptic is the word for the pall of smoke that was on the go yesterday," Mr McCook said.

View 5 Images Locals described seeing enormous clouds of smoke (Image: Patricia Eccles/PA Wire)

UK weather model shows 45C heat surge in what would be hottest day ever seen READ MORE :

UK weather maps show 40C heatwave within days as 18 counties hit 39C or more READ MORE :

The smoke has changed direction, and on Saturday at midday he said it was blowing towards Aberdeenshire and the North Sea, but the flames were still “very plain to see” from the outskirts of Nethy Bridge.

‌



Duncan Ferguson, a resident in Glenmore near Aviemore, said police visited his home last Wednesday and told residents to "leave your pets and go".

He said the fire could become severe and affect property unless it was contained quickly. "It's going to be bad, it's going to be major unless they get hold of it. It's heathland at the minute, but it's started to burn in the upper area of the regeneration of the Caledonian pine forest," he added.

"Once it comes down into there, it's dry, dry ground, with a real load to burn. It's just going to get hotter and hotter."

‌



Evacuations and smoke advisories are still in place after Police Scotland declared a major incident as emergency services battled the wildfire in the Cairngorms National Park.

Powerful winds caused the out-of-control wildfire to behave unpredictably, emergency services previously said.

View 5 Images The wildfire has torn through the Cairngorms National Park (Image: RSPB Scotland/PA Wire)

‌



In an update on Saturday morning, Police Scotland said residents in a small area of properties north-west of Dorback Lodge (Lain Thatchan) had been evacuated as a precaution.

The Scottish Government said a fire break was established around nearby villages overnight, with additional breaks now being built the as Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) deploys more resources to tackle the inferno.

A smoke advisory is also in place for Tomintoul, where residents have been advised to keep windows and doors closed due to smoke from the wildfire.

‌



"If you are affected by smoke, stay indoors where possible, keep windows and doors closed, and avoid strenuous outdoor activity," SFRS said.

The service also requested more heavy machinery, such as bulldozers, to help with the response.

"Operators who can provide suitable plant machinery to support the ongoing multi-agency response are asked to report to the Village Hall in Nethy Bridge," SFRS said.

‌



View 5 Images The wildfire was first reported on July 15 (Image: RSPB Scotland/PA Wire)

On the ground, Mr McCook said there was a major increase in firefighting units from the SFRS in and around the village, plus multiple wildfire response units.

"I think a lot of people are running on adrenaline," he said.

‌



"A lot of people are upset, angry and frustrated at the ongoing situation because the Scottish Government said a week ago [on Wednesday] that they had enough resources to deal with it, and they said on Thursday that the fire was contained.

"My argument with that is, if you said the fire was contained and you had enough resources last Wednesday and Thursday, why are we still fighting it 10 days later and it’s still running out of control? It is still not controlled in any way shape or form."

On Saturday, emergency services said there were nine fire appliances at the scene, supported by specialist wildfire resources.

‌



SFRS said it has maintained a "significant operational response" since the wildfire was first reported on July 15.

More than 500 firefighters have tackled the blaze over the last 10 days, alongside specialist wildfire appliances, all-terrain vehicles, helicopter water-bombing operations and partner agencies.

View 5 Images Some residents were told to leave their pets behind (Image: RSPB Scotland/PA Wire)

‌



The update came after First Minister John Swinney chaired a meeting of the Scottish Government’s Resilience Room (SGoRR) on Friday night.

The meeting was attended by several ministers and representatives from emergency services, including SFRS and Police Scotland.

On Friday, the First Minister told PA: "I would obviously ask people in the region to follow all of the advice that is available and to respect the exclusion zone that’s been put in place.

‌



"This is an incident that we felt was moving in a positive direction earlier this week, but with the change of weather circumstances – which is an illustration of just the scale and difficulty of the situation that we are managing – it has moved in the other direction."

His comments came as smoke from the wildfire near Glenmore drifted as far as Aberdeen due to changing wind conditions.

The fire, which broke out near the village of Glenmore on Wednesday last week, led to residents and campsites being evacuated. It covered about six square kilometres of heather and small trees at its height.

Article continues below

Evacuated residents are being directed to a dedicated respite centre at the Macdonald Aviemore Resort.

Members of the public are asked to avoid affected areas in the Cairngorms National Park. SFRS said the area remains unsafe due to firefighting operations, rapidly changing fire conditions and helicopter activity.

News.title: The 'life-changing' side effect for women from Mounjaro and Wegovy
News.content:
The 'life-changing' side effect for women from Mounjaro and Wegovy

A doctor has claimed that women 'increase the risk' by taking weight loss jabs

View 3 Images Taking weight loss medication could have this 'side effect' (Image: Scott Olson/Getty Images)

The weight-loss jabs like Mounjaro and Wegovy being taken by millions across the UK could come with a surprise side effect for some women that could be life-changing. People online are apparently referring to these surprises as 'Ozempic babies', according to ITV's Dr Amir Khan, who recently talked about the fertility improvement that may come with the drug.

‌



Several people are claiming there is a link between people taking the drugs and finding it easier to fall pregnant after years of struggling. But doctors are warning this isn’t something to mess around with.

‌



Anyone taking the injections should treat contraception seriously, because the body changes linked to major weight loss can make it easier to conceive. The big concern is that these injections are not licensed for pregnancy, meaning they’re not meant to be used if you’re trying for a baby or think you might already be pregnant.

‌



That’s why experts say planning matters. If you’re on the jabs and not looking for a little one, you may need extra precautions to avoid a shock.

ITV regular Dr Amir Khan laid it out on the No Appointments Necessary podcast, saying: "There is this thing online called an 'Ozempic baby' where people who have been on these weight loss jabs who have struggled to get pregnant previously are finding that they're getting pregnant.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



"If you are trying for a baby or you may be pregnant, you must not take these medications because they are not licensed for pregnancy. These are accidental pregnancies that are happening."

He also suggested the shift may be strongest in women with insulin resistance and conditions such as PCOS, which can affect periods and ovulation. Dr Khan added: "I don't think the jabs themselves are causing the pregnancy, but they're changing the biology enough in these ladies for them to increase the risk of getting pregnant.

"If you're trying to get pregnant, you must not take these jabs. I'm not saying they're harmful in pregnancy, but we don't have any evidence to say one way or another."

‌



View 3 Images One woman claimed that the side effect was 'unexpected but the best thing ever' (stock) (Image: Getty Images)

While the nickname is "Ozempic baby", most people under the ITV doctor's video are reporting these experiences after using Mounjaro and Wegovy. In the comments under one video, women swapped stories of surprise pregnancies — sometimes even when they thought they were covered.

One person wrote: "I got pregnant on Mounjaro. Very unexpected but the best thing ever!" Another said: "I got pregnant with our third after struggling for 18 months with our first and second, and I was on the pill! My doctor said that [certain medications] can reduce the effectiveness of the pill, as well as having PCOS insulin resistance."

‌



A third added: "I am an example of this too. Fell pregnant (after years of trying and nothing) after six months of being on Mounjaro ." And someone else claimed: "Got pregnant with twins on Mounjaro. I've never had a regular period in my life. If a drug is regulating your hormones then it’s going to help."

View 3 Images Women taking injections of Mounjaro or Wegovy could become 'more fertile'

How does this all link up?

Experts say it’s likely an indirect fertility 'boost' that comes from losing a significant amount of weight, which is known to improve insulin sensitivity and help regulate hormones. This could help restore more regular ovulation in some women, especially those with PCOS.

Article continues below

Professor Gerard Conway, of the London Lauriston Clinic, said: "Many women with PCOS have insulin resistance, which leads to higher testosterone levels and more irregular periods. With longer gaps between periods, ovulation is impaired, so the chances of conceiving are reduced. Mounjaro-induced weight loss (typically 5-15% of body weight) may improve insulin sensitivity, decrease androgen levels, and restore ovulatory cycles, enhancing chances of conception."

Even so, the key point is that neither Mounjaro nor Wegovy is a fertility treatment. Current UK guidance says stopping at least a month before trying to conceive for Mounjaro, and at least two months for Wegovy is important.

News.title: 'Hannibal the Cannibal' killer on hunger strike and wants to move back to glass box cell
News.content:
Robert Maudsley, the quadruple killer dubbed 'Hannibal the Cannibal', has gone on hunger strike again in a grim protest about his prison conditions.

Britain's longest serving prisoner, Maudsley has just spent his 52nd consecutive birthday behind bars. He turned 73 last month and it was his second birthday in Whitemoor, Cambs., after decades in Wakefield jail.

He has asked to move back to his 'glass cage' in the West Yorkshire prison dubbed 'Monster Mansion,' because it holds so many dangerous inmates.

View 4 Images Maudsley has spent almost 48 years in a single cell (Image: BBC)

‌



He has now spent almost 48 years in a single cell, the equivalent of more than 17,500 consecutive days in solitary confinement.

But his request to return to Wakefield has so far been denied. He has been on a hunger strike refusing prison food for two months, which has sparked fears about his health due to his age.

He also went on hunger strike to protest his move from Wakefield last year. He told his girlfriend, Londoner Loveinia Grace MacKenney, 71, that he feels "threatened" and is refusing to cooperate with prison staff.

View 4 Images Robert Maudsley's partner Loveinia MacKenney (Image: Daily Mirror)

‌



"He feels intimidated," she told the Mirror. "He feels bullied and he is at an age when he is extremely vulnerable. He is refusing to interact with staff because he cannot trust them. He does not want to see the psychologist.

"They want to discuss the trauma of his early life when he was attacked and abused and he does not want to go through that again.

"He has not had any visits and is refusing food again, he has gone on hunger strike, refusing food for the past two months.

"He will not see any nurses or medical staff, he has had enough. I am very worried about his health and state of mind."

‌



Loveinia, who speaks to her partner every week and writes to him regularly, added: "He does not sound like the same person, he just sounds very weak."

She said his exercise was now in a tiny 10ft x 10ft yard with 20 ft high walls, and his time in the shower is cut short.

The man she calls 'Bob' is said to have a high IQ and enjoyed reading and listening to classical music in Wakefield, where his previous crimes led to the nickname 'Hannibal the Cannibal'.

However, prison staff removed his TV and radio during a dispute there, and he was moved to Whitemoor in April last year.

‌



Maudsley became the UK's longest serving prisoner after the death of Moors murderer Ian Brady, who served 51 years, in 2017.

Maudsley was sentenced to life in 1974 for the manslaughter of John Farrell, a 30-year-old child abuser. He then killed three men behind bars.

View 4 Images One of Maudsley's cards to his partner Loveinia MacKenney (Image: Daily Mirror)

After killing his last two victims, he was said to have told a prison guard: “There’ll be two short on the roll call." He earned his 'Hannibal the Cannibal' nickname after one victim was found with a spoon in his skull, leading to rumours - later proven false - that he had eaten the man's brains. Maudsley spent decades at Wakefield, with special measures in place so prison staff could see him before they entered his cell.

‌



View 4 Images Prison psychiatrist Dr Bob Johnson, who interviewed Robert Maudsley, believes he should be freed (Image: YouTube/@shaunattwoodOFFICIAL)

Due to the Perspex window on his cell, he has been compared to the fictional character Hannibal Lecter, played by Anthony Hopkins in "The Silence of the Lambs."

The Ministry of Justice refused to comment on his latest hunger strike, and his complaints about visits from friends and relatives, saying they do not comment on individual prisoners.

A source stressed that Maudsley has access to a phone, has half an hour per day outside for exercise, and is allowed a daily shower.

News.title: 'As Mayor every decision will be about making life cheaper and easier for us all'
News.content:
'As Mayor every decision will be about making life cheaper and easier for us all'

'I’ll build on the work Andy did and make sure every young person has the careers advice, work placements and pathway to help them get a successful job', Labour's Greater Manchester Mayor candidate Bev Craig writes

View 2 Images Bev Craig hopes to replace Andy Burnham as the Mayor of Greater Manchester (Image: Peter Byrne/PA Wire)

This Thursday, the people of Greater Manchester will take part in the biggest by-election our country has ever seen.

‌



The choice is clear: either we choose to make things easier and cheaper for all of us, or we give power to those who want to spend their time trying to divide us.

‌



I firmly believe that on Thursday we will choose to move forward together and build a future that works for us all. In Greater Manchester we’ve always forged our own path.

‌



It’s no accident that we’re the home of the industrial revolution, the trade union and cooperative movements, the suffragettes and the fight for equal rights.

We have led the fight back from the de-industrialisation that left many of our communities abandoned. But despite boasting the fastest economic growth in the country, too many people still feel that life is too hard.

Inside No10 North as Andy Burnham sets up his new power base READ MORE :

View 2 Images Bev Craig has been doing Parkrun in every Manchester borough (Image: Steve Allen)

‌



That’s why I’ve set myself a simple test if I become Mayor - every decision I make will make life cheaper and easier for us all. I’ll start by putting more money in people’s pockets with free bus travel for all 11–18-year-olds – saving families £500 a year and sending a clear message that every young person here can go wherever they want to go.

The success of Greater Manchester depends on us all feeling the benefits, and too often people see the success of Greater Manchester but they don’t feel it. That’s why Andy Burnham and I set up the Good Growth Fund to help spread growth to every postcode. While he works to do this across the country as Prime Minister, I’ll make it happen here as Mayor.

Good growth isn’t a slogan, it's about well paid, secure jobs and restoring pride in your town centre. As Mayor, I’ll build on the work Andy did and make sure every young person has the careers advice, work placements and pathway to help them get a successful job. I’ll also use the money that’s being generated by the growth in our city centre and use it to create a Hight Streets Fund so all our town centres can get back their sense of pride. I’ll crack down on the vape shops and dodgy businesses blighting communities and back the local independents that light up our high streets.

‌



I’m taking on the fight against grievance and division with a positive, optimistic campaign of the can-do attitude of this place. Radical and realistic, because you beat divisive populism by delivering more money in people’s pockets and hope of a better future.

With Andy in No10 (North!), me as Mayor and the spirit of this place, there’s no limit to what we can achieve.

'A new generation of council housing'

I grew up in a council house and when times got tough, having a secure roof over my head was a literal lifeline for me and my family. But today, too many people just aren’t able to get a good, secure home they can afford.

‌



As Leader of Manchester I set out to change that. Last year we built more council and social homes than in the last 25 years and as Mayor I’d go even further.

I’ll build a new generation of council housing, 50,000 homes across all our boroughs that everyone can afford.

A new generation of council homes helping our next generation succeed. I’m proud Andy Burnham is backing my plans and as Prime Minister is just as committed to building council homes, so people have the same security I had growing up.

Article continues below

'Parkrun in every borough'

I’m running for Mayor, literally. As part of my campaign, I’m doing a Parkrun in every borough of Greater Manchester. A shout out to all the amazing volunteers that keep our sports and running clubs alive.

I have loved being joined by loads of supporters, the odd Secretary of State and even the new Prime Minister! I have strict rules for politicians though, no short shorts allowed!

'We need a Mayor who stands up for ordinary people'

With such a big by-election, all indications are it could be close. The first poll had Labour on 33 and Reform on 30. Just because there’s a bin fight happening down south, please don’t think that your vote won’t matter. We need a Mayor with a track record of standing up for ordinary people and getting stuff done.

News.title: EasyJet passengers 'collapsing, given no water and forced to sleep outside' in 24 hours of 'chaos'
News.content:
EasyJet passengers 'collapsing, given no water and forced to sleep outside' in 24 hours of 'chaos'

EXCLUSIVE: A tourist on a delayed EasyJet flight has claimed he and fellow passengers were given 'no food or water' and left to sleep outside by staff at Tivat Airport in Montenegro

View 4 Images Passengers have reportedly fainted due to overcrowding at Tivat Airport after a delayed EasyJet flight (Image: Dr Ron Roberts)

A desperate EasyJet customer claims he and his fellow passengers they have been left with "no food and water" after being stranded at an airport.

Dr Ron Roberts, 70, complained to the Mirror that the budget airline has in his view, "abandoned" travellers at Montenegro's Tivat Airport for over 24 hours without food, water, accommodation, or any EasyJet staff around to help - and said that "suffocating" overcrowding caused a passenger to collapse.

He had been due to fly back to London Luton at 12:40 yesterday, but remains stuck in the airport this afternoon more than 24 hours on amid what he describes as "absolute chaos".

‌



View 4 Images EasyJet passengers remained stuck in the airport 24 hours after they were due to depart (Image: Dr Ron Roberts)

Dr Roberts, who is travelling alone after his wife returned from holiday early to visit her sister, told the Mirror he'd got to the airport early, but said the flight was continually delayed and airport staff failed to help passengers or provide information. He claimed: "It was absolute chaos. They wouldn't do anything. They left people without food or water."

The retired psychology lecturer claimed he and other passengers from the delayed flight were "forced to sleep in the street" after airport staff told them to find their own hotels for the night when the airport was closing. He complained: "We were all thrown out of the airport. They said you've got to go and... you've got to go and arrange your own accommodation and travel. Even though they'd already told us there's no free accommodation in the area. I said it's not possible to do that."

View 4 Images One traveller claimed the airline had showed a 'complete contempt for passengers' (file photo) (Image: PA)

Dr Roberts that he returned to the airport when it reopened, but as of this afternoon he and his fellow travellers remain stuck in a corridor near departures as they wait for details on their flight home.

To add to the misery, Dr Roberts claimed hungry passengers were being told that they will not be able to re-enter the airport if they go to the café next door - the only place they can buy food. He said the partner of someone in the same corridor "went out to get something - and they won't let him back in."

‌



Dr Roberts warned that the situation had deteriorated overnight from being uncomfortable to "dangerously unhealthy" - and said he had witnessed a man fainting in the corridor this morning.

He said: "I'm an old Liverpool fan, if you imagine trying to get into the Kop in the 1960s or 70s, the entire airport is like that... It's rammed, suffocating, you can't breathe here. It is dangerously unhealthy. And nobody cares."

View 4 Images EasyJet said they were 'looking into the experience in the airport' with their ground handling provider (Image: Dr Ron Roberts)

‌



"My health is getting endangered, I called the doctor this morning. The guy down there is just told us he's on stage four cancer, he's fainted. They called medical staff and they will not do anything. There's no law here, it is I am not exaggerating, it's completely lawless."

Dr Roberts said in his view the airline had showed a "complete contempt for passengers" throughout their time in the airport, claiming: "They're not interested - it's as if people's health are expendable."

A spokesperson for EasyJet told the Mirror: "Flight EZY2638 from Tivat to London Luton yesterday was delayed overnight due to the aircraft experiencing a bird strike on a previous flight. Unfortunately, the flight has been delayed departing today due to air traffic control restrictions.

"We have been doing all possible to minimise the impact of the disruption and while we always look to secure hotel accommodation, as there was very limited availability, we advised customers they would be reimbursed for booking they own. While this was outside of our control, we are very sorry for the difficulty this caused.

"Our customers' safety and wellbeing is our highest priority and we are looking into the experience in the airport with our ground handling provider at Tivat, as this is not the level of support we expect for our customers."

A Foreign Office spokesperson said they are "in contact with the local authorities" about the situation at the airport.

News.title: Donald Trump 'jokes' about running for third term as US president
News.content:
Donald Trump 'jokes' about running for third term as US president

The US president made the comments at the White House Correspondents' dinner on Friday night, where he also took aim at the 'fake news media' and joked about celebrity supporter Nicki Minaj

View 4 Images President Donald Trump spoke at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner (Image: AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

Donald Trump apparently joked he will run for a third term before donning a red 'Trump 2028' campaign cap at the White House Correspondents' dinner.

‌



The US president, 80, is already half-way through his second term in office, the limit set by the US Constitution which says "No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice". Speaking at the black tie event on Friday night, Trump said: "I won three times, now I'm gonna do it again! It should be easy. I'm getting very good at running for president.

‌



"I won three times, did very well the second time by the way, a rigged election, but we don't have to talk about it." Earlier in the same speech, Trump said: "I'll run again."

‌



View 4 Images Trump tossed the "Trump 2028" hat into the audience at the end of his speech (Image: AP Photo/Rod Lamkey)

Gianni Infantino complaint rejected after Donald Trump World Cup interference READ MORE :

He added: "As I said three months ago, the show must go on." He added: "Just like my presidency, the second time is always better and the third time will be better yet... I'm only kidding!".

It is not the first time the president has spoken about running for a third term, which although unconstitutional is not unprecedented. Franklin D. Roosevelt served four terms as president from 1933 until his death in 1945, after which the Constitution was legally changed.

‌



Speaking about the prospect of serving a third term during a previous interview with NBC, Trump claimed "there are methods which you could do it". At the time, he said: "I'm not joking... a lot of people want me to do it. But, I basically tell them we have a long way to go, you know, it's very early in the administration." In January, he told supporters that it would be "the greatest honour of my life to serve not once, but twice or three times or four times". But he later claimed his comments were meant as a joke for the "fake news media".

View 4 Images National Guard personnel patrolling near the Waldorf Astoria Hotel (Image: Matt Kaminsky/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Friday night's rescheduled event took place amid high security at the Waldorf Astoria Washington DC, three months after the original event at the Washington Hilton had to be postponed due to an alleged assassination attempt. Trump spoke about what he described as "the attempted mass murder" and joked pop star Nicki Minaj, who is one of his most prominent supporters, began twerking after gun shots rang out.

‌



He said: "After hearing the gunshots, many people yelled, 'Get down!' which caused Nicki Minaj to start twerking. Can you believe it? She's the only one that really understood what that meant."

Trump also used the opportunity to make insults towards the "fake news" media, claiming: “This is really the largest group of ‘Trump Derangement Syndrome’ people put together at one time."

He added: “You people have no idea how lucky you are. When I’m gone, you’re all going to be broke. Your business model is going to be finished. There’s not going to be anybody to report on. Nobody gives a damn about anybody else. I want to save your ratings.”

Article continues below

View 4 Images President Trump salutes while White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt (L) and White House Correspondents Association President Weijia Jiang (R) stand during the National Anthem (Image: Getty Images)

The president was also left looking awkward as reporters for The Wall Street Journal were handed awards for their coverage of the Jeffrey Epstein scandal that had inspired him to launch an unsuccessful $10 billion defamation lawsuit last year.

Trump shrugged and smiled as their reporting was described before shaking hands with some of the winners. He joked it had “not been an easy evening” hearing about their work.

News.title: Turkey's Erdogan sacks politician for wearing cycling gear and sparks huge protests
News.content:
Turkey's Erdogan sacks politician for wearing cycling gear and sparks huge protests

Turkey's President Erdogan has fired a popular regional governor who championed sport after photographs emerged of him wearing 'inappropriate' tights on a bicycle

View 2 Images President Recep Tayyip Erdogan sacked the regional governor amid the 'cycling tights' controversy (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

A politician has been sacked after pictures emerged of him wearing tights on his bike - sparking a wave of protests from fellow cyclists.

Mehmet Fatih Cicekli, the governor of Ardahan province in eastern Turkey, was dismissed on July 17 by a presidential decree signed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

It came after some Turkish politicians criticised him for wearing cycling tights during a public event promoting the sport, and for posting the photos on social media.

Inan Akgun Alp, a member of the main opposition Republican People's Party, accused Mr Cicekli of prioritising social media over official duties - and said the tight-fitting clothing was inappropriate for a governor.

View 2 Images Governor of Ardahan province, Mehmet Fatih Cicekli, was pictured in tights on a bicycle tour (Image: Halil Ibrahim Ataman/IHA via AP)

Ben Needham’s grandfather dies without the answers he spent decades seeking READ MORE :

Saudi Arabia nuclear deal with US sparks fears of arms race in unstable region READ MORE :

He said during a debate on Turkish television last week: "He goes around in tights, spends all day cycling, with bodyguards in front of him, cycling in tights until the evening.

"A governor cannot wander around the city centre like this."

Samil Tayyar, from Erdogan's ruling party, said the attire violated cultural norms - particularly in a conservative, traditional province like Ardahan. He argued that other politicians wore jogging bottoms while cycling.

"People can wear whatever they want in their private lives, but a governor cannot visit the public in tights while on duty; it does not align with the seriousness of the state. In a traditional social setting like Ardahan, it is completely unacceptable", he later wrote on X (formerly Twitter).

Mr Cicekli, who was appointed governor in January by Erdogan, defended himself by arguing that what he wore was normal cycling attire.

He vowed to "keep pedalling" and said: I am an athlete who practices sailing, rowing and cycling. The clothes I'm wearing are sportswear".

A petition to try and get him reinstated has gathered more than 10,000 signatures, with supporters saying he had played a vital role in promoting sports, youth activities and bicycle tourism.

Article continues below

In an emotional farewell to his supporters in Ardahan on Wednesday, Mr Cicekli said: "I believe that I have not let down those who vouched for me and stood by me throughout my journey until now. I believe that this is the greatest honour of all."

He was mobbed by supportive local cyclists as he left the province, Halk TV reported.

Nacho Sanchez Amor, a member of the European Parliament from Spain who monitors Turkey in his role as rapporteur, spoke out in support for Mr Cicekli and suggested Mr Alp was promoting the ruling party's "Islamist conservative agenda."

News.title: Spain and France wildfires: Brits among 200,000 fleeing scorched tourist areas
News.content:
More than 200,000 people in France and Spain have been evacuated as wildfires continue to tear through vast areas of Europe - with temperatures expected to surge higher next week

Huge wildfires are ravaging parts of south-west France and central Spain, forcing the evacuation of an estimated 200,000 people - including British tourists.

French authorities have ordered the immediate evacuation of suburbs in Bordeaux - the largest city in the affected region - as the flames shift towards the area.

British families were among those evacuated from a Bordeaux hotel at 3.30am as staff warned smoke had been travelling over from the raging fires around 20-miles away in the Cap Ferret peninsula.

Around 141,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in France's Gironde and Landes departments, the French interior ministry said. Some residents and holidaymakers even fled by boat as flames swept through the popular tourist area of Cap Ferret on France's Atlantic coast.

In Spain, 60,000 have been forced to leave their homes in towns west of Madrid, the Spanish interior ministry said. Wildfires in the Madrid region and the nearby province of Ávila have prompted the government to declare a national emergency over wildfires for the first time.

News.title: Tourists tell BBC how their holiday turned into race to escape fires
News.content:
Families have relived how their tranquil holidays in France turned into a race to escape raging wildfires.

Tourists told the BBC of emergency alerts in the middle of the night, desperate drives just metres from six-storey high flames and the sight of people flocking to beaches with their suitcases.

Huge forest fires in south-west France and central Spain have displaced more than 220,000 people, with the French military drafted in to help and the Spanish government declaring a national emergency.

Winds and continued heat are still helping to fan the flames with some tourists reporting smelling acrid smoke like a "bonfire" far outside the affected areas.

Flights to Bordeaux and Madrid, the closest cities to the blaze-hit regions, are currently not affected. Earlier on Saturday, a French foreign minister described the fires as a "tragedy" but urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans.

Among those caught up in the crisis is Zac Morrison, who arrived in Cap Ferret - a popular peninsula blanketed with pine trees 40 miles (65km) south-west of Bordeaux - on Thursday.

The 21-year-old from London, who is on holiday with 10 members of his family, woke up to two text alerts at 04:00 and 06:00 local time ordering him to evacuate "by all means necessary".

News.title: Police declare 'major incident' over Cairngorms wildfire
News.content:
A major incident has been declared by emergency services as they continue to tackle a wildfire which has been burning in the Cairngorms National Park for 10 days.

Some residents of the village of Nethy Bridge have been evacuated as a precaution.

But a local resident told the BBC the wildfire should have been declared a major incident sooner and communication from authorities had been "pretty poor".

The Scottish government said a fire break had been established around Nethy Bridge overnight and new fire breaks were being constructed.

First Minister John Swinney, who held a meeting of the Scottish government's resilience committee early on Saturday, said additional police and fire service resources were being deployed to assist with the evacuation.

He said that it was "essential people avoid the affected areas."

Swinney continued: "The wind has changed direction overnight, which means the track of the fire has altered once again and the threat to Nethy Bridge has reduced, for the moment at least.

"Ground and helicopter resources are being focused on the current path of the fire and new fire breaks constructed."

Smoke from the wildfire can now be seen 59 miles away in Aberdeen following a change in wind direction.

News.title: Laura Kuenssberg goes behind the scenes with Andy Burnham in his first week as PM
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has just completed his first week as prime minister, with new policy decisions being made and the much discussed No 10 North taking centre stage.

The BBC's Laura Kuenssberg met Burnham for his first sit-down interview since taking charge and got an exclusive behind the scenes look at the new Manchester office.

Andy Burnham: The Laura Kuenssberg Interview will be available across BBC News on Sunday.

News.title: Sean McCann, Madeleine's brother, makes Commonwealths final
News.content:
Sean McCann - the younger brother of Madeleine McCann - qualified for Saturday's 400m freestyle final at the Commonwealth Games by coming through his morning heat in Glasgow.

With parents Kate and Gerry in the stands, McCann finished fourth in his heat and crept into the final as the last of the eight qualifiers at his first major championships.

"I am buzzing," the 21-year-old said. "It wasn't really an expectation coming in given how strong the field was but delighted to see I have made it."

McCann, a chemical engineering student at Loughborough University where he trains, grew up in England but qualifies for Scotland through his father.

News.title: Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous: What you had to say about wedding rule changes
News.content:
The day Sam and Courtney Scholey became husband and wife didn't feel like their wedding day.

There was no walking down the aisle, no rings exchanged, no wedding dress, and no music.

That all came several days later, when the pair had a bespoke ceremony led by a celebrant who knew them, at a venue in the Oxfordshire countryside. It was their dream wedding - but it wasn't legal in England and Wales.

And so in April, they forked out hundreds of pounds to quietly sign papers at a library in Buckingham.

"For us, that day was as insignificant as possible," Courtney told the BBC. "It was just the words we had to say to make it legally binding."

The Scholeys are one of a growing number of couples who feel the rigid rules around weddings are making getting married more stressful, more expensive and less meaningful.

But under new proposals announced this month - described by the government as the biggest shake-up of wedding laws in 200 years - couples in England and Wales could have the freedom to hold official marriage ceremonies in a wider array of unconventional locations, from forests to beaches, as long as the location is approved by a registered officiant.

It's welcome news for Nicky Brown, who said she wants to exchange vows in a wildly picturesque corner of Wales, with just her mum and her partner's mum as witnesses.

"I'd be quite happy to get married in a field full of sheep," the 57-year-old told the BBC.

But some say the sacred tradition of marriage is being perverted.

News.title: How the mystery of dead animals dumped in villages led to a hidden world of illegal hunts
News.content:
On a remote Cambridgeshire farm, where his nearest neighbour is half a mile away, Mathew Latta was making lunch when the peace was shattered by the sound of loud exhausts.

Latta ran to the window to see a convoy of more than a dozen 4x4s heading towards his farm. His iron gates were cut open with an angle grinder and concrete blocks were shifted out of the way to clear the convoy's path.

The vehicles drove right over his fields at speed, tearing up the crops and skirting the fence by the family's garden. Then more than 70 people got out of the vehicles, men dressed in military fatigues and balaclavas, cheering and playing music.

Dogs were brought out on leads and began to hunt hares.

"They were all stood up on their cars with binoculars," says Latta. "I would say this is 100% a properly organised coursing event, with competitors and competitive dogs. People watching the course - and watching and betting on that sport. It was quite terrifying."

Warning: This story contains images of dead animals

Latta and his family were trapped in their home. They kept calling the police, but nobody came. His daughter, then aged seven, was terrified and kept asking: "Are these men gonna come inside, daddy?"

More than three hours later, the bloodsport was finally over and the crowd dispersed. They left behind four cars, one of them a burnt-out wreck. It emerged that, earlier that day, the convoy had rampaged through an area 20 miles (32km) long in the county, forcing other cars off the road and even robbing a petrol station.

News.title: The pop band who went from playing for rescue dogs to selling out arenas
News.content:
Every band has to earn its stripes. Some have it harder than others.

At AC/DC's first gig, the club owner cut the power because they were too noisy. Sam Smith started at barn dances, singing on top of a haystack. At Robert Smith's first concert, he got so drunk that he sang David Bowie's Suffragette City while the rest of the band played Jimi Hendrix's Foxy Lady.

But LA pop trio Muna can top them all.

At the start of their career, the band got a call from their record label. We know you've just flown overnight from London, they said, but you have to get to Las Vegas.

Why? Because they'd been booked to play Pet-A-Palooza, a dog adoption festival sponsored by the local radio station. If they turned up, the station would support their new single.

"We were all sick, so it was doomed from the start," recalls guitarist Josette Maskin.

"It was an acoustic set, but we didn't have a sound guy, and the guitar started feeding back."

The noise, according to singer Katie Gavin, was like an unholy screech.

"The dogs were getting upset," says Maskin, wincing at the memory. "They just howled the whole time.

"We were mortified, but looking back, it is so funny. And I've gotten to share those experiences with some of my best friends, and that's what life is really about."

News.title: ADHD has rewired the workplace. This is what it means for bosses and workers
News.content:
Taking one of the UK's biggest grocery chains to an employment tribunal was something that Ryan Toghill says almost took over his life.

"It was all I could think about for 18 months and more," he says.

The deputy store manager at Lidl, who'd told his bosses he'd been diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), was called to a disciplinary meeting after breaking company rules by using equipment he hadn't been trained to use. After that meeting, Ryan was dismissed for gross misconduct.

He successfully appealed the decision and was offered a lower-paid role. He rejected it and took his case to a tribunal. Eventually, he was awarded more than Â£45,000 when the judge found his former employer hadn't fully taken his ADHD diagnosis into account during the disciplinary process.

The judgement found reasonable adjustments during the process hadn't been offered to him, such as additional breaks.

He'd been described by a manager as showing "a lack of remorse," something the tribunal found was clearly linked with his communication differences associated with having ADHD.

"I don't show a lot of emotions," Ryan explains. "I could be incredibly happy, angry, upset, or remorseful, and my facial expressions and tone of voice would essentially remain the same."

The tribunal upheld part of his claims for unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal and a failure to make reasonable adjustments. Lidl says it's "committed to ensuring that everyone receives the reasonable adjustments, clear communication and support they need to thrive."

Campaigners, lawyers and HR teams say cases like this highlight a shift that businesses should be paying attention to.

Thousands of people have been diagnosed as neurodivergent in the last few years, an umbrella term that covers autism, ADHD and other conditions such as dyslexia and Tourette's syndrome.

Since the pandemic in particular, diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism have been rising, and they're featuring more regularly in disputes in employment tribunals.

News.title: Twenty firefighters taken to hospital after explosion in Essex
News.content:
Twenty firefighters were taken to hospital after a blaze ripped through an industrial unit and spread to a fertiliser store, triggering a major explosion.

The fire service declared a major incident on Friday, as more than 100 firefighters tackled the flames at Highlands Farm, near the village of Rettendon, Essex.

Three fire engines and two fire service cars were destroyed in the blaze.

Speaking at a media conference on Saturday, Rick Hylton, Essex's chief fire officer, praised the "remarkable professionalism, courage and commitment" of the fire crews.

News.title: Six men arrested over fatal stabbing in south London
News.content:
Six men have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a 22-year-old man was fatally stabbed in Clapham, south-west London, the Metropolitan Police has said.

Police were called at 04:37 BST following reports of a man attending hospital with a stab wound. He later died in hospital, the force said.

The incident is believed to have taken place around Tremadoc Road and Clapham High Street.

Police said four of the suspects also attended hospital with stab wounds and are continuing to receive treatment, although their injuries are not believed to be life-threatening or life-changing.

Alongside the four men in hospital â three aged 22 and one 24 â officers also arrested two further men, aged 27 and 23, at the hospital on suspicion of murder. They remain in police custody.

The Met said it understood the fatally injured man was stabbed at about 04:20. It added that officers were carrying out inquiries in and around Tremadoc Road and Clapham High Street to establish the full circumstances around the incident.

Det Ch Insp Sarah Lee, who is leading the investigation, said those in the area would continue to notice an increased police presence throughout Saturday.

The family of the man who died have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.

Supt Mark Gallacher, a policing lead for the area, described the incident as "tragic".

"We understand that this will cause concern among the local community and specialist detectives are doing everything possible to determine what has happened," he added.

The Met urged witnesses or people with information about the incident to contact police on 101, quoting reference 1474/25July.

Information can also be provided anonymously to independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: It's the cocktail taking young drinkers by storm - but the packaging is 'unrecyclable'
News.content:
Cleaning up after pre-drinks, AÃ©dÃ©n Rooney puts his empty BuzzBallz in the recycling.

"It's plastic and metal, so I'd just assume it's recyclable," he said.

The company behind the bright, pre-mixed cocktails that have taken Gen Z by storm said they were recyclable on its website, but experts say this is not true.

BuzzBallz cannot be recycled as the PET plastic ball cannot be separated from the aluminium lid, global environmental action body WRAP said.

"It's greenwashing. I'm shocked," AÃ©dÃ©n said.

BuzzBallz blamed a website error for claiming they were recyclable via Terracycle, a US-only scheme, but did not comment on its now-deleted FAQ that said they were recyclable where UK councils allow.

News.title: Letters by pre-Smiths Morrissey set for auction
News.content:
Letters written by a young Morrissey before he formed The Smiths are to go to auction where they are expected to sell for Â£22,000.

The archive of letters, written to Birmingham pen friend, Simon Pitt, who would go on to become the city's poet laureate, by the singer between the ages of 14 and 20, includes one in which Morrissey says "my ambition is to be a rock 'n' roll star or an actor, or a writer".

Another letter dated a number of weeks later adds: "I always said I was a genius, but nobody listened."

The letters, written between 1974 and 1979, are expected to fetch a combined Â£22,000 estimate when they go on sale in London.

News.title: Heatwave conditions to return for many as UK temperatures to peak at 35C
News.content:
For most of England and Wales the third heatwave of the year ended last weekend when cooler air arrived, dropping maximum temperatures widely to 20-24C.

However, two locations - Usk and Exeter - have continued to just reach their heatwave criteria since then and have now reached 20 consecutive days - the longest run so far this year.

As temperatures drop further over the weekend, and parts of the UK see a little rain, even these local heatwaves are likely to come to an end.

However, it may only be a temporary break.

Next week, high pressure is set to build close to the south of the UK meaning rain-bearing weather fronts will stall.

Any wet weather will become confined to northern and western areas - especially north-west Scotland - and in southern parts of the UK temperatures look set to climb once again.

This could well mean a fourth heatwave is on the cards - although according to the Met Office isolated high temperatures might not be enough.

They say that: "If only one or two stations reach heatwave criteria, that would not be defined as a heatwave."

News.title: Horror fall overshadows gymnastics silver at Commonwealths
News.content:
A sickening injury to England's Gabriel Langton overshadowed his team's silver medal in the men's team gymnastics final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The 19-year-old, from the City of Birmingham Gymnastics Club, needed lengthy treatment on the mat after a horrible fall in the final rotation of the evening at The Arena.

Langton fell head first to the floor after missing his catch on the horizontal metal bar, three metres in the air, leading to a lengthy delay to the action as he was tended to by up to a dozen medical staff.

He was eventually led away on a trolley after being moved on to a stretcher with his head and neck braced and left to huge applause from the packed crowd who had spent much of the previous 10 minutes in hushed silence.

Langton was seen to be conscious and moving his legs and arms before leaving the arena floor, while team officials later said he was moving and speaking to doctors.

In a statement, Team England said: "We are grateful to the medical teams who responded immediately to provide assistance.

"He has been taken to hospital and we will share more information when it is available."

When competition resumed, his England team-mates were unable to overhaul their deficit to Canada who claimed their first gold medal in the event in 20 years, having finished second to England at the past two games.

Langton, a late call-up to Team England in the place of the injured six-time Olympic medallist Max Whitlock, was unable to join his teammates on the podium as England collected their silver medals.

Team-mate Luke Whitehouse, who was first on to the apparatus after the competition restarted and posted a relatively low score of 11.700, said: "When something like that happens, you've just got to forget about it and reset. I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time."

Whitehouse added: "From what we've heard, he's doing OK. Gymnastics is such a dangerous sport and things like this remind us of that. It's one of those things you have to put out of your mind."

Felix Dolci, who helped Canada to gold and led qualifying for the all-around competition, said: "It's terrible but it goes to show that gymnastics is a very, very difficult and complicated sport. It's dangerous you know sometimes.

"All our thoughts go to Gabriel and the team. Pushing through this is definitely not easy, England stayed focussed, they stayed in the zone, a huge shout out to them because that's not an easy one.

"For any gymnast that was on the field of play, seeing this not only is difficult, but something you never want to see. It goes to show how hard the sport is."

Hamish Carter from Team Scotland - who narrowly missed out on a bronze medal to Australia in the final rotation - said: "I didn't actually see what happened. I'm just so happy that he's alright and, having experienced that, anything could have happened.

"We've walked away with no medal but I'm thinking of Gabe in this moment."

News.title: Murder investigation begins after teen dies in Luton stabbing
News.content:
Police have launched a murder investigation after a teenage boy died following a stabbing in Luton.

Bedfordshire Police said officers responded to reports of violent disorder in Kingsway Recreation Ground at about 18:30 on Friday, where a number of teenagers were seen carrying large knives.

A 17-year-old, who has not been identified, was taken to hospital with multiple stab wounds but was pronounced dead shortly after, the force said.

One teenage boy has been arrested on suspicion of violent disorder and is in police custody for questioning. A second was arrested but remains in hospital with serious but non-life threatening injuries.

Police are appealing to the public for information.

In a statement, Det Ch Insp Nick Gardener condemned the "horrific violence" that has "sadly cost a teenage boy his life today".

"Our thoughts are first and foremost with the loved ones of the boy who lost his life in such tragic circumstances," he said.

Such incidents have "a significant impact on our communities", he said.

He also urged the public to contact police with any information they have and not to share any images and videos circulating on social media.

An increased police presence and patrols will remain in the area.

Zanib Raja, a councillor for the Biscot Ward in Luton, asked people not to share alleged videos of the incident online.

In a statement on Facebook, she said: "A tragic incident took place today in Kingsway Park, a place many of us grew up in, played in, and built memories in.

"A place that should be safe for families, children, and every resident of our town. Instead, a man lost his life in broad daylight. A family has been shattered. Luton is hurting."

Raja urged the community to come together.

News.title: Wildfire burning one month on is 'the size of a small town'
News.content:
As darkness set in over the Peak District one Wednesday night in June, calls started to come in to Derbyshire's fire service over smoke starting to rise from the moorland overlooking the town.

More than a month on, the Tintwistle Moor fire is now a sprawling, smouldering blaze the size of a small town, which can be seen from space.

Declared a major incident on 13 July, it has come in tandem with a prolonged spell of hot, dry weather that shows little sign of easing soon, pushing the country's firefighting resources to their limits.

Now Dr Kirsten Lees, environmental sciences lecturer, specialising in zero carbon at the University of Derby, has told the BBC Tintwistle is on a par with the biggest wildfires ever seen in England - and it's still burning.

When questioned about her assertion the fire could be one of the largest in recent memory in England, she said: "It may well be, yes."

With hosepipe bans in force across several English regions and more restrictions likely to follow, gardeners face some tough choices.

When every drop counts, which plants deserve your precious water from the water butt, and which should you leave to fend for themselves?

As someone who has researched how British gardeners need to adapt to respond to our changing climate, I can tell you that not all garden plants are created equal when it comes to water needs.

Some plants will bounce back from a summer scorching, while others may never recover.

Top plants to prioritise for watering

open image in gallery Hydrangeas adopt a conservative strategy when it comes to drought ( Alamy/PA )

1. New woody plants

Any woody plant installed in the last 12-18 months should be your absolute priority. These haven’t yet developed the deep root systems needed to find moisture reserves and going without enough water the first year or so after planting could kill them.

Water thoroughly and add a deep mulch of wood chips to help the soil hold water. For young trees you can install a watering bag around the trunk but you still need to top it up.

2. Hydrangeas

Hydrangeas adopt a conservative strategy when it comes to drought. They shut their stomata (leaf pores) rapidly when they sense dry soil, and keep them closed until consistent moisture returns. They often drop their leaves too.

This can mean many weeks without growth, after even a relatively short drought period. So if you want to keep them looking at their best, they need consistent watering. You can cut growth back to reduce water loss, and save the the plant at the cost of flowers.

3. Moisture loving trees

Japanese maples (Acer palmatum), along with other moisture-loving trees like birch and beech, are prone to serious die-back during summer droughts. Their shallow root systems and large leaves make them particularly vulnerable to water stress. Water and mulch them.

About the author Alastair Culham is an Associate Professor of Botany at the University of Reading. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

4. Soft herbaceous plants

Astilbe, dicentra, filipendula, heuchera, primula, trollius and many other soft herbaceous plants require good moisture levels and may not survive prolonged drought.

5. Shallow-rooted shrubs

Rhododendrons and azaleas are shallow-rooted shrubs particularly susceptible to drought stress, especially the large-leaved evergreen species which are also prone to wind damage when stressed.

6. Clematis

Many clematis varieties struggle with drought. Since they’re often grown for their spectacular flowering displays, maintaining adequate moisture around the roots is crucial, especially for autumn-flowering varieties, or spring-flowering varieties which flower on the previous year’s growth.

A gravel mulch can help keep the roots cool and damp. However, clematis orientalis, terniflora, and evergreens such as C. cirrhosa can be surprisingly tolerant of a hot dry period.

open image in gallery Many clematis varieties struggle with drought ( Getty/iStock )

7. Ripening vegetables

If you’re growing vegetables, prioritise crops approaching harvest and those that split when moisture returns after drought, such as carrots. Runner beans and courgettes need moist soil to keep cropping and potato yields are heavily influenced by water levels.

8. All the pots

Anything in pots has limited access to soil moisture reserves and will need regular attention. Move containers to shadier spots if possible. Always use a pot saucer to hold water and prevent it draining away.

Plants that can survive without extra water

Research into plant water-stress shows that many common garden plants are surprisingly resilient.

Forsythia adopts a risk-taking strategy. It keeps growing and photosynthesising even when soil moisture becomes limited, gambling that it can regrow after damage. This makes it remarkably drought-tolerant. It is also tolerant of heavy pruning which can save it in severe conditions.

Mediterranean shrubs like lavender, rosemary, sage and thyme are naturally adapted to dry conditions. Their grey, hairy or waxy leaves are evolved to conserve moisture. Soil conditions are crucial though. If the plants are deep rooted they will draw water up, but if your soil is shallow or compacted they might well be less drought tolerant.

open image in gallery Mediterranean shrubs like lavender, rosemary, sage and thyme are naturally adapted to dry conditions ( Getty )

Sedums, sempervivums and other succulents store water in their fleshy leaves and can survive extended dry periods. RHS research identifies Sedum spectabile as particularly reliable under stress.

Ornamental grasses generally have efficient root systems and many species actually prefer drier conditions once established.

Established shrubs including cistus, phlomis, buddleja, cotoneaster, berberis and viburnum have deep roots and proven track records for drought survival. The RHS report identifies these as garden stalwarts, with high stress resilience.

Some trees, including eucalyptus, bay (Laurus nobilis) and holm oak are remarkably drought tolerant.

Those to sacrifice

Grass lawns are thirsty and can be left to go dormant. If you have a newly seeded or turfed lawn from this year, some limited watering may be justified. But in general, embrace the golden colour of water-stressed lawns. As long as you don’t create too many bare patches from over-use, the green colour and growth will come back when it rains.

Annual bedding plants like busy lizzies and begonias have shallow root systems and high water demands. However, they are only there for one season and are easily replaceable, so prioritise them for watering only if they’re particularly important to your garden’s summer display and you can spare the water. You could save some by potting them up and enjoying a display that needs less water.

When you do water, research shows that technique is crucial. Water thoroughly but less frequently to encourage deep root growth. Focus water at the base of plants rather than on leaves, and water in early morning or evening to reduce evaporation.

Consider “split-root” watering for established shrubs – water one side of the plant thoroughly, then switch to the other side two to three weeks later. This keeps plants hydrated while chemical signals from the dry side’s roots prevent excessive new growth that would increase water demands.

This drought is a taste of Britain’s gardening future. The plants struggling most in this year’s drought are likely to become increasingly unsuitable for British gardens without intensive irrigation.

Be willing to swap out plants that suffer in drought for new plants that are more tolerant. Refresh plantings to adapt to the new climate.

Three fire engines and two fire officers’ cars were destroyed in a blaze at an industrial unit in Essex yesterday, while 20 firefighters were sent to hospital following the incident.

Firefighters were faced with the “large and rapidly developing” blaze on Friday evening following a fertiliser explosion.

Rick Hylton, chief fire officer and chief executive at Essex County Fire and Rescue Service, gave an update on the fire in a press conference on Saturday afternoon.

He said: “The fire and explosion has ... destroyed three fire engines and two officer cars that were being used to respond to the incident.

“This underlines the scale and intensity of the conditions our crews faced.”

Mr Hylton said that 20 firefighters had “attended hospital” following the incident.

open image in gallery Roads are closed and people are being asked to avoid the area ( PA )

“Of that 20, four suffered minor injuries, and the remainder were precautionary assessments, including checks for issues such as hearing loss following the explosion.

“I am pleased to confirm all of those firefighters have now been discharged from hospital.”

Firefighters will continue working into the weekend at the site of the huge industrial blaze.

The fire, which prompted the evacuation of nearby homes, was declared a major incident on Friday afternoon.

Emergency services were first alerted to the inferno on Southend Road, between East Hanningfield and Rettendon, at 4.50pm on Friday, Essex County Fire and Rescue Service said.

open image in gallery Smoke billows from a fire at an Essex industrial unit ( Reuters )

Several industrial units and an adjacent field were engulfed in flames. About 100 firefighters were originally deployed to combat the extensive fire.

Mr Hylton said: “The incident is now under control, although firefighters will remain at the scene, dealing with the remaining hotspots and supporting the transition into the recovery phase.”

People are being asked to stay away from the area so that firefighters can continue their operations.

In Wisconsin's progressive capital city of Madison, where liberal residents have long embraced their history of political activism and protest, a police shooting this week has disrupted some of the largest and most popular summertime events and once again put the spotlight on persistent and deep racial divisions.

Corey Ruiz, who is identified as Black or Latino in Wisconsin court records, was shot and killed by a Madison police officer on Wednesday after a brief scuffle at the intersection of a city street just yards away from a popular 52-year-old food co-op in the heart of the city's most liberal neighborhood.

It marks the third time since 2012 that Madison police have shot and killed someone in the same neighborhood. The shooting has sparked renewed calls for police reforms and forced the city that is 70% white to once again reckon with calls from the Black community to address racial justice issues.

Pressure from protesters, and sympathy for their cause, has also led to the cancellation or disruption of many of Madison's signature summertime events.

“Our community has spoken loud and clear: this is NOT business as usual,” Black activist Clyde Mayberry posted on Facebook on Friday amid a string of cancellations. “Your decisions have helped ensure that this city continues to acknowledge the pain, the loss, and the call for accountability.”

Protesters took to the streets hours after the shooting, disrupting a popular Wisconsin Chamber Orchestra outdoor concert at the state Capitol that attracts about 30,000 every week in the summer. Protesters, many of whom were Black, stood over white concert attendees sitting at tables near the stage that cost as much as $1,800 to rent for the night.

Concert organizers canceled the event.

Threats of a protest on Thursday led the city to postpone the grand opening of a new public market, just a few blocks away from where the shooting occurred. A popular neighborhood festival near the shooting called AtwoodFest, scheduled to begin on Saturday, was also canceled in the face of potential protests.

“Our community and our Marquette neighbors witnessed another horrific officer-involved shooting just blocks from our festival grounds, leaving us in deep pain and justified anger,” organizers of the festival wrote. “In acknowledgment of what has happened far too often in our community and our country as a whole, this year’s AtwoodFest, themed ‘The Heartbeat of the Neighborhood,’ is canceled.”

And on Saturday, the popular downtown farmers market that attracts about 20,000 people each week around the Capitol building, was scheduled to shut down nearly four hours earlier than usual in solidarity with protesters.

“We mourn with our community,” market organizers posted on social media. “And we agree - business cannot proceed as usual.”

Investigations into the shooting continue. Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represents the Ruiz family, said on Friday at a new conference in the Capitol that the officer who fired the shots should face criminal charges.

Madison Police Chief John Patterson, who is white, has tried to calm tensions, even allowing protesters to overtake a news conference that he was leading along with the mayor inside the police department's downtown headquarters on Thursday.

Patterson took questions from angry protesters, one of whom held a sign just feet away from the chief that said “corrupt cops deserve to die too.” After one protester hurled an insult at Patterson, the chief calmly responded, “I appreciate you being here.”

News.title: Scrutiny of WNBA intensifies as mounting discord around the league looms over All-Star festivities
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

The WNBA has never been bigger.

More people are watching. More are investing. Salaries for many players are higher than ever. But mounting turmoil and discord have been a part of this transformative period that has featured a landmark collective bargaining agreement, league expansion and skyrocketing player recognition.

It seems to have reached a new flashpoint, as discussions about race, gender and sexuality made headlines ahead of Saturday’s WNBA All-Star Game. Race-driven conversations resurfaced after an incident between Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark and Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas, while players continued to voice frustrations with WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert and leadership over what they say is a lack of protection from social media harassment and divisive remarks.

“It is a moment to be celebrated without a doubt,” said Ketra Armstrong, sport management professor and director of the Center for Race and Ethnicity in Sport at the University of Michigan. “We want to celebrate what’s great. But sometimes, the progress can overshadow, still, where the perils are.”

Issues of race, gender and representation have been an undercurrent throughout the league's history. Debates over those issues have grown as women's sports have exploded. And they remain a challenge that shape the WNBA's — and most other pro sports leagues, for that matter — public and online discourse.

“This is what a sports league" is, said David Berri, sports economist and economics professor at Southern Utah University. He cited the NFL’s Rooney Rule as an example. “If a sports league is going to get attention, you’re going to get attention for these things as well.”

Growth has magnified broader cultural debates

Contentious conversations also spread to issues of transgender athletes and harassment.

WNBA veteran Brianna Turner said on social media this week that her former team, the Fever, fired a male employee last season for sexual harassment. Turner, who was with Indiana last season but now plays for Las Vegas, said Indiana players were encouraged not to discuss the firing.

Turner’s comments came as she defended transgender athletes days after Indiana forward Sophie Cunningham spoke on transgender athletes competing in women’s sports.

“I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I’m like, ‘I never once said that,’” Cunningham was quoted as saying in a story published by ESPN. “I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.”

The WNBA’s conversations about race were thrust back into the spotlight after Toronto Tempo coach Sandy Brondello was suspended one game for referring to Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese as a “protected species.”

The comment, picked up by the broadcast after Reese drew a foul on Toronto player Nyara Sabally, quickly drew criticism.

Brondello, a former player who has won two WNBA titles, is Australian. The “protected species” phrase is used in Australian sports to express frustration over a lack of calls against a player. However, in the U.S., the phrase suggests that someone isn’t human and could be seen as derogatory toward Black people. Brondello later apologized. Reese accepted, saying she appreciated the league’s swift action.

“It’s a much bigger platform now. Everything that happens is news,” Berri said. “There were hard fouls 10 years ago. Nobody paid any attention to that. It ends up being because of the coverage now, everything gets magnified ... which is good. I mean, this is what we wanted.”

‘A lot to celebrate,’ but race still matters

Clark has repeatedly attempted to downplay the noise surrounding her, but she has become a springboard for projections far beyond the game itself.

“It’s basketball," she said in a recent ESPN interview. "When I walk out of the locker room I shouldn’t be fearful of what the conversation is going to be. It’s emotionally exhausting. It’s draining. It makes your shoulders tense because people don’t want to talk about the basketball. They just want to stir it up and make something else.”

The WNBA retroactively assessed Thomas a flagrant foul and suspended her one game after the veteran made contact with her fist to Clark’s throat in a June 24 matchup.

The play, which Thomas has said was an accident, gained widespread attention and ignited debates over officiating, with coaches, pundits and lawmakers weighing in on whether the league needs to take action about physical play involving Clark.

Thomas, who is Black and in her 12th WNBA season, said after the incident she had received death threats, part of increased online vitriol players have faced in recent years. Chelsea Gray of the Las Vegas Aces recently posted a message from a man that included a racial slur. And Engelbert this week met with a pair of player committees to discuss what more can be done to protect players from online harassment.

Since she entered the league, Clark and her WNBA peers have become proxies for long-standing American issues — from race, gender and sexual orientation to who receives attention and who doesn't.

“There’s a lot to celebrate,” Armstrong said, “but race still matters. Race will always matter. It just depends on how we make it matter.”

News.title: A road trip through New England revealed the region’s vast cultural legacy
News.content:
