Sports.title: Inside LeBron James's family feud with new Philadelphia 76ers teammate amid the bombshell move that rocked the NBA
Sports.content:
LeBron James sent shockwaves through the NBA on Friday when he announced the final stop in his remarkable career would be with the Philadelphia 76ers.

The 41-year-old, who left the Los Angeles Lakers after eight seasons, admitted he thought he had played his final game in the NBA, but has decided instead to sign a two-year deal – worth around $8 million – with the Sixers.

But he did so without any guarantee he would walk into a welcoming environment. Yes, the pieces seem to be in place in America's birthplace for instant success, but talks were needed 'to clear the air' before their superstar's arrival.

There would have definitely been an awkward reunion with Jaylen Brown, whose trade from the Boston Celtics to Philadelphia earlier in the offseason is believed to have been a major factor in the recruitment of James.

While with the Celtics, Brown went viral for some unflattering comments he made about James' son, Bronny, after he was drafted by his dad's Lakers back in 2024.

In a blunt assessment of the then-rookie's ability, Brown said: 'I don't think Bronny is a pro.' Brown also rattled the cage of another new teammate, Joel Embiid, earlier this year.

LeBron James, pictured with wife Savannah, stunned the NBA by signing with the Sixers

After being eliminated in the first round of the playoffs by the Sixers, Brown said: 'Flopping has ruined our league. Joel Embiid is one of the greatest players that has played basketball, but he flops. He knows it too.'

But The Daily Mail understands Sixers executives have been trying to smooth things over behind the scenes in recent weeks. Honest discussions have taken place and the team's stars have buried the hatchet ahead of James' arrival.

A source told us: 'Any issues LeBron may have had with Jaylen (Brown) ultimately took a backseat because winning changes everything. The opportunity to join what the Sixers could become was simply too good to pass up.

'He's already won championships by changing teams in Miami and Cleveland, so returning to either situation would have felt like a step backward.

'And while Golden State had been viewed as the frontrunner for a while, it increasingly looked like more of a retirement tour than a true championship destination, especially with how difficult the path to the NBA Finals is in the Western Conference.

'The Eastern Conference presents a much more realistic road back to the Finals, particularly with the talent Philadelphia already has in place.'

They continued: 'Jaylen also had past issues with Joel Embiid, but conversations have been had, everything has been smoothed over. Tyrese Maxey's presence - along with his connection with Rich Paul - helped reassure everyone involved.

'In the end, it became the obvious choice. Everyone spoke with LeBron, cleared the air and made sure there would be no lingering problems.'

One of James' new teammates is Jaylen Brown, who questioned his son Bronny's ability

Brown's blockbuster trade from the Celtics is believed to have been key in recruiting James

It remains to be seen what James' wife, Savannah, will do. After eight years in Los Angeles and the glamorous lifestyle that comes with it, it is unclear how she feels about the prospect of returning to the East Coast.

Like her husband, Savannah was born in Akron, Ohio and the pair met when James was playing high school football and she was cheerleading for the rival team.

They share three children - Bronny, Bryce and Zhuri - but our source says James has made a promise to them that this will be his final shot at an elusive fifth NBA championship.

They added: 'Just as importantly, his wife and kids fully supported the move after LeBron assured them that this would be his final chapter. Once this is over, he's done.'

The NBA's all-time leading scorer made the announcement on social media Friday, saying it will be his 'last decision' and that it comes after he strongly considered retirement.

The Sixers, who went 45-37 last season and were swept in the second round by the NBA champion New York Knicks and have not won an NBA championship since 1983, quickly emerged as favourites to win the championship with most betting sites.

'I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energize a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time,' James said.

A four-time NBA champion, James wrote he was 'done' when his 23rd NBA season ended and that it was his last with the Lakers.

'I was pretty sure I played my last game. I was honest at that last press conference when I said I needed to look at myself and deicide if I still love this game,' James wrote. 'I still truly love this game, and I have more to give.'

Joel Embiid (right) also had issues with Brown but the team is focused on winning with James

Our source has said LeBron has promised his family this will be his final contract in the NBA

The 41-year-old James is set to sign a modest $8-million, two-year contract with the Sixers, according to ESPN. He made nearly $53 million last season.

'I'm not going for money. I'm not going for family,' James wrote. 'What am I really playing for at this point? I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning.'

James celebrated his decision on Instagram with a career highlight reel set to Philadelphia rapper Meek Mill's 'Dreams and Nightmares,' the adopted sports anthem of city sports teams.

The video ends with the lyric, 'hold up, wait a minute. Y'all thought I was finished?' and cuts to a Sixers' logo. Philadelphia will be praying he can deliver one final special run.

Sports.title: Donald Trump weighs in on Bryson DeChambeau controversy at The Open... after American star threatened to call the President during meltdown
Sports.content:
Donald Trump has weighed in on Bryson DeChambeau's heated rules dispute at The Open Championship, calling the penalty against the American star a 'tough call.'

Speaking on Friday, Trump addressed the drama that unfolded at Royal Birkdale, where DeChambeau was docked two strokes during his second round for improving his lie in the deep rough on the fifth hole.

The penalty sparked a furious reaction from the LIV Golf star, who reportedly threatened to call Trump for assistance in having the ruling overturned.

When asked if there was a precedent for someone in his position acting as a 'fixer' for athletes facing sports disputes, Trump rejected the label and reframed his role.

'Well, it's not a fix. You mean being a judge?' Trump replied when questioned about his involvement in high-profile sports controversies.

'You know, I thought the Bryson call was a tough call,' Trump added.

Donald Trump has weighed in on Bryson DeChambeau's heated rules dispute at The Open

DeChambeau was hit with the penalty on the second day after 'inadvertently improving his lie'

Fox’s @PDoocy: “When Tiger Woods was about to get arrested, he called you. Now we know that when Bryson DeChambeau was having a dispute with a rules official this week, he wanted to call you. You got involved with a red card for the U.S. men’s soccer team. Is there a precedent… pic.twitter.com/nPBC3dGycv — Curtis Houck (@CurtisHouck) July 24, 2026

'I saw him walking around. I see a lot of people there walking around looking for their ball in weeds. I've been watching that. So, I thought it was a tough call against him.'

Trump then drew a comparison to his recent intervention regarding a red card issued to U.S. Men's National Team star Folarin Balogun during the World Cup, defending his decision to reach out to FIFA President Gianni Infantino.

'I thought the red card was a very tough call, and it worked out brilliantly,' Trump said.

'Look, supposing that they didn't let him play and we lost, everyone would have been angry, right? The way it was that they lost with their best player, now everyone's happy, including Belgium.'

'Of course, they lost their next game, so they're not that happy either, but it worked out great,' he continued. 'Gianni did a good job in making that call. All I did, I asked for a review. I thought that call was not a good call.'

Despite DeChambeau's frustration on the course and his threats to get the president involved, R&A Chief Executive Mark Darbon confirmed that Trump never reached out regarding the golf penalty.

Darbon maintained that the ruling against DeChambeau was 'clear-cut' from a rules perspective, emphasizing that the decision was made strictly to uphold the integrity of the championship regardless of the player involved.

DeChambeau reportedly tried to get Trump involved in the dispute at The Open

The American was subsequently embroiled in a dramatic argument with officials at The Open

In losing the argument, DeChambeau toppled from one shot off the 36-hole lead to three back, before sliding further down the leaderboard on Sunday.

While Scottie Scheffler insisted DeChambeau was not a 'cheat', Rory McIlroy was scathing of his rival's antics.

Speaking on Saturday, the world No 2 said: 'I was up in the players' lounge watching it with a few other players and as soon as he made the step into the ball, we all sort of looked at each other and we were like, "That didn't seem right". Then when I heard that he was called in by the rules officials, it was pretty obvious for why.'

McIlroy added: 'I think a lot of it's performative. I think a lot of it is for attention. To hold the tournament hostage like that and to have all of us, players, volunteers, everyone waiting on him to depart, I didn't feel like it was a great look.'

Sports.title: The ultimate football bromance reunited as Morgan Rogers seals £117m move to Chelsea: England star and Cole Palmer share a celebration, grew up together at Man City and are linked by a tragic bond
Sports.content:
Monday, November 2, 2020. St George’s Park, Burton-on-Trent. The FA Youth Cup final between Manchester City and Chelsea. It is 2-2 as we approach the 83rd minute. Morgan Rogers has already scored for City, a tidy finish to a low cross cut back by Liam Delap.

Then Delap breaks behind. He shoots. The ball bobbles beyond Chelsea defender Levi Colwill and trickles towards the back post, where Cole Palmer is waiting. He taps in for 3-2 and that’s that at the FA’s national football centre. City win, Chelsea lose.

Those in attendance might never have guessed what a Chelsea connection this youth match involving City would carry nearly six years later, now that Rogers is signing for £117million, the most expensive fee ever paid for a British player.

Both 18 years old at the time, neither Rogers nor Palmer performed their now customary ‘Cold’ celebrations after scoring. That trademark came later in their careers.

Instead, when Palmer grabbed the winner for Carlos Vicens’ academy class of 2020 at City, he lifted his shirt to reveal a tribute to Jeremy Wisten, his former team-mate who had died by suicide just nine days before.

Young footballers form bonds when they dream of making it big together, and we will never know what might have become of Wisten, a teenager who wrestled with his release by City. It was a poignant gesture by Palmer to reveal a ‘GBNF’ (‘Gone But Never Forgotten’) undershirt so that his late friend was involved in their first FA Youth Cup triumph since 2008.

Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers have been friends and team-mates since their days in Man City's academy

The pair share a celebration but Rogers' £117m move to Chelsea will also see them share the pitch for the first time in nearly six years

Watching back this final, it is striking how all three of City’s goals involved a player now owned by Chelsea. For their first, Delap occupied Chelsea’s centre backs as Palmer squeezed a pass by Colwill for the unmarked James McAtee to finish.

For their second, Colwill was marking Palmer as Delap crossed and Rogers scored.

For their third, Delap’s saved shot crept to Palmer to complete the 3-2 scoreline, with Colwill smashing the ball into the back of the net in frustration while City celebrated. Now they are all set to be team-mates at Stamford Bridge moving forward in a case of graduates reunited. Once City’s next generation. Suddenly Chelsea’s future.

With Rogers and Palmer in particular, this £117m move from Aston Villa rekindles a friendship, it being no secret that the two are close. They have described each other as best friends in football. They are on WhatsApp and FaceTime almost daily, as we all are with our own pals. Both believed in what the other was capable of achieving back when they were with City, and so for them personally, it is rather nice that they are teaming up again at Chelsea.

While away with England, Rogers’ team-mates liked jesting on the ownership of his celebration. Jude Bellingham was asked during one interview whose was better: his or Rogers’. Sitting next to Rogers, Bellingham pondered and said: ‘Mine or Cole’s?’ Chelsea’s content team will be buzzing with ideas for how they can play on this ‘Cold’ competition.

Rogers did it first while playing for Middlesbrough, but technically, Palmer owns it. He has it trademarked with the UK Intellectual Property Office for commercial reasons. It entered the register in November 2025, and is not due for renewal until November 2034.

Palmer debuted it in a 3-2 win away at Luton in December 2023 and has since told reporters that he did it as ‘a nod’ to Rogers. They’re mates, so Rogers does not mind too much that he pinched it from him. From Chelsea's perspective, they will hope they can score enough goals between them to take turns and share it amicably.

Palmer may have seen this move coming. Before the end of the last season, several Chelsea players held talks with the club’s owners and directors, Palmer included. It was at a time when he was being linked to Manchester United despite Chelsea sources tagging him as one of their untouchable assets. Assurances were made, and also to Reece James when the captain signed his new contract through to 2032. Palmer spoke at length with James about what he was told.

Chelsea has kept a close eye on Rogers since he was at Middlesborough (pictured in 2024)

Palmer celebrated his friend's signing with a touching Instagram post documenting their bond

Chelsea promised they were now going to recruit ‘ready-made’ signings this summer. Missing out on Champions League football – or any form of European qualification for that matter – was a complication. But they have spent big to beat Arsenal to the signing of Rogers. He meets that ‘ready-made’ criteria. James is said to have been pleading his club’s case while they were both away at this summer's World Cup.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso had his first behind-closed-doors friendly at the weekend, with Daily Mail Sport revealing the scoreline was 3-1 and the scorers were Delap, Jamie Gittens and Emmanuel Emegha. One source also told us they used a 4-2-3-1 formation. One solution would be Palmer at No 10 and Rogers on the left, or Rogers at No 10 and Palmer on the right. If Alonso uses a 3-4-2-1, both could feature behind Joao Pedro as the starting striker.

Their versatility gives Alonso options, and while Rogers has been a long-term target for Chelsea, the 44-year-old Spaniard very much sanctioned this transfer after arriving. We can sometimes suspect it is hot air when a new manager is telling us how he is on the same page as those above him, but in this particular case, it is true.

Rogers will be due some downtime after his World Cup exploits with England, three weeks being the usual break. That means he may miss their pre-season tour of Australia and Asia. Whenever he rocks up, coldness could ensue. Certainly, after spending £117m to bring the boys back together, Chelsea hope it will be positively Siberian.

Sports.title: Barcelona release statement as Nou Camp worker dies during stadium redevelopment
Sports.content:
Barcelona release statement as Nou Camp worker dies during stadium redevelopment

Barcelona have said they regret that a worker has died while working on the Nou Camp renovation, as club president Joan Laporta offered his personal condolences

View 2 Images A worker has died during the redevelopment of the Nou Camp

A man who was working on the Nou Camp renovation has died, with Barcelona offering their support to his grieving family.

‌



The 54-year-old, who has not been named, is thought to have died as a result of "a blow" while working on Friday, the Catalan regional police said. The iconic stadium has been undergoing major work for almost three years and the emergency services were called to the stadium. His death has led to an investigation.

‌



Work at the stadium began in June 2023 and is expected to be completed in early 2028, as Barcelona look to bolster their capacity to 105,000 - making it one of the largest grounds in the world.

‌



The club put out a statement following the tragedy which read: "FC Barcelona deeply regrets the death of the worker who lost his life yesterday in the workplace accident that occurred during the renovation works at Spotify Camp Nou. The club wishes to express its deepest condolences and extend its heartfelt support to his family, friends, and colleagues.

Arsenal exploring stunning Vinicius Junior transfer as Real Madrid star's move approved READ MORE :

"FC Barcelona president Joan Laporta wishes to personally convey his condolences to the family and places himself at their disposal on behalf of the entire club."

Barcelona's rivals, Real Madrid, have revamped the Bernabeu over the past decade, making it one of the most iconic and aesthetically impressive stadiums in the world. Barca have now responded as they look to modernise their stadium.

‌



They returned to their iconic home back in November after more than two years when they beat Athletic Bilbao in front of a reduced capacity of 45,401 with cranes and construction work still very much taking place. The overall project is set to cost around £1.1billion.

View 2 Images Barcelona returned to a partially finished Nou Camp back in November

Since moving back to the Nou Camp, Barcelona have won every single home game in La Liga. The only team to secure a result there was Atletico Madrid, who registered a 2-0 victory en route to knocking out the Catalans in the last eight of the Champions League.

Article continues below

Barcelona memorably won the first El Clasico back at the Nou Camp in May by downing Real 2-0, in turn securing La Liga. Hansi Flick's side are eyeing up a hat-trick of Spanish titles as they prepare for a full season back into their long-term home.

Sports.title: Kate and Gerry McCann cheer on Madeleine's brother Sean at Commonwealth Games
Sports.content:
Kate and Gerry McCann cheer on Madeleine's brother Sean at Commonwealth Games

Sean McCann this week spoke proudly of swimming for Scotland at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow - a welcome positive story for the family who have endured hell since three-year-old Madeleine's disappearance in 2007

View 5 Images Kate and Gerry McCann photographed with their daughter Amelie as they cheer on son Sean McCann at the Commonwealth Games (Image: Stuart Wallace/Shutterstock)

Kate and Gerry McCann proudly cheered on their son Sean at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow today.

‌



The couple were watching Madeleine's younger brother represent Scotland in the 400m individual freestyle swimming event at the competition. Sean's twin sister Amelie was also supporting her sibling alongside them from the stands inside Tollcross International Swimming Centre.

‌



Kate, 58, was wearing a t-shirt decorated with the words 'Yes Sir, I can boogie' in reference to the 1977 Baccara hit, which has become a Scottish football anthem.

‌



View 5 Images The McCanns gave their full-throated support to Sean (Image: Stuart Wallace/Shutterstock)

Madeleine McCann's brother opens up about Commonwealth Games journey and making big decision READ MORE :

Sean and Amelie, both now 21, were aged just two when Madeleine disappeared from her family’s holiday apartment in Praia da Luz, Portugal, on May 3, 2007. The three-year-old’s disappearance prompted a worldwide manhunt, but she has never been found.

Sean has previously spoken about his training regime and dedication to the sport, and how he one day wants to make the Olympics.

‌



View 5 Images Sean pictured after finishing fourth in a Men's 400m individual Freestyle heat (Image: Stuart Wallace/Shutterstock)

The Leicester athlete, who studies chemical engineering at Loughborough University, began competing aged eight and previously raced for Scotland at the 2023 Commonwealth Youth Games in Trinidad and Tobago, competing in the 400m and 1500m freestyle.

Sean, who was brought up in England, but competes for Scotland due to his dad’s Scottish roots, is a keen sea swimmer and has been part of the Scottish Swimming programme since his teens.

‌



View 5 Images Madeleine was three when she vanished on holiday (Image: PA/PA Wire)

He appeared in British colours at the European junior open water championships in Corfu in 2023 and finished third in the 800m freestyle and fourth in the 1500m at the British Championships earlier this year.

McCann previously competed at the 2024 Championships, which doubled as Team GB's Olympic trials. His progression to the senior Commonwealth Games comes after representing Scotland at the 2023 Commonwealth Youth Games in Trinidad and Tobago.

‌



He finished fifth in the 400m freestyle and seventh in the 1,500m freestyle there and also raced for Great Britain at the 2025 European Open Water Championships in Croatia. Speaking about his expectations for Glasgow, he said: "I'm going in as more of an underdog. I don't feel like there's any pressure on me. I should be able to go in and perform at my best."

Talking about his first swimming experience with his mum, Sean previously said: “I hated it at first, didn’t want to go, but then after a while, it grew on me and I am still here now.”

View 5 Images The family looked as though they were enjoying watching Sean compete in Glasgow (Image: Stuart Wallace/Shutterstock)

Article continues below

He began swimming competitively at the age of eight, when he joined a local triathlon club, and two years later he was selected to swim for City of Leicester and went on to win county and regional titles.

He has said previously: “In order to have achieved this, I have had to remain extremely dedicated, getting up at 4am multiple mornings a week to train, since the age of 11.

“I train nine times a week in the pool, as well as three gym sessions, totalling over 20 hours of training per week. I’m aiming to compete at the 2026 Commonwealth Games and also the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.”

Sports.title: Inside Josh Kerr's gruelling preparation to break fastest mile record as runner admits 'dark days'
Sports.content:
Inside Josh Kerr's gruelling preparation to break fastest mile record as runner admits 'dark days'

EXCLUSIVE: The flying Scot tells how 'Project 222' - the number of seconds required to break the world mile record that had stood for 27 years - meant every aspect of his life was tailored to a specific day

Josh Kerr celebrates Olympic silver medal with first drink since Christmas

The term 'Man on a Mission' could have been coined for the all-conquering King of the Track Josh Kerr. The 28-year-old Scot set his goal to break the world mile record eight months in advance. "Project 222" - the number of seconds required to break a record that had stood for 27 years - meant every aspect of his life was tailored to the specific day and event when he would line up to run faster over the distance than any man in history. That he smashed the record with almost half a second to spare, running three minutes and 42.66 seconds, is testament to his superhuman dedication and determination.

‌



View 4 Images Josh Kerr breaking the mile record (Image: Adam Davy/PA Wire)

‌



These are the faces of dozens of tragic Brits who lost their lives in open water READ MORE :

UK weather model shows 45C heat surge in what would be hottest day ever seen READ MORE :

His place in history inevitably led to comparisons with the late Sir Roger Bannister, the distinguished British medic who became the first man to run the mile in under four minutes in 1954. In many ways the two men could not be more different.

‌



Bannister had completed a shift as a junior doctor at a London hospital before getting a train, having lunch with Chris Chataway and pacemaker Chris Brasher before taking to the track.

He freely admitted that he would have given up athletics altogether if he had won an Olympic Gold medal at the Helsinki 1952 games. He was criticised for training 'away from the spotlight' because he was so nervous in competition. What the two men shared was a steely determination to push themselves to the absolute limits of human endurance. Kerr's preparations included taking ice baths lasting exactly three minutes and 42 seconds, matching his new mile time.

He would go to bed at 8:30 p.m. in an oxygen-boosting altitude chamber at his home in Albuquerque, New Mexico.

‌



View 4 Images Josh Kerr in the ice bath which he used for training before he broke his mile record (Image: Mirrorpix)

Albuquerque is around 5,250 ft above sea level. Kerr's altitude chamber gives him another 3,000 ft. The former 1500m world champion and double Olympic medallist ate spinach with almost every meal.

He fasted for 16 to 18 hours, starting around 6:30pm on a Tuesday until around 12:30pm the next day. And some of his methods were just bizarre. He would also take sodium bicarbonate, otherwise known as baking soda, before every race, which experts say delays muscle fatigue. Now he has turned his attention to the Commonwealth Games and the same mile event in his home country on Saturday. Few would bet against him. Kerr said that the "darkest" aspects of his life came not in training, but in the time away from his loved ones due to the sacrifices he makes.

‌



He is married to Larimar Rodriguez, whom he met on his first day at university and who now works as a dermatologist at a hospital in Albuquerque. He was just 17. They have a 'relaxed' home life, but Kerr admits his dedication comes at a cost.

View 4 Images Josh Kerr and partner Larimar Rodriguez (Image: Instagram)

“Most of the dark places don't happen on the track for me," he said as he prepared for the Games which opened on Thursday in Glasgow. "Those are the most fun times that I have. "You know, the hard sessions are kind of where I live. I take pride that I can push and manipulate my body to get ready to go. It's mostly the time off the track, the other 23 hours of the day, living that boring lifestyle, that are the hardest. But they allow me to turn up and do my job as well as I can during that one or two hours that I'm specifically training. "So those are the quiet moments where you've got to convince yourself that you're doing it for the right reasons. And then you're spending time away from the people you love for the right reasons and the result will come.” Asked why he had set himself his world record goal so publicly, he joked: "Bold, brave or stupid, one of those works pretty well. If you want to have a moment in sport, you have to tell people about it.

‌



"I'm a businessman at the end of the day. I want to big up my product and I believe in myself. I knew that the people around me knew how to peak my performance just at the right time. "I just needed to turn up to train every day ready and be willing to go to the deep depths of some dark places to get myself in the right position at the right time. The best plans come together like that. You need a little bit of luck on your side as well, and the British weather was on our side." He celebrated his mile record with a beer and a steak but admitted he was 'still coming down from my floating space' this week. "But yes I had a good day," he said. "It's starting to settle in for sure. Events like that come at you from all angles.

"It's going to take a while for me to come back to Earth." Kerr is about to land back in Scotland, where his athletics journey began as a teenager on the track where he is going for gold on Saturday August 1.

In July 2011, almost 15 years to the day that he will run the Commonwealth Mile, the record books show Edinburgh-born Kerr ran 4m 30.91 as a 13-year-old. He also threw the shot 7m 34cm and achieved 1m 55cm in the high jump.

‌



He recalled: “I grew up in youth academies for future Commonwealth Games hopefuls, and that experience will never leave me. I still have the T-shirt that says, "Scottish Commonwealth Games hopeful." It was a bit of a rough T-shirt back then but there’s definitely a lot of memories held in it.

"So, to be able to go out there and represent my country, in my country, in front of a home crowd, in the Commonwealth Games, that's all I want for my career.”

Bullied at school, sport was an escape for the young Bannister; he would climb over fences at night to find somewhere to run, once injuring himself when he ran into an obstacle after dark.

‌



He also spoke of his determination and sacrifice and admitted the last few seconds of his record-breaking run seemed "never-ending." Afterwards he "felt like an exploded flashlight, no will to live".

He held his world record for only 46 days before the Australian John Landy broke it. The two men were due to face one another at the Empire Games at Vancouver in August, and both knew that this battle would mean more to Bannister than the four-minute mile and more to Landy than the world record.

View 4 Images Sir Roger Bannister with Chris Chataway (right) and Chris Brasher on the day Bannister broke the mile record (Image: Hulton Archive)

‌



The clash turned into a huge media fanfare, and 40 million people watched it on television while 100m listened on radio. It became one of the most exciting duels of all time as Bannister overtook Landy on the last lap.

In looking around, Landy had lost a valuable fraction of a second - and Bannister grabbed his chance and overtook him at 3 minutes 58.8 seconds.

Bannister went on to win the European Championships before disappearing from the athletics scene at 25 to become a distinguished medic and a fellow of Pembroke College, Oxford.

‌



Kerr is unlikely to disappear from the limelight any time soon.

* Fans are encouraged not to miss out and get their hands on their tickets today, available at glasgow2026.com/tickets.

Sports.title: Super Bowl champion dies by suicide aged 38 as heartbroken wife pays tribute
Sports.content:
Super Bowl champion dies by suicide aged 38 as heartbroken wife pays tribute

Tributes have been paid to former NFL star and Super Bowl champion Jordan Devey after he died by suicide at the age of 38, leaving behind wife Linsey and four children

View 3 Images Jordan Devey leaves behind four children (Image: Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images)

Super Bowl champion Jordan Devey has died by suicide at the age of 38, his wife has confirmed in a heartbreaking statement.

‌



Devey represented the Baltimore Ravens, New England Patriots, San Francisco 49ers, Kansas City Chiefs and Las Vegas Raiders during a seven-year career in the NFL.

‌



Playing as a guard and an offensive tackle, he won the Super Bowl with the Patriots in February 2015 and made 44 appearances in the NFL in total, including 21 as a starter.

‌



Devey's wife Linsey has confirmed his sad passing in a post on Instagram. "Today would have been our 15th year anniversary," she wrote.

English gymnast taken to hospital after sickening fall onto his head at Commonwealth Games READ MORE :

Tony Bellew hammers 'disgraceful' Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury plan over controversial venue READ MORE :

"We have filled the walls of our homes and hearts with countless memories, joys, struggles, and triumphs.

"We brought 4 beautiful children into this world that have your eyes, freckles, and compassion. You were our hero and our hearts ache in your absence. We love you. We miss you. And as you said in your last words to me, 'we’ll talk soon.'"

‌



A fundraising page has been set up for the Devey family and has raised $90,000 (£67,570) from 441 donations at the time of writing. The page describes Devey as "a devoted husband to Linsey and a loving father to their four children".

"Tragically, Jordan took his own life, leaving his family to navigate an incredibly difficult and heartbreaking time," it reads.

View 3 Images Linsey Devey shared a photo of herself with Jordan in hospital (Image: Instagram/ldevey)

‌



"As they face overwhelming emotional and financial challenges, including mounting medical expenses, the community is coming together to support Linsey and their children.

"The funds raised will help ease the financial burden, allowing them to focus on healing and moving forward without the added stress of immediate expenses.

"If you are able, please consider donating to support Linsey and their four children during this difficult time."

‌



View 3 Images Jordan Devey played for Kansas City Chiefs during his NFL career (Image: Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

There has been an outpouring of messages of support, with Devey's role as a high school coach inspiring the next generation of American football players.

"Jordan spent countless hours volunteering as a coach for his own children’s teams and for the athletes at Eagle High School, where he was deeply loved by the players who saw him as a mentor, role model, and friend," the fundraiser adds.

Article continues below

"His commitment to uplifting those around him extended far beyond sports, as he faithfully served in his church, offering support, counsel, and friendship to anyone in need."

A friend of the family wrote on Instagram: "We’ve been hit by a hurricane of sadness for the Deveys. We can’t imagine life without Jordan and love Linsey and the kids like the family. Please pray for them- pray for angels to hold them up. We’re shattered."

If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text Crisis Text Line at 741741.

Sports.title: Tony Bellew hammers 'disgraceful' Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury plan over controversial venue
Sports.content:
Tony Bellew hammers 'disgraceful' Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury plan over controversial venue

Anthony Joshua's fight with Tyson Fury is yet to have its venue confirmed and Eddie Hearn has been hammered by Tony Bellew after talk of it being held at Madison Square Garden

View 2 Images Tony Bellew took Eddie Hearn to town over the prospect of the fight being in the USA (Image: DAZN)

Tony Bellew has called out Eddie Hearn over potential plans to stage Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury in America, claiming its a "disgrace" and "no one cares" in the US.

The fight between the two British heavyweights has been a decade in the making and, provided both men come through their fights this week, is set to take place in the coming months.

But given the interest and the powerbrokers involved, there is doubt over whether the fight would actually be held in the UK. That would be a blow to British fans and, when Hearn talked up the desire to have it in America, Bellew underlined the fact that the biggest number of pay-per-view buys will likely be in the UK.

The Matchroom boss, also Joshua's promoter, said: "These people want the fight to be in the US, that's the reality of the situation" which led to a frustrated rant from ex-professional boxer Bellew.

He said on DAZN: "American boxing is dead, no one cares. No one cares in America. It's disgraceful, what are we going there for?"

The former cruiserweight champion continued: "I'm just sick of it, we're appealing to America - why? America doesn't care about us. When have America cared about boxing? They want what we've got. We've got the best crowds in the world, the most passionate fans in the world, and that's why it should be with us.

"These are the two stalwarts of British boxing, these two have put boxing back on the map, no one cares in America. No one's cared in American since Evander Holyfield retired and Mike Tyson left, no one cares, so why do we need it there? New York and Madison Square Gardens, that's great, go and watch the Knicks."

View 2 Images Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua could finally fight are years of waiting (Image: Getty)

Hearn said on Friday night that Madison Square Garden in New York is the preferred choice of Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Al-Sheikh, WWE president and TKO board member Nick Khan, as well as streaming service Netflix.

Speaking to The Athletic at the weigh-in of Joshua’s fight against Kristian Prenga, Hearn said: “They’ve had a decent offer from MSG. And time zones as well; I think the aim would be to do it at three o’clock in the morning UK time, which would be 10pm in the U.S. (Eastern Time)”.

Article continues below

If Joshua emerges victorious from his fight in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia Hearn says there is a possibility that the fight with Fury could be officially announced.

The contract that Joshua has signed stipulates that the fight must be held in the UK but Hearn claimed “quite a few bits in the contract that haven’t been adhered to. They’re not necessarily material breaches, but where the fight is, is a material breach.”

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
