"There's a lot of mistrust in vaccines in Nigeria, but there's some highly influential champions for cervical cancer in the country that I think are doing phenomenal work in driving public awareness," Dent says.

In another project in Cote d'Ivoire, BIO Ventures helped create a public awareness campaign with video s on commuter buses, encouraging men to get regular screenings for prostate cancer. Steps like these, Dent says, can help countries prepare for a future where cancer diagnoses are increasingly common.

An optimistic outlook

Titilayo, the mother of three, says she hopes to inspire others to watch for early signs of cancer, and to pursue treatment if diagnosed. She says it isn't an easy task; cancer survivors in her community face stigma, gossip and rejection, especially if they have undergone a mastectomy. Others face financial hardship and difficulty returning to work.

But she now shows no evidence of disease. Her girls are older and she is optimistic about the future.

"I still insist that my life is worth more than any trauma or emotional issue," Titilayo says. She wants to make sure the women around her feel the same.

World.title: Trump is hellbent on tariffs. Here are 5 implications
World.content:
Trump is hellbent on tariffs. Here are 5 implications

toggle caption Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images North America

President Trump's second term has been marked by intense economic uncertainty, from the war with Iran to tensions with countries around the world – and there appears to be no reprieve coming.

The White House said on Thursday the U.S. would replace a temporary 10% tariff it had imposed earlier this year with a batch of new ones covering dozens of countries.

The new levies, which kicked in on Friday after midnight, range from 10% to 12.5%, and they are meant to be more legally durable — though economists still say they are likely to be challenged.

Here are five takeaways as Trump remains fixated on tariffs.

1. No immediate relief for American households

It's already been a rough ride for many families, with the cost of living remaining a top concern after years of high inflation.

Things may not get better anytime soon. The renewed tensions with Iran are threatening to push up gas prices and broader energy costs — raising the prospect that inflation could once again pick up after prices had finally seemed to ease in June.

Sponsor Message

The national average for gas prices is back up above $4 a gallon , according to AAA, after dipping below that level in late June as crude prices once again surge.

Loading...

Meanwhile, the average 30-year mortgage rate this week hit its highest in nearly a year and remains historically high.

Now Trump's determination to find new legal ways to justify tariffs on imported goods threaten to burden households for longer.

The new tariffs are not significantly higher than the ones they are replacing, and there are carveouts in place.

But they are still higher than when Trump's second term started, with a current average rate of 11% , according to the Budget Lab at Yale University.

The prospect of continued tariffs could extend the financial burden on Americans – imposing an additional cost of about $1,100 on households, according to Budget Lab.

2. The path to lower interest rates is tougher

New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh inherited a challenging job when he was sworn in back in May.

Inflation remains a top concern for policy makers even though the U.S. economy has been relatively stable recently.

If inflation starts to rise, the Fed may need to raise rates – in a rebuke to President Trump who appointed Warsh hoping the central bank would be more willing to cut rates instead.

Sponsor Message

Trump's determination to extend his tariffs – and his administration's threat to impose additional ones – will keep additional economic uncertainty in place

"If there are tariffs imposed and if they stick, that is certainly going to drive up the prices of imports, which is going to add to inflation," says Eswar Prasad, a professor at Cornell University.

Loading...

3. More uncertainty for businesses that rely on imports

Ever since Trump imposed his initial set of tariffs last year, businesses have faced a period of intense volatility.

Business owners were able to get some reprieve after the Supreme Court struck down many of Trump's tariffs – allowing many to get refunds from the import taxes they had already paid.

But Trump's determination to continue to impose tariffs threaten to prolong the uncertainty. The president responded to the Supreme Court setback with a temporary 10% tariff, drawing fresh legal challenges.

The new set of tariffs are intended to be more legally durable. Nonetheless more court fights could still be coming, meaning the question of whether tariffs will ultimately remain could continue to cast a shadow on businesses, warns Prasad.

"It is going to have a dampening effect on business investment," says Prasad. "Businesses crave certainty and this is going to introduce a whole lot of uncertainty which could potentially lead them to holding back from investment, which will [then] have some implications [on hiring]," he says.

In addition, the administration is threatening additional tariffs, including one on pharmaceuticals and import duties on additional countries.

4. The administration argues there will be benefits — but at what cost?

Despite the warnings from economists and policy experts, the Trump administration has argued tariffs are vital as leverage to obtain key concessions from other countries on trade agreements.

Trump has also argued tariffs will put pressure on American manufacturers to stop importing goods from other countries and instead start creating jobs in the U.S. However, despite tariffs that were imposed during his first term and since the beginning of his second, none of that has yet materialized.

Sponsor Message

Tariffs, though, have brought more revenue from the government. The Budget Lab projects that tariffs will raise $1.9 trillion in revenue for the U.S.

But Natasha Sarin, president of the Budget Lab argues, that revenue gains need to be weighed against the projected economic costs, including the uptick in inflation and a decline in economic growth.

"The way that [tariffs] are bringing in that revenue isn't incredibly efficient," she says. "The fact that the economy isn't growing as fast as it would be in a counterfactual world without tariffs levied at these levels, you never make up that. It's sort of a permanent decline in the economic strength as a result of this type of policy."

toggle caption Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images

5. The global economy could continue to bear the tariff fallout

Countries around the world face the prospect of continued pressure from the Trump administration.

The expected rise in energy costs from the U.S. war with Iran had already led the International Monetary Fund to lower its outlook for the global economy early this month.

Trump's determination to extend tariffs could continue to put countries on guard. Just this month, the White House threatened to impose additional tariffs on Canada, over reasons including a boycott of eight Canadian provinces on American liquor.

The global economy – and American households – have already been dealing with over a year of tariff uncertainty. With Trump hellbent on tariffs, that is unlikely to change anytime soon.

World.title: Democrats in Maine gather to replace Graham Platner in the race against Susan Collins
World.content:
Democrats in Maine gather to replace Graham Platner in the race against Susan Collins

toggle caption Graeme Sloan/Getty Images

Democrats are gathering in Bangor, Maine, on Saturday to formally nominate a new candidate for U.S. Senate, as the party looks to move past the scandal-plagued campaign of Graham Platner and refocus its sights on unseating longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins.

It's a Senate matchup with far-reaching political implications. Democrats need to net a total of four seats to win back control of the chamber this fall, and party officials see the contest in Maine as one of their best opportunities.

The race was thrown into turmoil earlier this month when Platner, the party's initial nominee, ended his campaign after a woman he previously dated came forward and accused him of raping her in 2021. Platner has denied the allegation, but it was the final straw for Democrats after months of controversy surrounding him.

Sponsor Message

Now, after an abbreviated and chaotic search for a replacement, Maine Democrats are hoping to rally behind a new candidate who can harness the same energy and momentum of the Platner campaign.

The apparent front-runner heading into Saturday's convention is Troy Jackson. The former president of the Maine Senate has already garnered support from the bulk of elected delegates who will cast ballots for the nominee, and nearly every one of his primary rivals has dropped out of the race.

Maintaining Platner's movement, without the baggage

Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from northern Maine, is running on an economic populist message that mirrors much of what Platner emphasized in his campaign, rejecting the Democratic establishment and focusing on affordability concerns, backing policies like Medicare for All and raising taxes on the ultra-wealthy and large corporations.

Like other more progressive candidates on the left, Jackson is pushing for the abolishment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and an end to U.S. military aid to Israel. He's also advocating for Congress to pass civil rights legislation protecting LGBTQ Americans and federalize the right to an abortion — two issues where he's changed his views after taking more conservative stances during his early years in public office.

Sponsor Message

When asked about Jackson's history with reproductive rights, Democratic state Sen. Stacy Brenner argued that it wasn't a deterrent in supporting him.

"What I find compelling about legislators and policymakers is when they are able to evolve with the thinking of where their heart is, where their mind is, when they learn about data and when they hear stories [from] their constituents," said Brenner, who also has a background as a farmer and nurse.

"That's what's happened for Troy," she added.

Jackson supporters celebrate his lengthy tenure in Maine politics as well as his blue-collar roots. And despite recent reporting in The Washington Post and CNN describing Jackson as exhibiting a short temper with colleagues during his time in office, he has faced minimal public pushback from state leaders in the lead-up to the convention.

A tough road ahead for the nominee

While Collins has faced competitive challengers before, Democrats see the fifth-term incumbent as particularly vulnerable this year. She's running in a state carried by Kamala Harris in 2024, and at a moment when many voters have soured on President Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran.

Still, even if Jackson is able to claim the nomination, he will face a difficult path to victory, with only about 100 days before voting ends on Nov. 3 to build up a war chest and make his case to voters.

In Collins, he would be facing off against one of the most senior Republican incumbents in the Senate. Collins, who has held her seat for 30 years, holds a massive fundraising edge, reporting $11 million in cash on hand, according to latest Federal Election Commission filings.

toggle caption Scott Eisen/Getty Images

But Jackson's campaign argues that it has momentum, reporting a fundraising haul of more than $1 million since he announced his run.

"This campaign is powered by people who are sick of watching billionaires and corporations buy influence while working families get screwed," Jackson said in a statement Wednesday.

Sponsor Message

"Together, we're building the grassroots movement it will take to defeat Susan Collins and give Maine a senator who answers to working people."

World.title: Trump returns to correspondents' dinner 3 months after shooting
World.content:
Trump returns to correspondents' dinner 3 months after shooting

toggle caption Rod Lamkey/AP Photo

President Donald Trump returned to the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association dinner Friday night, delivering a rambling, hour-long speech that praised some journalists, took potshots at others, made jokes about public figures' weight and intellect, and quipped about a third presidential term.

He assured the crowd of journalists, though, that he'd scrapped the most biting parts of his remarks.

"That was going to be a doozy," Trump said about the speech he'd been prepared to give in April, before a gunman upended the original dinner and forced its postponement.

"As I said three months ago, the show must go on," the president said to begin his remarks, hailing the decision to reschedule the dinner. He referred to "the attempted mass murder" that could have happened that night in April, but then moved largely to humor — and insults.

Sponsor Message

Trump's return to the correspondents' dinner — and his promise to come back next year as well — represented a notable moment in his relationship with the news media, which he has attacked, sued and taken administrative action against since he began his second term early last year. Among the audience members were reporters he had denounced and barred from events.

Trump's sometimes off-color speech, which lasted just over an hour, was full of vague potshots directed at individuals he doesn't like — from Jane Fonda to Bruce Springsteen to "Barack Hussein Obama." The audience, reacting at first with some friendly laughs, slowly quieted to scattered titters as the insults piled up.

toggle caption Rod Lamkey/AP Photo

Among other targets of Trump's humor: Late-night hosts Jimmy Fallon and Jimmy Kimmel; Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.; California Gov. Gavin Newsom; former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie; and Trump's own speechwriters, whose jokes he sometimes criticized even as he delivered them. Some of the comments flirted with racism.

The president also spent some time expressing pride in the ballroom at the Waldorf Astoria hotel, formerly the Trump International Hotel. "It's great to be back at a place that I know very well, because I built it," Trump said.

He also made reference to the journalism awards that had been handed out earlier in the evening, most of them for stories challenging him and his administration. "Do I have a say in those awards?" he asked with a grimace.

Sponsor Message

He made a brief mention of the Iran war and several remarks about the ballroom he is building at the White House. He also used the occasion to joke about the possibility he would serve a third term — something barred by the U.S. Constitution's 22nd Amendment.

"Just like my presidency, the second time is always better," the president quipped. "And the third time will be better yet."

He added: "I'm only kidding." Then, at the end, he donned a red cap that said "Trump 2028" and delivered the "scoop" that he was running again.

It was a very different dinner than the previous one

Earlier, Trump had entered the ballroom to polite applause, and was thanked for his support by outgoing White House Correspondents' Association president Weijia Jiang of CBS News. After dinner, he then sat through more than an hour of awards presentations.

One of the winners, Tyler Pager of the New York Times, was in fact one of the reporters who had been subpoenaed by Trump's Justice Department over his reporting about Trump's Qatari-gifted Air Force One jet. Those subpoenas were withdrawn on Thursday in a New York courtroom — just one of the arenas where the president, in his second term, has been seeking to control media coverage that displeases him.

The rescheduled dinner was taking place at a smaller venue this time that held only about 700 people. Security was markedly tighter. Guests entered via a single entrance, through two ID checks and past a detection dog, armed officers and security guards. There was no red carpet and no separate cocktail receptions preceding the dinner.

"Let's try this again," Jiang quipped, welcoming the crowd. The White House press corps, she noted, "always have a follow-up." Turning serious, she referred back to the trauma and confusion of the original dinner in April.

Sponsor Message

"Tonight our message is this: We are back," she said. "We will not be intimidated. We refuse to let an act of violence have the final word."

Early in his speech, Trump signaled that he had decided to tone it down. But he kept some zingers. Like this one, to the media-heavy audience: "This is really the largest group of 'Trump Derangement Syndrome' people put together at one time."

People received awards for bravery during April shooting

Besides the pared-down approach, there was another change at Friday's dinner: two additional awards. One was presented to Victor Gonzales, the Secret Service agent who was staffing a security checkpoint in April and was struck in his protective vest.

Gonzales "placed himself directly in harm's way and engaged the armed suspect," Jiang said. "He stayed in the fight and the attacker was stopped."

A second award was presented to the staff of the Washington Hilton hotel, site of the first dinner, hailed for professionalism under pressure.

toggle caption Cliff Owen/AP Photo

The dress code this time was a looser "black tie optional," and dinner included grilled peach and burrata salad, lobster and beef Wellington. The evening, as in April, featured entertainment by mentalist Oz Pearlman — who this time got the chance to do his act..

Jiang and her fellow board members had worked hard to bring about this WHCA dinner 2.0, not wanting to let a violent act — or the image of colleagues hiding under tables — remain the final thought. Announcing the rescheduling, she emphasized the dinner's stated purpose: "A celebration of a free press and the vital role of journalism in our democracy for over a century."

There's still lots of criticism of the event

But it's also clear that some people felt the dinner should not be rescheduled at all.

Many never thought it was much of a good look in the first place, with the sight of journalists in formal wear cozying up to their sources, or the objects of their reporting.

Sponsor Message

"It undermines the public faith in how the press does its work, and it makes it look like we are pals with the people we cover," Kelly McBride, an ethics expert at the Poynter Institute, a journalism think tank, said when the deliberations were taking place.

The new dinner came at a time of fast-increasing tension between the media and a president who, in his second term, has tried to exert pressure on media outlets he is unhappy with in a variety of ways. That pressure has ranged from sanctions against members of the White House press corps to regulatory actions through the Federal Communications Commission to outright lawsuits. Those tensions have only escalated since April.

Trump, though, ended with an attempt to mend fences 00 to a point. "I have a lot of respect for your profession," he told the assembled journalists. He also touted his own success, and declared: "When I'm not around, you're all gonna be broke."

And he concluded about the evening: "I didn't know what to expect. It's far worse than I originally thought."

World.title: Paramount says it will pause its Warner acquisition while legal challenges play out
World.content:
Paramount says it will pause its Warner acquisition while legal challenges play out

Jae C. Hong/Associated Press



The blockbuster merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery is on hold — possibly for many months — as two legal challenges to the $111 billion deal play out in court.

In a legal filing in federal court in California on Friday, Paramount says it has agreed not to take any steps to acquire Warner until June 1, 2027, or five days after the lawsuits are resolved, if that comes first.

The proposed deal would unite Paramount and Warner's film studios, streamers Paramount+ and HBO, and dozens of cable channels, along with CBS and CNN.

Sponsor Message

But Paramount is battling a pair of lawsuits filed by a consortium of 12 states and from the Writers Guild of America, which represents many entertainment professionals who work in Hollywood.

The Democratic attorneys general and the Writers Guild allege that Paramount's purchase of Warner Bros. would reduce competition, hurting filmgoers along with TV and news consumers and especially those who create entertainment programming and the news content that the public relies on.

Earlier this week, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted a temporary restraining order to pause the acquisition. Martínez-Olguín has yet to sign the agreement filed Friday.

In a statement, New York Attorney General Leticia James wrote, "Halting this merger while our case proceeds is a critical victory in our efforts to uphold the law and protect the film and television industries."

"Our argument against this illegal merger is straightforward: When too few corporations have too much power in markets central to American life, it makes things more expensive, and it makes things worse," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

The delay will have huge financial costs for Paramount. Starting Oct. 1, Paramount has to pay Warner shareholders a "ticking consideration" of roughly $650 million for every 90 days the deal is set back. If the deal is not closed by June 4, 2027, Paramount would have to pay Warner $7 billion according to the terms of the deal that Warner shareholders approved.

Sponsor Message

A Paramount spokesperson confirmed those fees are not affected by the latest development.

Paramount said in a statement that the company looks forward to going to trial.

"Today's agreement is a significant win because the result is exactly what we have sought from the outset: a direct path to a trial based on the evidence," the statement said. "This is the fastest and clearest way to prove that this transaction is good for competition, good for consumers, and good for creators, a conclusion dozens of competition authorities around the world have already reached."

The proposed deal has gotten scrutiny outside Hollywood for the relationship between Paramount's controlling family and President Trump — especially because two major newsrooms would be under that family's control.

The merger is largely bankrolled by Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison and a close ally of Trump. Trump has long accused CNN of being "fake news" and has publicly mused about what he'd like to do to the cable news giant.

World.title: He spent years playing and coaching hockey alongside Russians. Then Putin invaded Ukraine
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Oleksandr Matviychuk sifts through a stack of hockey medals hanging in his Kyiv apartment, the 51-year-old proudly shows off one earned during his decade playing for Ukraine's national team starting in 1999.

His eyes are then drawn to a medal he earned during the five seasons he played in Russia's Kontinental Hockey League between 1998 and 2003.

Back then, Russians were his teammates and some of his fiercest competitors on the ice. Now, he struggles to even think about facing off against them again. Anger blurs his ability to envision it.

"It's tough to imagine going in the same ring with them," he said, speaking to CBC News a few hours after Russian ballistic missiles killed at least 28 people in an attack on the Kyiv area in the early hours of July 6.

"They just tried to kill my people. Why should I feel anything different?"

Matviychuk shows off some of the hockey medals he won during his career as an elite player and coach. He spent five seasons playing in Russia, including in Moscow and St. Petersburg. (Vitalli Virchenko/CBC)

Off the ice and onto the front

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, the decades Matviychuk spent playing and coaching hockey came to an abrupt end once he signed up to fight.

Then, in June 2025, his time at the front ended violently after he was shot in the face while trying to help evacuate a group of Ukrainian soldiers who had been surrounded by Russian forces.

At one point, he said, doctors weren't sure he was going to live. But more than a year and nearly a dozen surgeries later, his face has been largely reconstructed.

A surgical team operates on Matviychuk in June 2026. During this surgery, plastic surgeons focused on the area around his upper lip. (Vitalii Virchenko/CBC)

Matviychuk now spends most of his time at his dacha, or rural cottage, valuing the quiet time by himself. He doesn't like venturing outside because of the way people look at him. Even though Ukrainians are now used to seeing people scarred by the violence of war, he says, some still can't help but stare.

"I don't like them feeling sorry for me," he said. "I don't like it. I prefer to stay at home and do not enjoy going out."

At one time, hockey took Matviychuk all over the world, including to North Bay, Ont., where he spent two seasons, between 1994 and 1996, playing in the Ontario Hockey League. He fondly remembers tournaments in Calgary and points out a novelty hockey stick in his apartment that was signed by other players after a youth tournament.

WATCH | 'I don't like them feeling sorry for me,' says soldier disfigured by war: Ukrainian hockey player injured in war longs to return to game he loves | Duration 2:38 After trading in his hockey skates for a military uniform, Oleksandr Matviychuk sustained severe injuries on the battlefield. The former Ukrainian national team player is now undergoing reconstructive surgery in Kyiv and longs to return the game he loves.

Matviychuk had taken a Ukrainian youth team to a tournament in Belarus just a few days before Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the start of what he called a "special military operation." He remembers many of the parents were concerned about the trip because of repeated warnings from the U.S. that Russia was poised to invade Ukraine.

Matviychuk assured them everything would be fine, convinced Russia wouldn't invade. When it did, he started reaching out to the Russian players he still kept in touch with.

"Most of the Russians … they kind of act like … that bird that's hiding its head in the sand, just saying, 'No, no it's not happening …. We're not doing anything,'" he said. "Some guys were saying, 'Please don't go fight. You'll get killed.'"

Matviychuk playing for Ukraine in a 2005 game against Finland at the IIHF Men's World Championship in Innsbruck, Austria. He hasn't been back on the ice since his injury because the cold air could make it harder for him to breathe through his nose. (Jeff Gross/Getty Images)

Around the same time, he said, some of his hockey contacts in Canada offered him a coaching role in Alberta — a pathway to get him out of the country — but he turned it down because he didn't feel right leaving.

Instead, Matviychuk was assigned to Ukraine's military intelligence agency, known by its acronym GUR. He had no prior military experience and didn't know how to shoot a gun, but sports had made him strong and scrappy, and he was used to working as part of a team.

But the analogy only goes so far.

"On ice, when you get blood, you just put a little snow on it, and it stops right away."

War, he says, is much dirtier.

A photo shared on Instagram by Matviychuk's daughter shows her father in Eastern Ukraine before his injury. (Alina Yeroshkina/Instagram)

'The war is not over'

Over the past four years, Matviychuk was sent on missions across Ukraine, including over the border during incursions into Russia. While he couldn't disclose specific details, he spoke of harrowing experiences, ruined villages and nearly impossible missions that sometimes didn't go as planned.

In June 2025, his team was sent to help a group of Ukrainian troops leave an area surrounded by Russians. Their task was to evacuate them and take up new positions. When they arrived, they encountered Russian forces immediately.

"We just had to fight ... as soon as we realized that this was not our guys who [we] were supposed to meet."

The Russian troops started shooting, and one member of Matviychuk's team was killed right away. Four others, including Matviychuk, were severely injured.

"We had one guy who was totally unwounded, and he took care of the rest of the Russians, so we could get out."

Dr. Leylya Omerova, middle, says facial injuries can be especially tough for patients' mental state because it can make them insecure when they go out in public. (Vitalii Virchenko/CBC)

Shot in the face and arm, Matviychuk applied his own tourniquet to his limb to stop the bleeding. He remembers walking himself to an evacuation vehicle while holding his gun, fully aware that his face was "hanging" off.

The next thing he remembers is waking up in a hospital in Dnipro, Ukraine. He was initially treated there before being moved to Kyiv.

"When he came to us, he didn't have a nose — the nose was destroyed," said Leylya Omerova, a Kyiv-based plastic surgeon.

"This kind of injury gives patients not only physical suffering but mental and psychological suffering."

Surgeons reconstructed his nose, jaw and lips, and he has at least one more surgery planned for the fall.

These two images taken my medical staff show how his face was changed over the course of several surgeries. The image on the right was taken near the beginning of his facial reconstruction while the one on the left is more recent (submitted/Dr. Leylya Omerova)

Back at his apartment, he shows off some of the newest medals added to his collection. The awards were given to him for his military service, but he admits he doesn't really know what each one represents.

They aren't like his hockey medals, where the trophies and team pictures hanging on the wall bring back fond memories of competition and camaraderie.

"I want to go back to [hockey], but I don't feel free to do it," he said. "The war is not over."

World.title: Canadian intern at NATO military headquarters in Belgium faces spying charges
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Canadian woman of Chinese origin who was an intern at NATO's military headquarters in Belgium has been arrested on spying charges, Belgian prosecutors said Saturday.

"She is suspected of spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization," the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office said in a statement.

The woman was as an intern at NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) in the Belgian city of Mons, it said. No further details of her identity or the country or organization she's suspected of spying for were given.

SHAPE is NATO's top military headquarters, the base of Allied Command Operations, which is responsible for planning and carrying out all operations of the 32-member transatlantic security alliance.

LISTEN | Canada's relationship with NATO: Just Asking 59:35 Footing the NATO bill: What Canada’s growing defence budget actually buys you Canada went to this week’s NATO summit in Turkey with a promise to spend 5 percent of its GDP in defence by 2035. But what does NATO, and Canada’s military strategy, really mean for everyday Canadian life? Lieutenant General the Honorable Andrew Leslie is a retired commander of the Canadian Army and former MP. Alexander Lanoszka is an associate professor in the department of political science at the University of Waterloo.

The suspect had come to the attention of SHAPE’s security services, which reported her to Belgian intelligence officials, according to the statement.

Investigators searched the suspect's home and her workplace at SHAPE, and she was placed under arrest on Friday.

A SHAPE spokesperson said there was no indication that NATO or SHAPE operational readiness, command and control arrangements or ongoing tasks had been affected.

"SHAPE continues to fulfil its responsibilities without interruption."

The prosecutor's office said it would make no further comment as investigations continued.

CBC News reached out to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) and the Department of National Defence and will update this story with any response.

World.title: Interprovincial booze rules may be easing, but other trade barriers still remain
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Interprovincial trade barriers were back in the spotlight this week as Canada's premiers mused about how to deal with new tariff threats from U.S. President Donald Trump at their annual summer meeting.

On Tuesday, a new deal was announced that will see nine provinces across Canada introduce direct-to-consumer alcohol sales following an agreement signed by their premiers.

It's the latest step in a larger push that started last year to address interprovincial trade barriers across Canada in an effort to boost the country's economy in the trade war with the United States.

The 2026 edition of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB) report card on interprovincial co-operation gave most of the provinces and territories an A, while giving the federal government an A+, in recognition of the progress made toward reducing these barriers through different mutual recognition legislation and/or policies.

"Over the years, we've seen a little bit of progress here and there, but last year really kicked things off," said SeoRhin Yoo, senior policy analyst of interprovincial affairs at CFIB.

But a litany of barriers remain. Here's a look at some key ones and how they hinder the free flow of goods, services and labour between provinces.

Food production

Navigating a combination of federal and provincial laws regulating food safety can make it difficult and costly for food producers to sell their products outside their home province or territory.

Under federal regulation, food businesses must meet federal requirements under the Safe Food for Canadians Act and be licensed by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) if their products cross borders.

And while the interprovincial trade of food in Canada is a federal responsibility, the regulation of food produced within a province is primarily a provincial one.

WATCH | Why interprovincial trade barriers are tough to remove: Why are provincial trade barriers still a thing? | Duration 7:10 More interprovincial trade is being touted as one potential countermeasure to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariff threats, but complicated barriers stand in the way. CBC’s Ellen Mauro breaks down why free trade within Canada is so difficult and what needs to happen to get more goods flowing across the country.

That means food producers or food product processors that are provincially inspected can't move product outside their home province unless they undergo federal inspection.

That can be costly for small businesses, Yoo said.

"It can range from tens of thousands of dollars just to get a licence, but it can be even more when we're thinking about all the upgrades that they have to make to their equipment just so they can fit federal standards, even though there's no problem with provincially inspected food," she said.

"Small businesses just don't have the money to do that, so that's a big visible barrier."

Labour movement

Depending on the profession, different provincial certification standards can make it harder for workers to transfer skills and take advantage of new job opportunities in another part of the country.

For example, in some jurisdictions, dental hygienists give injections for dental freezing, while in others that task is outside the scope of their role, meaning dental hygienists may require additional training if they move provinces.

Psychologists and nurses may also require additional coursework in order to practise in another part of the country.

While trade of goods may be more visible, barriers to job transfes have a much bigger impact on the economy because it can lead to labour supply issues if it's too expensive and cumbersome for people to take opportunities in provinces where their services are needed, said Charles De Land, vice-president of research at the Canada West Foundation, a Calgary-based think-tank focused on issues impacting the country's western provinces.

"You end up with mismatches of labour supply and demand and potentially … not having the labour available where you need it and also making costs higher for people to actually transfer and move," he said.

"And if it takes a long time to get recertified in a particular province, that doesn't help them and that doesn't help the labour market that they're working in."

Trucking rules

Different rules between provinces around highway standards, the size of vehicles and when trucks can be driven have been creating headaches for the trucking industry for years.

In B.C., certain types of trucks can only be driven at night , but in Alberta, they can only be driven during the day. That leaves truckers only a small window of time when they can cross provincial borders.

WATCH | Trucking companies face interprovincial issues in daily dealings : Prairie trucking companies face interprovincial issues in daily dealings | Duration 2:38 The Manitoba Trucking Association says businesses in the industry continue to grapple with interprovincial issues every day, despite a national conversation on alleviating barriers in light of American tariffs. One company on the Manitoba-Saskatchewan border says navigating two sets of provincial rules adds administrative burdens to its daily operations.

Last year, a gravel and trucking company on the Manitoba-Saskatchewan border spoke out about the headaches of having to navigate two sets of provincial rules, including on where they can transport gravel and when their vehicles need to be safetied.

However, earlier this year federal, provincial and territorial transportation ministers signed a memorandum of understanding aimed at streamlining commercial transport across Canada and alleviating some of these headaches.

World.title: Nursing home booze ban inspires Minnesota woman to fight for her right to party
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Interview with Anita LeBrun: As It Happens 6:32 Minnesota grandmother wins law change allowing nursing home to serve booze

Anita LeBrun can soon — legally — enjoy a nice glass of pinot grigio served at her assisted living facility. She's earned it, given LeBrun is the reason nursing homes in Minnesota can now serve booze.

"It's just kind of fun when you say, 'Well, today's happy hour,' and with a drink, it just makes it all the better," the 82-year-old grandmother of five told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.

LeBrun testified in front of Minnesota lawmakers twice, arguing that laws that prevented assisted living facilities from serving drinks were unreasonable and should be changed.

And those lawmakers agreed, passing what has been coined the "Grandparents' Happy Hour" bill, allowing facilities to serve alcohol to residents and guests at special events without a licence, as long as they notify the state ahead of time.

To celebrate, Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz even visited LeBrun's assisted living facility, where the two enjoyed a toast following a ceremonial signing of the bill.

"Growing older shouldn't mean giving up the freedoms you've enjoyed your whole life," said Walz in a Facebook post.

Walz, centre, performs the ceremonial signing of the bill while Lebrun, left, watches. (Submitted by Amira Choice Champlin)

Broken booze rules

LeBrun first decided to challenge state legislation after Amira Choice Champlin, the assisted living facility where she lives in Champlin, Minn., was told by local officials that it had broken the rules at an event in April of 2025.

The facility had just finished some renovations, and was going to have a toast with some champagne. But staff were told by the Champlin Police Department that was not allowed.

And that wasn't all. Previously, the facility had served its residents drinks on Tuesdays and Fridays, with a limit of two per person. But the facility was told that also wasn't allowed. Happy hour was over.

It wasn't that alcohol was strictly forbidden. LeBrun and her fellow residents were welcome to partake in their own rooms, with their own booze, and bring a drink to a community event. But with no liquor license, having drinks served by the facility was strictly off limits.

LeBrun spoke in front of state lawmakers twice, arguing for a change to the restriction. (MNHouseInfo/YouTube)

LeBrun would actually purchase wine to share with others, as her two daughters would offer to stop at the liquor store before they came for visits (though someone else had to take care of the beer, she says).

But she says most residents don't have cars, so purchasing their own booze isn't easy. You can take the bus, but LeBrun says it can be hard to get out some days.

"And in the snow, you know Minneapolis is pretty chilly in the winter with lots of snow and ice, so that's very hard too," said LeBrun. "It's hard to bring boxes of wine on the bus."

'Happy hour at the place where we call home'

In testimony, facility executive director Abigail Dahl told lawmakers that getting a permit would bring a lot of cost and red tape, and the permit just didn't fit the facility's situation.

"Assisted living and nursing home dining operations are already operating under a comprehensive public health regulatory framework designed to prevent foodborne illness and protect residents," said Dahl.

"Requiring a liquor license is simply red tape without value. It's duplicative, not protective."

LeBrun says she was nervous to testify before the state legislature. She had never done anything like that before.

So, with her daughters' help, she would practice in front of the mirror.

"Just because we are older, and living in assisted living, doesn't mean we should have fewer freedoms than anyone else," she told the state legislature.

"This amendment is simply putting into law what many people assume is already allowed: happy hour at the place where we call home."

In April the bill was passed with a vote of 129 to one. It was then signed into law by Gov. Walz in July.

LeBrun said she was nervous to speak in front of state lawmakers, but encouragement from her daughters and some prep work in front of a mirror got her through. (Submitted by Amira Choice Champlin)

"This was never just about serving alcohol," said Sara Luehmann, float executive director of Ebenezer, which operates senior housing in the U.S.

"It was about preserving our residents' independence, dignity, and the right to make their own choices … Challenging this restriction was about recognizing that autonomy doesn't end with age, it should be respected and protected throughout every stage of life."

The bill will take effect in August, meaning licensed facilities will be able to serve liquor. And in August, Amira Choice Champlin will be taking advantage of that.

It will be hosting an all-day party to celebrate the new legislation. There will be an Elvis impersonator, live music, all-day food, and — of course — booze.

"After you have just a little glass of wine, you can talk to people, reminisce, and everybody's just more relaxed," said LeBrun.

World.title: Waymo’s driverless cars involved in 68% fewer crashes than human drivers, U.S. study finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Waymo driverless cars were involved in 68 per cent fewer crashes than human drivers over a three-year period across four U.S. cities, according to new data from the U.S. Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.

There were 89 police-reportable Waymo-involved crashes in San Francisco, Phoenix, Los Angeles and Austin between 2021 and 2024, the study released Thursday says.

There were 901,525 police-reported human-caused and involved crashes in that same period, in the same places, excluding on interstates and highways.

"It's sort of the dream we've had as researchers for the last 10 to 20 years to see this technology actually be practised in the real world in a way that's significant," said Steven Waslander, director of the University of Toronto Robotics Institute, who was not involved in the study.

Of the 89 Waymo-involved crashes, 72 per cent took place while the involved Waymo was completely driverless. About half had passenger occupants at the time.

The numbers translate to about 80 million kilometres of driverless Waymo operation, compared with 355 billion kilometres by human drivers in the same places over that three-year period, the study said.

WATCH | Waymo robotaxis now way safer than human drivers: report: Waymo robotaxis now way safer than human drivers: report | Duration 2:05 Google's Waymo robotaxis now cause far fewer, and less serious, accidents than human drivers in four major U.S. cities, according to a new report that also calls for better monitoring of self-driving vehicle fleets.

The research was ultimately quantified in terms of crashes per million vehicle miles travelled. In total, human drivers had a crash rate of 4.06 crashes per million vehicle miles travelled, and Waymo vehicles sat at 1.28 crashes per million vehicle miles travelled, leaving Waymo 68 per cent lower in its rate.

The independent study of Alphabet’s driverless vehicles used data collected from police and Waymo, as well as from federal databases.

According to the U.S. Department of Transportation , crashes involving autonomous vehicles must be reported if automated driving systems were used "within 30 seconds of the crash and the crash resulted in certain property damage or injury."

Waymo is operational in 11 U.S. states and has plans to expand to the United Kingdom and Japan. It has also been lobbying to get programs up and running in Canada.

A Waymo driverless vehicle sits at Bronx Community College in the Bronx borough of New York City on Oct. 16. (Shannon Stapleton/Reuters)

‘Promising’ for the driverless industry

The types of crashes are important to consider when looking at the data, Eric Teoh, director of statistical services at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, told CBC News in an interview.

Teoh sees the study results offering a positive outlook on the future of driverless vehicles, particularly with Waymo's vehicles being involved less often than human-driven vehicles in crashes causing injuries or fatalities.

"In addition to being less frequent, they are also the less egregious types of crash. They're not rear-ending people. They're not getting into head-on crashes as much," he said.

"These results are promising for Waymo, for the driverless industry in general."

Be that as it may, Waymo only reports its data voluntarily, and Teoh said governments in the U.S. should make datasets more readily available and easier to understand.

For Canadians, however, they may not be riding without a driver any time soon. Waymo has had little success breaking into Canadian markets with its lobbying, although it has registered for the Automated Vehicle Pilot Program in Ontario.

In an email, Braman Thillainathan, a spokesperson for Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow, said "the mayor’s priority is protecting jobs in Toronto," and added that Waymo must demonstrate that its vehicles will "not put people out of work or undermine workers’ livelihoods."

B.C. laws prohibit the class of autonomous vehicles that Waymo falls under

Experts point out climate is another hurdle when thinking about expansion into Canada.

A Waymo driverless vehicle navigates a street in Los Angeles on March 18. (Mike Blake/Reuters)

‘We have our winters’

"We have a fairly significantly different climate [in Canada] from what's happening down in the U.S., where they started originally," Waslander said. "We have our winters, we have difficult driving in those scenes."

Although the driverless collision rates may seem low in comparison to those of human drivers, instances of technical difficulties have gone viral on social media.

Moments like a Waymo driving into a flooded roadway or stopping in the path of a tram end up in compilations with millions of views , drawing skepticism about data suggesting they’re on the cutting edge.

"Waymo's produced evidence in this regard before … there's always been a certain amount of healthy skepticism of whether this could be trusted, whether they had their thumb on the scale in some way," Andrew Miller, author of The End of Driving, a textbook about the future of automated driving in cities, said in an interview.

The vehicles are still learning, too, Miller said.

"For instance, they would know what a stop sign looks like, but they're confused when it's a stop sign that is being held by construction worker."

Miller said these vehicles won't be taking over just yet.

"By 2030, it could be that most people in the downtown core have got an app on their phone they can use to summon a driverless ride-hail vehicle. I don't think it'll be bigger than that."

World.title: Tornado warnings are rising faster than actual tornadoes. Is that a good thing?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If you feel like you've been inundated with tornado warnings this year, it's not just you.

Canada is not only on track for a potentially record-setting tornado year, but warnings from Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) are outpacing the twisters.

The federal weather agency says it had sent out 124 warnings across the country by July 22, at which point it said 74 tornadoes had actually touched down.

By comparison, ECCC issued 107 warnings all of last year and recorded 116 tornadoes touching down. In 2024, the agency issued 100 warnings and logged 132 tornadoes.

The agency provided CBC News with data going back to 2017, and this year has already seen by far the most alerts.

ECCC's tornado warnings have increased significantly over the past 10 years. In 2018, for example, just 34 warnings were issued and 105 touched down.

A spokesperson said in an email the number of warnings could sometimes fall below the number of tornadoes touching down "even if they were perfectly forecasted," because several tornadoes can form in one group, but the forecaster may only send out a single warning for the affected region.

ECCC did not provide further comment on the numbers by deadline.

'You can't be dithering'

The uptick is good news to David Sills, director of Western University's Northern Tornadoes Project (NTP) in London, Ont., which tracks tornadoes across the country and sends teams out to survey damages.

"Certainly there can be false alarms when you send out those warnings, but that's the choice: either you're increasing the number and having a bit more false alarms, or you're just missing tornadoes," Sills said.

NTP issued a failing "report card" for ECCC's warning system in 2022, based on data from 2019 to 2021 that found the agency was missing twisters and was behind target on its warnings both in terms of frequency and timing.

"I know that's hard for a lot forecasters. They don't want to have false alarms," Sills said. "But if you want to get lead time with these things, you have to make quick decisions.… You can't be dithering about making a decision on a tornado warning."

He says this year has been his team's busiest since the project launched in 2017, with numbers on track for a record high across Canada. NTP has tracked 83 tornadoes so far in 2026, with 70 of those touching down in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.

Concerns of 'warning fatigue'

But Greg Johnson, a storm chaser based in Regina, is less impressed by all the warnings.

"I've seen storms that have no chance of producing a tornado. And I'm getting a thing on my phone and I'm literally standing looking at the thing and going, there is no way that this should be tornado-warned," he said.

Johnson says part of the problem is the warnings are broadcast over such wide regions they go out to people who, in some cases, are so far away from the storm they can't even see it.

He worries people will get "warning fatigue" from too many alerts for storms that don't actually put them in danger.

WATCH | What's behind the higher tornado count: Canada on track for historic tornado season | Duration 2:11 There have already been 83 confirmed tornadoes in Canada this season, with 70 of them in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. This is partly due to the summer’s weather but Environment Canada says it’s also because of improved tracking efforts.

"If you're getting warnings every day and you're not seeing any tornadoes, next time the warning comes, you go, 'Damn, well, I'm not gonna change what I'm doing just because of this dumb warning, because I get these every day,'" he said.

Johnson says he understands forecasters don't want to miss a tornado, but there should be a "happy medium."

Forecasting a challenge: ECCC

Meteorologists rely on computer modelling and Doppler radars to track and forecast storms.

An Environment Canada spokesperson said tornadoes are challenging to predict, as only 20 per cent of severe thunderstorms form tornadoes and instead of detecting most tornadoes directly, radar is used to examine the structure of the thunderstorm and wind patterns to see whether the right conditions exist for a tornado.

Experts told CBC News that forecasting is more precise in the U.S., where there are more tornadoes, denser populations and more forecasters looking at radar systems.

Peter Kimbell, a warning preparedness meteorologist with ECCC, told CBC's Ottawa Morning that improvements to the current system are in the works.

ECCC forecasters in Toronto are responsible for deciding when to transmit tornado warnings through Canada's Alert Ready system, and Kimbell said the technology can sometimes be slow to catch up — sometimes causing forecasters to issue warnings to an area that's wider than the immediate danger zone.

"So maybe there’s a bit of an overwarning going on now, but 20, 30, 40 years ago, we weren’t even able to do that at all, and so the risk was that no one really got the warning," he said.

World.title: 'A subtle mistake': How a single underscore led to an innocent Halifax man's conviction
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Halifax man who spent 18 months in jail for child luring and possession of child pornography after an investigative mix-up between two nearly identical online usernames has been acquitted on all charges on appeal.

The error leading to Brandon Klayme's conviction came down to the difference between one underscore — a keyboard symbol used in email addresses or usernames to represent a space — and two, said Nova Scotia's top court in a decision released Thursday.

"If the correct username had been used at the start of the investigation, the subsequent steps in the investigation would not have led to Mr. Klayme," wrote the three-member appeal panel.

Halifax Regional Police arrested Klayme in February 2020 in relation to an investigation by police in Wisconsin into sexual conversations, video calls and the exchange of intimate images between a 12-year-old girl and a man on the messaging platform Kik.

A case of 2 usernames

The man went by the username fus__ro_dah, with two underscores between "fus" and "ro," the decision said.

But when U.S. authorities tried to track down the email and IP addresses connected to the man's account, they mistakenly retrieved the information belonging to Klayme, who had an almost in distinguishable username, save for one key detail: fus_ro_dah, with just one underscore between "fus" and "ro."

While t he girl had described to police the physical features of the man with whom she had been communicating, court documents said investigators were unable to conduct a detailed interview with her because she was receiving medical care due to a deep depression.

"The Wisconsin police identified Mr. Klayme as the offender using the incorrect username. His conviction rested on the internet username being attributed to him,” the appeal panel wrote.

Klayme was found guilty of child luring, making sexually explicit content available to a minor and possession of child pornography following an April 2023 trial in Dartmouth provincial court. He was sentenced to 18 months in jail followed by 18 months probation.

A subtle mistake that changed the course of my life - Brandon Klayme

The Appeal Court decision said no evidence was found linking Klayme to the girl, the Kik conversations, or the intimate images.

It wasn’t until earlier this year that Klayme’s legal team discovered the username discrepancy.

Klayme had denied 'any involvement'

“We noticed the problem when we were working on the appeal arguments this spring,” wrote Klayme’s defence lawyer, Zeb Brown, in an email to CBC News.

“We were trying to figure out why the digital forensic evidence pointed at him given his denial of any involvement.”

In an affidavit submitted for the appeal, Klayme said the subpoena by Wisconsin police “contained a subtle mistake that changed the course of my life.”

In addition to an acquittal entered on the charges, the sentence and ancillary orders against Klayme were vacated.

"This is not a situation where an acquittal is entered because the Crown has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt the essential elements of an offence or an error during the trial made the verdict unsafe," the appeal panel wrote.

"In these circumstances, Mr. Klayme is factually innocent of the offences. He should never have been charged, let alone convicted."

The correct username likely would have identified someone in California, according to the decision.

World.title: Parks Canada charges hikers after grizzly bear run-in with off-leash dog in Banff National Park
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A pair of hikers with an off-leash dog were charged after coming close to a well-known grizzly bear on a popular hiking trail in Banff National Park.

Parks Canada charged them after a social media video on TikTok generated several million views since being posted July 21. The video, recorded by a woman, shows a man with bear spray and a small off-leash dog running between the two of them as grizzly bear No. 142 walks toward them on the trail.

James Eastham, a spokesperson for Parks Canada’s Lake Louise, Yoho and Kootenay field unit, said an investigation by park wardens led to charges since the dog was off-leash.

“Failure to keep your pets leashed in the national parks poses risks to pets and wildlife,” he said in an email. “Bears and other wildlife may react aggressively toward dogs they view as threats, resulting in their injury or death.”

The law says people have to keep their pets on a leash of three metres or less in national parks. If found guilty, the two could face a fine of up to $25,000.

WATCH | 2 hikers and dog encounter grizzly bear in Banff National Park: 2 hikers and dog encounter grizzly bear in Banff National Park | Duration 0:14 A clip of a video posted to the TikTok account twohumanstwodogs shows a close grizzly bear encounter on a hiking trail in Banff National Park. Parks Canada has charged the two hikers because their dog was off-leash.

The incident took place on Taylor Lake trail, about 15 kilometres southeast of Lake Louise.

CBC reached out to the two people charged, but didn’t hear back before publishing the story.

Staying safe with wildlife

In the roughly 90-second video, the man is heard yelling at bear 142 to “back off” and “get out of here” several times.

Bear 142 walks along the trail until she moves into the woods at the end of the video.

Nick de Ruyter, program director of WildSmart for the Biosphere Institute of the Bow Valley, said it was good the pair had bear spray, but the focus should be on the animal rather than filming.

“The safety of them, their pets and other people is far more important than getting that video,” he said.

He praised Parks Canada for moving ahead with charges since “there was so much time in the video to grab the dog and put it on a leash.”

De Ruyter focuses on public education, but “after that, there needs to be some type of enforcement.”

“It’s not just ‘I’m going to take a quick selfie.’ There are consequences to those actions, and it will affect the wildlife.”

Parks Canada advises people encountering wildlife in the national park can happen at any time.

It recommends people make noise to avoid surprising wildlife, watch for signs such as tracks and scat, travel in larger groups, keep a distance from animals, and carry bear spray.

“Off-leash dogs can also cause wildlife stress, leading to them avoiding important habitats and sources of food,” Eastham said. “Always keep your pets on leash when visiting national parks.”

LISTEN | Bear activity is ramping up in the Rockies: Calgary Eyeopener 8:40 Bear activity is ramping up in the Rockies Politicians aren't the only ones in Kananaskis causing a raucous. What you need to know when encountering a bear, from Nick de Ruyter, WildSmart Program Director with the Biosphere Institute of the Bow Valley.

Bear well-known to Parks Canada

Bear 142 is one of Banff’s most famous grizzly bears.

The female grizzly is the daughter of bear 122 — also known as The Boss — and is estimated to be about 16 years old.

She has had several cubs in the national park. In 2020, bear 136 — known as Split Lip — killed and ate one of her cubs.

Bear 142 lost another cub earlier this year when it was hit and killed by a train near Protection Mountain campground close to the Bow Valley Parkway.

According to an access to information document obtained by CBC, it’s believed there were about 71 grizzly bears in Banff National Park between 2021 and 2023.

They’re a threatened species in Alberta, and the federal government considers them a species of special concern.
