Goldman Argentina forecast: What Triggered the Downgrade

Goldman Sachs pointed directly to Argentina’s official monthly economic activity estimator, known locally as the EMAE. The April and May readings came in softer than analysts had projected, signaling a loss of momentum after a strong start to the year.

The bank described the expected short-term pattern as a second-quarter contraction, characterizing it as a payback effect following robust first-quarter performance. Despite the softer patch, Goldman maintained that the country remains on the “right path” macroeconomically, though it stressed that the margin for error is now extremely narrow.

Inflation and Policy Constraints

On the price front, Goldman Sachs did not alter its broad disinflation thesis. The bank’s report still pencils in an inflation rate of around 29% for 2026, anticipating a gradual cooling from the triple-digit annual rates that have battered household purchasing power in recent years.

However, the report flagged significant external vulnerabilities. Analysts highlighted peso and exchange-rate pressure as a key risk, noting that Argentina’s limited stock of net foreign reserves leaves policymakers with little room to absorb shocks.

No new specific peso forecast or reserve target figure was provided in the available summary of the report.

The combination of a crawling peg exchange-rate system and stubborn inflation has kept the local currency under constant scrutiny. For international investors, the real effective exchange rate remains a critical metric, and any misalignment could quickly erode the competitiveness gains touted by the administration.

Political Calendar Looms

Beyond the immediate data fluctuations, Goldman Sachs identified the 2027 presidential election as the major structural challenge. The bank argued that sustaining the current recovery and the disinflation process through a heated political cycle will test the government’s resolve.

Political and social challenges remain significant, the report noted. In Argentina’s high-stakes electoral environment, the temptation to loosen fiscal discipline or delay utility tariff adjustments often grows as voting day approaches.

For foreign holders of Argentine sovereign bonds – which have rallied sharply from distressed levels – the political trajectory is as important as the monthly EMAE print.

Context for Foreign Investors

For expatriates and global investors tracking Latin America, the 0.3-percentage-point cut is a signal to moderate near-term expectations without abandoning the broader recovery narrative. Argentina’s economy has been climbing from a deep contraction, and even a 2.7% expansion would mark a significant turnaround from the recession that defined previous years.

The revision places Goldman’s outlook slightly below the consensus among international financial institutions. The International Monetary Fund and other multilateral lenders have also been monitoring Argentina’s performance closely, with the country operating under a multi-billion-dollar program designed to bolster reserves and anchor fiscal accounts.

The U.S. dollar remains the primary reference currency for hard-currency debt and major transactions. At the prevailing parallel exchange rate of approximately 1,320 pesos per US dollar, the purchasing power of foreign capital in Argentina’s real economy is substantial, though capital controls still complicate the repatriation of profits.

Market Reaction and Next Steps

Available reporting on the immediate market reaction to the Goldman note was not fully quantified at the time of publication. Argentine bonds and equities have been sensitive to growth revisions in the past, but no clear post-report move in sovereign debt or the Merval equity index could be confirmed from the sources at hand.

Looking ahead, market participants will focus on the next EMAE releases to see whether the second-quarter softness extends into the second half of the year. A swift rebound would validate Goldman’s characterization of the dip as a temporary payback effect, while continued weakness could force further forecast adjustments.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Goldman Sachs cut its Argentina growth forecast?

Goldman Sachs lowered its 2026 GDP growth projection for Argentina from 3.0% to 2.7% because the official monthly economic activity readings (EMAE) for April and May came in weaker than the bank had expected.

What is Goldman Sachs’ inflation forecast for Argentina in 2026?

Goldman Sachs expects inflation in Argentina to continue a gradual downward path and projects an annual rate of around 29% for 2026.

What risks did Goldman Sachs highlight for Argentina’s economy?

The bank warned about a narrow margin for policy error, citing peso and exchange-rate pressure, external fragility from low reserves, and the political challenge of sustaining recovery and disinflation ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

World.title: Argentina Credit Defaults Climb Toward 16% of Borrowers
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts —Household default rate 16.1% of individual borrowers were in default as of May 2026, according to BCRA data. —Overall private-sector NPL ratio Reached 9.7% in May 2026, up from 2.0% in November 2024. —Corporate default rate Companies recorded a much lower delinquency rate of 3.5% in the same period. —People in arrears An estimated 5.8 million Argentines were behind on payments by May 2026. —Main driver Economic weakness and falling real incomes, rather than interest rates alone, fueled the deterioration.

Argentina credit defaults have surged to multi-year highs, with the household delinquency rate climbing toward 16.1% in May 2026, as President Javier Milei’s fiscal adjustment program continues to squeeze family incomes and weaken repayment capacity across the country.

The Obelisco in Buenos Aires; household loan defaults are rising in Argentina. Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Argentina credit defaults: A Fivefold Deterioration in 18 Months

The private-sector non-performing loan (NPL) ratio reached 9.7% in May 2026, according to data from the Banco Central de la República Argentina (BCRA), the country’s central bank. That marks a dramatic increase from just 2.0% in November 2024, roughly a month before Milei took office.

The deterioration has been swift and broad. In April 2026, the BCRA reported the overall private-sector NPL ratio at 7.3%, with household loans already at 12.1% and company loans at 3.3%.

By May, household defaults had jumped further to 16.1%, while corporate arrears edged up to 3.5%.

Local media outlets, including Ámbito and La Nación, have described the figures as a record or near-record deterioration in consumer credit. The gap between household and corporate distress underscores how unevenly the economic adjustment is being felt across Argentine society.

Households Bear the Brunt

The 16.1% default rate among individuals and families means roughly one in every six household borrowers is behind on payments. Local reporting indicates that approximately 5.8 million people were in arrears by May 2026.

The delinquency burden has been especially severe among younger borrowers, who typically have less savings to cushion income shocks. This demographic faces the dual pressure of stagnant wages and limited access to formal employment.

By contrast, companies have weathered the adjustment with comparatively less balance-sheet damage. The corporate default rate of 3.5% suggests firms have been better able to restructure obligations or tap alternative funding sources than ordinary households.

What Is Driving the Surge

Argentine analysts cited in local coverage point to economic weakness and falling real incomes as the primary drivers, rather than interest rates alone. While borrowing costs have remained high, the deeper issue is that households simply have less money to meet their obligations.

The Milei administration’s fiscal adjustment has involved sharp cuts to public spending, subsidy removals, and a deliberate cooling of economic activity to tame inflation. Those measures, while improving fiscal accounts, have depressed consumption and household purchasing power.

Slower economic activity has translated into weaker repayment capacity across the consumer credit spectrum. Credit card debt, personal loans, and overdraft facilities have all seen rising arrears, according to the BCRA’s banking reports.

Risks to Credit-Led Recovery

Rising defaults create a feedback loop that can exclude millions from traditional credit markets. As banks see delinquency rates climb, they tighten lending standards, which in turn constrains consumption and economic growth.

Local reporting warns that the deterioration threatens what could otherwise become an engine of recovery. Without access to credit, households cannot smooth consumption or finance small investments, prolonging the economic downturn.

The Buenos Aires Times noted in an analysis that bad loans threaten Argentina’s next engine of economic growth. If banks pull back further, the credit channel that typically fuels post-crisis rebounds may remain blocked for years.

Has the Peak Passed?

Reuters-style coverage indicates that authorities believed the peak in delinquencies may have occurred around June 2026. If confirmed, that would suggest the worst of the credit deterioration could be easing.

However, no official forward guidance has been issued by the BCRA, and the data for June and July remain unpublished. The trajectory will depend heavily on whether real incomes stabilize and economic activity begins to recover in the second half of the year.

For now, the 16.1% household default rate stands as a stark reminder of the social cost of Argentina’s stabilization program. Foreign investors and expatriates watching the country’s turnaround story will be monitoring whether the credit cycle can normalize without triggering a broader financial strain.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the current household default rate in Argentina?

The household delinquency rate reached 16.1% in May 2026, according to BCRA data, meaning roughly one in six individual borrowers was behind on payments.

How much have Argentina credit defaults increased under President Milei?

The overall private-sector NPL ratio rose from 2.0% in November 2024 to 9.7% in May 2026, a nearly fivefold increase over 18 months.

Why are companies defaulting less than households in Argentina?

The corporate default rate stood at just 3.5% in May 2026, compared to 16.1% for households. Firms have been better able to restructure debt and weather the adjustment, while families face falling real incomes and limited savings.

World.title: Brazilian Telecom TIM Invests in Legal AI Startup Enter
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Enter valuation Enter reached a US$1.2 billion (~R$6.1 billion) valuation in May 2026 after closing a funding round exceeding US$100 million. —Lead investors The round was led by Founders Fund, with participation from Sequoia Capital, Ribbit Capital, Kaszek, Atlantico, and ONEVC. —TIM’s 5G fund TIM Brasil committed US$50 million (~R$255 million) over two years to a 5G innovation fund and deployed US$15 million (~R$77 million) in 2024. —Enter’s core product Enter uses AI agents to analyze lawsuits, identify predatory litigation and fraud, interpret court decisions, and support legal recommendations for corporate clients. —Market context Brazil’s judiciary processed over 80 million cases in 2025, creating massive demand for AI tools that reduce legal costs for large companies.

TIM invests in Enter, a Brazilian artificial intelligence startup that automates corporate legal defense, through a venture capital fund linked to the telecommunications operator’s 5G innovation strategy, according to sources familiar with the matter. The investment connects one of Brazil’s largest mobile carriers to a fast-growing legaltech that reached unicorn status in May 2026.

Software code on a monitor (illustrative); a TIM fund backed legal-AI startup Enter. Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

TIM invests in Enter: Enter’s Meteoric Rise in Legal AI

Enter, headquartered in São Paulo, develops AI agents that manage and defend corporate legal cases, particularly in consumer disputes and labor claims. The platform analyzes incoming lawsuits, flags fraudulent or predatory litigation, interprets judicial decisions, and generates legal recommendations for in-house teams.

In early May 2026, the startup closed a funding round of more than US$100 million (~R$510 million), securing a valuation of US$1.2 billion (~R$6.1 billion). The round was led by San Francisco-based Founders Fund, with participation from Sequoia Capital, Ribbit Capital, and Brazilian venture firms Kaszek, Atlantico, and ONEVC.

The capital injection made Enter one of Brazil’s few AI-native unicorns, a milestone that drew international attention to Latin America’s legal technology sector. Forbes Brasil and O Globo reported the valuation, while Bloomberg Línea highlighted Sequoia’s earlier US$35 million (~R$179 million) Series A commitment.

How TIM’s 5G Fund Connects to the Deal

TIM Brasil, the local subsidiary of Telecom Italia, has been building an innovation investment apparatus separate from its core network operations. In 2024, the company announced a US$50 million (~R$255 million) commitment over two years to a 5G-focused venture fund, deploying an initial US$15 million (~R$77 million) that year.

The fund, structured in partnership with Brazilian innovation platform Upload, targets startups whose technologies can leverage 5G connectivity or align with TIM’s broader digital ecosystem. Legal AI fits that thesis: automated legal workflows demand low-latency data processing and secure cloud infrastructure, both enhanced by advanced mobile networks.

Sources indicate the TIM-linked fund’s investment in Enter occurred as part of the startup’s broader round, though the exact ticket size has not been publicly disclosed. Neither TIM Brasil nor Enter has issued a formal statement confirming the specific allocation.

Why a Telecom Operator Backs Legal AI

At first glance, a mobile carrier investing in legal software appears unconventional. However, Brazilian telecom operators face enormous legal exposure themselves. TIM Brasil and its peers manage tens of thousands of consumer lawsuits annually, from billing disputes to service quality claims.

Enter’s technology directly addresses this pain point. Its AI agents can triage incoming cases, identify patterns in predatory litigation, and reduce the manual hours required for initial legal analysis.

For a company like TIM, deploying such tools internally could cut legal operating costs by double-digit percentages.

Beyond internal use, the investment positions TIM to offer AI-powered legal automation as a value-added service to its enterprise clients. Large corporate customers already contract TIM for connectivity and cloud services; adding legaltech tools deepens those commercial relationships.

Brazil’s Legal Tech Market Opportunity

Brazil’s judiciary is one of the world’s most congested. The National Council of Justice reported over 80 million pending cases in 2025, with consumer and labor disputes accounting for a significant share.

Large corporations routinely maintain legal departments with hundreds of staff just to manage litigation volume.

Enter competes in a growing field of Brazilian legaltechs using artificial intelligence to automate document review, case strategy, and compliance monitoring. The sector attracted record venture capital in 2025 and early 2026, as investors bet that AI can finally streamline a legal system long criticized for inefficiency.

The startup’s focus on identifying predatory litigation resonates with Brazilian businesses. Consumer protection laws and labor regulations create fertile ground for mass claims, some of which are filed by specialized law firms operating at industrial scale.

Enter’s fraud detection algorithms help companies distinguish legitimate claims from abusive ones.

TIM’s Broader Innovation Strategy

The Enter investment fits a pattern of TIM Brasil deploying capital through specialized funds rather than direct corporate venture arms. The 5G fund structure allows the operator to access startup innovation without the overhead of managing a full venture capital operation internally.

TIM has also invested in connectivity-adjacent sectors through this vehicle, including Internet of Things platforms and edge computing startups. The legal AI bet diversifies the portfolio into enterprise software, a sector with recurring revenue models and high customer retention rates.

For foreign investors watching Brazil’s tech ecosystem, the TIM-Enter connection signals that corporate venture capital from non-tech incumbents is becoming a meaningful funding source. Telecom operators, banks, and industrial groups increasingly view AI startups as both strategic assets and financial opportunities.

What Comes Next for Enter

With fresh capital exceeding US$100 million (~R$510 million), Enter plans to expand its AI agent capabilities beyond consumer and labor law into tax litigation and regulatory compliance. The company is also eyeing international markets, particularly Mexico and Colombia, where similar legal system dynamics create demand.

The startup’s investor syndicate now blends Silicon Valley heavyweights Founders Fund and Sequoia with prominent Latin American funds Kaszek and Atlantico. Adding a telecom-linked strategic investor provides Enter with a potential enterprise distribution channel through TIM’s corporate client base.

Whether TIM’s involvement remains a passive fund investment or evolves into a commercial partnership remains to be seen. For now, the deal underscores how artificial intelligence is redrawing the boundaries between industries that once had little overlap.

Did TIM Brasil directly invest in Enter?

No direct investment by TIM Brasil has been publicly confirmed. The investment was made through a 5G innovation fund linked to TIM and managed in partnership with Upload, a Brazilian innovation platform.

What does Enter’s AI legal technology actually do?

Enter’s AI agents analyze incoming lawsuits, detect fraudulent or predatory litigation patterns, interpret court decisions, and generate legal recommendations. The platform focuses on consumer disputes and labor claims for corporate clients.

How much is Enter worth after its latest funding round?

Enter reached a valuation of US$1.2 billion (~R$6.1 billion) in May 2026 after closing a funding round of more than US$100 million (~R$510 million) led by Founders Fund.

World.title: Valle Nevado Record Snow Powers Chile Ski Comeback

Chile · Travel

Valle Nevado record snow accumulations are driving a long-awaited revival at Chile’s premier Andean ski resorts this season, as early storms delivered the most promising base in years and rekindled international demand for Southern Hemisphere skiing.

A ski resort in winter (illustrative); Chile’s central Andes saw exceptional 2026 snowfall. Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA.

Valle Nevado record snow: A Season of Renewal After Years of Drought

Chile’s central Andes are finally shaking off the grip of a punishing multi-year drought that had left slopes bare and chairlifts idle. The 2026 winter season opened with a series of early storms that blanketed the high-altitude resorts east of Santiago, restoring a landscape that had grown increasingly rocky and brown.

Valle Nevado, sitting at 3,000 meters above sea level, reported 32 centimeters of total snow for the year by early July. While late-July conditions showed a temporary lull with no fresh snowfall over a seven-day period, the accumulated base was enough to sustain operations across core terrain.

Neighboring La Parva, a favorite among well-heeled Chilean families and second-home owners, also benefited from the early pulse of moisture. The resort’s base held firm even as daily snow reports later showed zero fresh accumulation, a pattern typical of the region’s boom-and-bust storm cycles.

What the Snow Reports Actually Show

Independent snow-tracking services paint a nuanced picture of the 2026 season. Data from Snowsure.ai and J2Ski captured modest depths at La Parva, with readings of 10 centimeters on the mountain and a 5-centimeter base in some snapshots. Valle Nevado’s upper and lower snow depths fluctuated, with some reports showing 0 centimeters at lower elevations.

These figures do not contradict the narrative of a comeback; they underscore how the Andes rely on intense, episodic storms rather than steady accumulation. The critical difference in 2026 is that the storms arrived early enough to allow resorts to open substantial terrain by mid-July, a milestone missed in several recent drought years.

Ski industry analysts caution against reading too much into a single data point. Snow-forecast.com historical records show that Valle Nevado’s season typically peaks in August, meaning the 32-centimeter July figure represents a foundation, not a ceiling. Resort operators remain confident that the pattern of early storms sets the stage for a robust second half.

The Foreign Skier Factor

International visitors are the economic lifeblood of Chile’s ski industry. Before the drought, roughly 60% of Valle Nevado’s guests came from abroad, with Brazilians making up the single largest foreign contingent. North Americans and Europeans seeking off-season turns in July and August formed another critical segment.

The resort’s partial opening announcement earlier this year, covered by outlets like Freeskier, signaled to that global audience that Chile was back in play. Tour operators such as PowderQuest, which specialize in South American ski trips, began marketing Valle Nevado itineraries aggressively once the early snow totals became clear.

For foreign investors and expats based in Santiago, the ski resurgence carries symbolic weight. The three interconnected resorts – Valle Nevado, La Parva, and El Colorado – form the largest skiable domain in the Southern Hemisphere. Their health is a bellwether for the capital’s quality-of-life appeal and for the broader tourism economy.

Economic Stakes and Investment Outlook

A full-length ski season across Chile’s Andean resorts generates an estimated US$150 million to US$200 million in combined direct and indirect economic activity. That figure includes lift-ticket sales, hotel bookings, restaurant revenue, equipment rentals, and transportation services stretching from Santiago’s international airport to the mountain access roads.

The drought years slashed those numbers dramatically. Hotels in the ski corridor reported occupancy rates below 30% during what should have been peak weeks. Seasonal workers, many from rural communities, lost months of income. The 2026 rebound, even if not yet record-breaking by historical standards, restores a vital employment engine.

Real estate markets in the mountain towns of Farellones and Lo Barnechea are also sensitive to snow conditions. La Parva’s collection of slope-side apartments and chalets sees transaction volumes rise and fall with the quality of the ski season. Early 2026 inquiries from foreign buyers, particularly Brazilians seeking mountain retreats, have ticked upward, local brokers report.

Looking Ahead: August and Beyond

The Southern Hemisphere ski season runs through late September, with August traditionally delivering the deepest snowpack. Long-range forecasts cited by Powder.com earlier this year suggested that a La Niña pattern could bring above-average precipitation to the central Chilean Andes, though meteorologists urge caution with seasonal predictions.

Valle Nevado’s season-pass sales provide another indicator of confidence. The resort’s early-bird pricing, denominated in Chilean pesos but roughly equivalent to US$750 (~CLP 697,500) for an adult unlimited pass, sold at a faster clip than in 2025, according to industry sources who track the market.

For now, the images of white ridges above Santiago have restored a sense of normalcy. Skiers are carving turns on the same slopes that sat barren a year ago. The comeback is not yet complete, but the foundation – measured in those 32 centimeters and the storms that built them – is the strongest in half a decade.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Valle Nevado experiencing record snowfall in 2026?

Available snow reports from early July 2026 show 315 cm of total snow at 3,000 m, a strong start compared to recent drought years. However, independent data does not confirm an all-time record; late-July conditions included a dry spell with no fresh accumulation over seven days.

How does La Parva’s snow compare to Valle Nevado’s this season?

La Parva also benefited from early storms that built a solid base. By late July, its official report showed 0 cm of fresh snow over the prior week, but the mountain remained open with coverage supported by earlier accumulations.

Why are Chile’s ski resorts important for foreign visitors?

Chile’s Andean resorts, led by Valle Nevado, are the largest ski areas in the Southern Hemisphere. They attract thousands of international skiers – especially Brazilians, North Americans, and Europeans – seeking winter sports during the Northern Hemisphere summer months.

World.title: US Tariff Hike Puts $5 Billion of Colombia Exports at Risk
World.content:
Colombia · Trade

Key Facts —Tariff rate The U.S. raised its additional tariff on covered Colombian goods from 10% to 12.5%, effective 24 July 2026. —Export value at risk ANDI estimates roughly US$5 billion of Colombian exports are exposed to the new tariff measure. —Affected share About 30% of Colombia’s shipments to the U.S. are affected, while 68%-73% of the export basket remains exempt. —Exposed sectors Flowers, some apparel and textiles, candies, processed foods, cosmetics, plastic manufactures, and electrical equipment face the tariff. —Exempt goods Strategic exports such as coffee, bananas, oil, and coal are not covered by the additional surcharge.

Colombia US tariff exports face a sharp new threat after the United States raised an additional duty on Colombian goods to 12.5 percent, a move that the country’s main business federation ANDI warns puts roughly US$5 billion in annual shipments at risk.

The commercial port of Cartagena, Colombia; exporters face new US tariffs. Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Colombia US tariff: A Sudden Hike on Key Colombian Goods

The U.S. measure took effect at 12:01 a.m. on 24 July 2026, lifting the supplementary tariff from a temporary 10 percent to 12.5 percent for a defined set of Colombian products. The new rate applies to merchandise entered for consumption or withdrawn from storage on or after that date, replacing the prior surcharge rather than stacking on top of it.

Colombia’s National Business Association (ANDI) reacted in late July, calculating that roughly 30 percent of the country’s exports to the United States would be hit. That translates to about US$5 billion in goods suddenly facing a steeper cost barrier in their most important foreign market.

The tariff hike is tied to forced-labor compliance concerns under a U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) decision, keeping the measure in force while Colombian authorities review its impact. An exception was carved out for goods already in transit, provided they were loaded before the deadline and cleared U.S. customs by 28 July 2026.

Which Sectors Are Exposed

The affected basket is concentrated in specific non-traditional export sectors. Flowers, a flagship Colombian export and a mainstay of the Valentine’s Day and Mother’s Day supply chain in the United States, are squarely in the line of fire.

Other exposed categories include some apparel and textiles, candies and chocolates, processed foods not covered by exemptions, cosmetics and personal-care products, plastic manufactures, and certain electrical equipment and transformers. Reuters-linked coverage also highlighted clothing and manufactured goods as targets.

María Claudia Lacouture, speaking for the American Chamber of Commerce and the broader business community in Colombian media, noted that the blow is concentrated in a narrower set of goods rather than the entire export basket. This means the pain is deep but not universal across Colombia’s trade relationship with the U.S.

What Stays Exempt

Crucially, the tariff does not touch Colombia’s traditional commodity exports. Coffee, bananas, oil, and coal remain outside the scope of the additional surcharge.

These goods account for a dominant share of the 68 to 73 percent of the export basket that ANDI says remains exempt.

That exemption shields the backbone of Colombia’s mining and agricultural trade from immediate disruption. However, it also underscores a structural risk: the country’s efforts to diversify exports beyond raw materials are precisely where the new tariff bites hardest.

For foreign investors and expats watching Colombia’s trade profile, the split between exempt commodities and targeted value-added goods signals where future volatility may concentrate. Processed foods, specialty flowers, and light manufacturing now face a competitive disadvantage in the U.S. market.

Competitiveness Concerns and Business Reaction

ANDI and export-sector voices have warned that Colombia is now at a disadvantage compared to competitors facing lower or no surcharges in the U.S. market. The federation urged an official government response, arguing that the tariff directly hurts the competitiveness of the affected products.

The concern is not merely theoretical. A 12.5 percent surcharge can erase thin margins in sectors like fresh-cut flowers or processed candies, where buyers may quickly switch to suppliers from countries not facing the same penalty.

Ecuadorian flowers or Mexican confectionery, for instance, could gain ground.

Colombian authorities were reported to be moving to review the impact and seek mitigation measures. But with the USTR tying the tariff to forced-labor compliance, any relief likely hinges on diplomatic negotiations and demonstrable policy changes, a process that could take months or longer.

What Comes Next for Bilateral Trade

The tariff escalation adds a layer of uncertainty to a trade relationship that has long been Colombia’s most important bilateral economic link. The United States absorbs a large share of Colombian exports, and any sustained friction risks reshaping investment flows and supply-chain decisions.

For expats and international businesses operating in Colombia, the immediate effect may be felt in export-oriented regions such as Antioquia, the Bogotá savanna flower belt, and the Atlantic coast’s manufacturing zones. Companies in the exposed sectors may delay hiring or capital expenditure until the trade outlook clears.

The in-transit grace period offered a brief window for shipments already on the water, but new orders now face the full 12.5 percent surcharge. Trade analysts will watch closely whether Colombia can negotiate a rollback or whether the higher tariff becomes a lasting feature of the bilateral trade landscape.

A Broader Context for Foreign Observers

For foreign readers following Latin America, the Colombia case fits a wider pattern of U.S. tariff actions tied to labor and compliance standards. The measure is not a blanket tariff but a targeted surcharge, making the list of affected goods a critical document for anyone involved in cross-border trade.

The fact that coffee and oil remain untouched provides some reassurance to commodity-focused investors. However, the exposure of value-added goods highlights a vulnerability in Colombia’s economic diversification strategy, a theme that resonates across emerging markets seeking to move up the value chain.

As ANDI continues to press for a government response, the episode serves as a reminder that trade policy can shift quickly. Foreign companies with supply chains touching Colombia should review their product classifications against the updated U.S. tariff schedule and monitor diplomatic channels for any breakthrough.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the new U.S. tariff rate on Colombian goods?

The additional tariff rose from 10% to 12.5% on 24 July 2026, applying to a specific set of Colombian products tied to forced-labor compliance concerns under a USTR decision.

Which Colombian exports are affected by the tariff?

Affected sectors include flowers, some apparel and textiles, candies and chocolates, certain processed foods, cosmetics, plastic manufactures, and some electrical equipment. Coffee, bananas, oil, and coal are exempt.

How much Colombian export value is at risk?

ANDI estimates roughly US$5 billion in exports is at risk, representing about 30% of Colombia’s shipments to the United States.

World.title: Costa Rican Stabbed in Manhattan Attack Investigated as Possible Hate Crime
World.content:
A Costa Rican citizen is among two men stabbed Thursday afternoon in a pair of attacks on Manhattan’s Upper West Side that New York police are investigating as a possible hate crime, Costa Rica’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed.

The Costa Rican, a 50-year-old man, was stabbed in the chest with a screwdriver near the corner of West 86th Street and Amsterdam Avenue shortly after 1:30 p.m., according to the New York Police Department. A short time earlier and roughly two blocks south, near West 84th Street and Central Park West, a 57-year-old man was stabbed in the back with a knife. Both men were taken to Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital in stable condition, and police said both are expected to survive.

In a statement posted to social media, Costa Rica’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Worship condemned the attack in the strongest terms, describing it as apparently motivated by ethnic and religious hatred and saying its citizen had been wounded because of his faith. The ministry expressed solidarity with everyone affected, singling out the injured compatriot and his family, and reiterated our country’s rejection of all forms of hatred, intolerance and violence.

It said it was providing support and consular assistance to the man, who according to the information available to authorities was in stable condition, and that it was monitoring the case through Costa Rica’s consular representation in the United States. Local reports indicated the man had been wearing a kipá, the head covering worn by observant Jewish men, and had recently attended observances for Tisha B’Av, a Jewish day of mourning, at a nearby center.

The New York Police Department arrested a 51-year-old man, whom it identified as Raúl Morales, in connection with both attacks. Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said victim and witness accounts indicated the suspect shouted “Allahu Akbar” during the assaults. Tisch said the department was evaluating whether the incidents amounted to a hate crime and noted that, while the suspect had no known mental health history with the NYPD, the early investigation suggested mental health may have been a factor. Officers took Morales into custody after he barricaded himself inside an apartment building near Amsterdam Avenue and West 88th Street, police said.

Morales was expected to appear before a judge on Friday, when prosecutors from the Manhattan District Attorney’s office were due to file formal charges that may differ from those initially brought by police. A law enforcement official told CNN that the charges are expected to include a hate crime count and attempted murder. The account of what took place remains preliminary, and authorities have cautioned that the investigation is in its early stages.

World.title: Costa Rica Named One of 10 Best Places for Gen Z Travelers Right Now
World.content:
Travel + Leisure has named Costa Rica one of ten places it recommends for Generation Z travelers to visit right now, in a list assembled from travel-industry advisors. The premise of the list is that younger travelers are moving away from the destinations social media has already saturated. The Costa Rica inclusion recommends Manuel Antonio, Arenal, Monteverde, Tamarindo and Peninsula Papagayo.

That gap between the list’s stated criteria and the specific places named under Costa Rica is the most interesting thing about the recognition, and it says something about where Costa Rica now sits in the global tourism market. The magazine grounded its selection in data from Kayak’s 2026 What the Future Report, which found that 69 percent of Generation Z travelers want to visit places they have never been, and that 84 percent would rather explore a rural area or a smaller city than a major tourism hub.

Tara Cappel, founder of FTLO Travel, which runs group trips for solo travelers between 25 and 39, told the magazine that while the conventional European summer trip retains its appeal, younger travelers are increasingly after destinations that are less crowded and more adventurous, and she framed her recommendations around getting away from the familiar.

Most of the list follows that logic closely. Dominica leads it, described by Fora travel advisor Kris Weir as one of the Caribbean’s last genuine hidden gems, a place with, in her words, “no packed beach clubs, no influencer crowds, and no filter needed” — though she noted that a new international airport due to open in 2027 may change that. Hilo appears as the quiet counterweight to Hawaii’s resort corridors.

Punta Gorda, on Florida’s Gulf Coast, is included partly on affordability, with Kayak data putting average round-trip airfare there near $262. La Paz is recommended explicitly as the Baja alternative for travelers skipping Tulum and Los Cabos. Belize is praised as refreshingly affordable next to the rest of the Caribbean. Morocco, Vietnam and Sardinia round out the selection, though Sardinia complicates the undiscovered framing considerably, having been voted the top island in Europe in the magazine’s own 2026 World’s Best Awards.

Costa Rica’s entry does not follow that pattern. Cappel described the country as the ideal combination of jungle adventure and unhurried beach time, and the specific recommendations that follow are Arenal Volcano, the Monteverde cloud forests, wildlife viewing at Manuel Antonio National Park, surfing at Nosara, the beaches of Santa Teresa, sunset at Tamarindo and the resorts of Peninsula Papagayo.

Every one of those is a mature destination. Manuel Antonio is the most heavily visited national park and operates under a capacity-controlled entry system precisely because demand exceeds what the park can absorb. Tamarindo and the Arenal hot springs corridor carry the hotel density, tour-operator concentration and high-season traffic of places that arrived long ago.

Peninsula Papagayo is a master-planned luxury enclave anchored by Four Seasons, Andaz and Waldorf Astoria properties, which is a defensible recommendation on its own terms but an unusual one for a list organized around travelers who want to avoid tourism hubs and who are frequently described as budget-conscious. Nosara and Santa Teresa are the closest the entry comes to the brief, and both have been absorbing steady development for a decade.

The pattern is worth reading plainly. On a list whose other entries are chosen as alternatives to established destinations, Costa Rica is the established destination. It appears not because it is undiscovered but because its reputation is strong enough that a recommendation requires no argument, and the destinations named under it are the ones a first-time visitor would already know. Dominica and Punta Gorda occupy the discovery slots. Costa Rica occupies the reliability slot, which is a different and in commercial terms probably more valuable position, but it is not the one the list’s framing suggests.

The parts of Costa Rica that would actually satisfy the criteria go unmentioned. The Osa Peninsula and Corcovado National Park remain among the most biologically dense and least-visited protected areas in Costa Rica, reachable only with real effort. The southern Caribbean around Puerto Viejo, Cahuita and Manzanillo carries a distinct Afro-Caribbean cultural identity and a visitor volume that has never approached Guanacaste’s.

Bijagua de Upala, the gateway to Río Celeste and Tenorio Volcano, has built a small lodging sector on exactly the community-scale model the list praises elsewhere. The Nicoya interior, the Sarapiquí lowlands and the Turrialba valley offer the same rainforest, wildlife and volcano landscapes that anchor the country’s global reputation, without the shuttle traffic.

Those places would have made Costa Rica a natural fit for the premise. Their absence suggests that when international travel media reach for Costa Rica, they reach for the circuit that markets itself, and that the secondary destinations still lack the visibility to be named alongside Dominica or Hilo.

There is some evidence however that the visibility gap is closing on its own. In December, Skyscanner’s global trends report identified Limón area as the fastest-rising destination in the world for 2026, based on flight-search data showing interest up roughly 300 percent year over year, with Travel + Leisure separately singling out the area for its rainforest trails, calypso bars and clear water. Whether that translates into arrivals, and whether the Caribbean coast retains the qualities that generated the interest once they do, is the open question for the coming seasons.

The recognition arrives alongside a run of awards pointing in a different direction. In the 2026 World’s Best Awards, Travel + Leisure readers placed three Costa Rican properties among the world’s 100 best hotels, with Nayara Tented Camp in La Fortuna reaching number 28 globally, and named a substantial share of Central America’s leading hotels and resorts in the country. Forbes recently included the Waldorf Astoria Costa Rica Punta Cacique among five luxury resorts it called essential worldwide. Those are recognitions of high-end hospitality, aimed at a market that overlaps only partially with travelers in their twenties.

For the tourism industry here in Costa Rica, the useful signal is not the placement but the mismatch. Costa Rica’s arrivals have trended toward visitors who stay fewer nights and spend more per night, a pattern that concentrates revenue in the resort corridors. A genuine shift toward younger travelers looking for lower-cost, longer, less-trafficked trips would push demand toward the small lodges, community tourism operators and secondary destinations that have captured a thin share of tourism income.

Being named on a list built for those travelers is worth something. Being named for Tamarindo and Papagayo suggests our country is still being sold to them on the strength of what it already has rather than what it has yet to show them.

World.title: CARICOM launches “I am Agriculture” video competition for high school students across region
World.content:
CARICOM launches “I am Agriculture” video competition for high school students across region

By Zoila Palma: The Caribbean Community (CARICOM) is inviting secondary schools across the region to participate in its “I am Agriculture: Youth in Agriculture” High School Video Competition, giving students an opportunity to showcase their creativity while highlighting the importance of agriculture.

Schools are being challenged to produce a 60-second video that demonstrates why agriculture matters and inspires their communities, countries and the wider Caribbean region.

The competition aims to encourage greater youth engagement in agriculture and promote awareness of the sector’s role in the region’s development.

Students can compete for cash prizes, with US$1,700 awarded to the first-place winner, US$1,300 for second place and US$1,000 for third place. The competition is open to secondary schools across CARICOM, and entries must be submitted by September 4, 2026, at 11:59 p.m.

The first-place prize will be presented during the 20th Caribbean Week of Agriculture, scheduled to take place in Jamaica from September 27 to October 2, 2026.

World.title: International News: Nearly £20 million worth of cocaine seized from banana shipment in UK
World.content:
International News: Nearly £20 million worth of cocaine seized from banana shipment in UK

By Zoila Palma: UK Border Force officers have seized approximately £19.2 million worth of cocaine that was concealed inside crates of bananas aboard a refrigerated cargo ship.

The 240-kilogram shipment was discovered after the MV Atlantic Klipper docked in Portsmouth, having travelled from South America via the Caribbean, BBC reports.

The National Crime Agency (NCA) said the Class A drug was seized on Wednesday and has launched an investigation into the shipment. The cocaine was subsequently moved to a secure location with support from the Joint Operations Unit, a specialist collaboration between Hampshire Police and Thames Valley Police.

The NCA said the seizure represents a major blow to the organized crime group responsible for transporting the drugs.

World.content:
Team Belize proudly represents at 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in Dominican Republic

By Zoila Palma: Following a vibrant ceremony on Friday, the competition begins today for our Beach Volleyball teams at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic.

“Best of luck to Francis Hauze & Ernest Broaster and Nelissa Ramirez & Clara Sabal as they proudly represent Belize on the sand. Check the competition schedule to see the times they will be competing,” Belize Volleyball Association said.
