Go Team Belize!,” the association expressed.

World.title: Belize achieves full membership in World Health Organization Global Drug Safety Monitoring Programme
World.content:
Belize achieves full membership in World Health Organization Global Drug Safety Monitoring Programme

By Zoila Palma: Belize has officially become a full member of the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Programme for International Drug Monitoring (PIDM), marking a major step forward in the country’s efforts to strengthen medicines safety and protect public health.

The achievement follows years of work by the Ministry of Health and Wellness to improve Belize’s national pharmacovigilance system, regulatory oversight and monitoring of medical products, with technical support from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). Belize initially joined the programme as an Associate Member in 2020.

According to PAHO, full membership recognizes Belize’s growing ability to “detect, assess, understand, and prevent adverse effects or other medicine-related problems,” while allowing the country to contribute data and expertise to the global monitoring network coordinated by WHO and the Uppsala Monitoring Centre (UMC).

PAHO has supported Belize through initiatives focused on post-marketing surveillance, adverse event reporting, health professional training, data exchange and participation in regional and international regulatory networks.

A key factor in Belize achieving full membership was improved interoperability and information exchange, strengthened through the Data Bridges project supported by PAHO.

“This enables the country to contribute to regional and global efforts to identify potential safety signals and respond to emerging risks associated with medical products,” PAHO noted.

Belize now has direct reporting links to global surveillance systems through VigiFlow/VigiBase and the Global Surveillance and Monitoring System (GSMS), while also strengthening its Drug Inspectorate Unit and expanding regulatory and surveillance activities.

“Strengthening regulatory systems remains a public health priority for the Pan American Health Organization,” PAHO said, noting that Member States endorsed a policy in 2022 aimed at strengthening national regulatory systems for medicines and other health technologies.

As a full PIDM member, Belize will have greater opportunities to collaborate internationally, access global safety analyses and information, and contribute to the detection of medicine-related risks, including those linked to substandard and falsified medical products.

World.title: International News: U.S. Department of Agriculture announces phased reopening of cattle imports from Mexico
World.content:
International News: U.S. Department of Agriculture announces phased reopening of cattle imports from Mexico

By Zoila Palma: The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) has announced plans for a phased reopening of southern U.S. ports to livestock trade, beginning August 24, 2026, following a year-long closure aimed at preventing the spread of New World screwworm (NWS).

The Douglas, Arizona, port of entry, which borders Sonora, Mexico, will reopen first, while operational preparations will begin for the potential reopening of the Santa Teresa and Columbus ports in New Mexico. Every animal entering the United States through the reopened ports will undergo a full USDA inspection to ensure it shows no signs of NWS.

“Protecting the United States from NWS and pushing this pest out of Mexico and back to the Darien Gap is a top priority at USDA and has the full attention of the Trump Administration,” U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins said. She added that the closure of southern ports had been “a tough but necessary action to control the spread of NWS in Mexico and protect the American livestock industry.”

USDA said Sonora and Chihuahua have been identified as the lowest-risk Mexican states for NWS because of their established animal health and inspection programs and their distance from southern Mexico, where most cases are concentrated.

The USDA said the closest active case to the Douglas port was approximately 325 miles away, detected on July 22, 2026. “Thanks to the work across the federal government as well as state, local, and industry partners, it is now safe to reopen the Douglas, Arizona, port in 30 days to resume the hundreds year old movement of cattle,” Rollins said.

The reopening process will remain flexible and dependent on Mexico’s progress in meeting milestones under the Joint Action Plan.

USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service will evaluate the results of the initial reopening before considering the resumption of live cattle, bison and horse trade through Santa Teresa and Columbus.

However, USDA warned that port reopenings could be paused if increased NWS risks are identified in Sonora or Chihuahua through post-opening audits or other information.

World.title: October court date set for Elvira Mulholland; accused of attempting to murder her husband
World.content:
October court date set for Elvira Mulholland; accused of attempting to murder her husband

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A tentative October 2, 2026 court date has been set in the attempted murder case against Elvira Mulholland, who is accused of shooting her husband during a domestic dispute in 2024.

Mulholland appeared before Justice Candace Nanton in the High Court on Friday, represented by attorney Dr. Lynden Jones. She remains out on High Court bail.

The defence informed the court that Mulholland is also currently on trial in the Magistrate’s Court for an alleged robbery arising from the same incident. That trial, which began in April, is scheduled to continue on August 3.

Justice Nanton adjourned the attempted murder matter until October 2 for a case management conference, by which time the lower court proceedings are expected to have concluded. A firm trial date could then be determined.

Police allege that on October 25, 2024, Mulholland followed her husband, Jeffrey Mulholland, along the Coastal Road, ran his pickup truck off the road and shot him with his own licensed firearm following a struggle.

She was committed to stand trial in the High Court after a preliminary inquiry concluded in July 2025.

World.title: Collin Francis found stable to stand trial for murder of Nestor Vasquez Jr. but Court says it won’t accept just one evaluation
World.content:
Collin Francis found stable to stand trial for murder of Nestor Vasquez Jr. but Court says it won’t accept just one evaluation

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The murder case against Collin Francis Jr. could take a significant turn when it returns to the High Court on Tuesday, July 28, 2026.

Francis had previously been found unfit to enter a plea and was ordered to undergo psychiatric evaluations every six months for two years. However, Justice Nigel Pilgrim was informed on Friday that only one evaluation had been completed.

The June 29, 2026 report, prepared by psychiatrist Dr. Denethia Usher, found that Francis is now stable, taking his medication and considered fit to enter a plea. The report also noted that his condition had improved while he was away from marijuana.

The prosecution indicated that the Director of Public Prosecutions’ office was prepared to proceed to trial. Justice Pilgrim, however, said he would not allow the case to proceed to trial based solely on the single evaluation.

The judge asked whether the prosecution would consider accepting a guilty plea, but the Crown said instructions would first have to be obtained from the DPP.

Francis is charged with the 2019 murder of 60-year-old Nestor Vasquez Jr., who was fatally injured while the two men were detained in a cell at the Queen Street Police Station.

The matter was adjourned until Tuesday for the prosecution to indicate how it intends to proceed.

World.title: BDF volunteer soldier Mark Nolberto sentenced to nearly 18 Years for raping 17-year-old girl and videoing it; Says his sentence is ‘unjust’
World.content:
BDF volunteer soldier Mark Nolberto sentenced to nearly 18 Years for raping 17-year-old girl and videoing it; Says his sentence is ‘unjust’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: High Court Justice Candace Nanton today sentenced 31-year-old Belize Defence Force (BDF) volunteer soldier Mark Anthony Nolberto to 17 years, 10 months, and 3 weeks in prison following his conviction on two counts of rape against a 17-year-old girl.

Justice Nanton ordered that the sentences for both counts run concurrently. In addition to his prison term, Nolberto must undergo counseling as well as medical and psychiatric treatment while incarcerated. Upon his release, he will be legally required to report his residential address to the Commissioner of Police and the Department of Human Development.

The convictions stem from an incident where Nolberto struck the minor with a metal cup, forced her into his residence, subjected her to physical and sexual assault, and recorded the act on his mobile phone—video footage that was later extracted by police and presented as evidence in court.

In delivering the sentence, Justice Nanton classified the harm as severe and noted the high degree of offender culpability, pointing to the victim’s age, the violent nature of the attack, and Nolberto’s lack of remorse throughout the trial. Starting from a 19-year baseline, the judge deducted two years for Nolberto’s prior lack of a criminal record and community service, added one year to reflect the overall severity of the crime, and credited 40 days for time served on remand.

Defense attorney Orson “OJ” Elrington had requested a suspended sentence, but Justice Nanton rejected the plea, citing statutory laws that restrict suspended sentences to offenses carrying maximum terms of three years or less. Under Belizean law, rape carries a mandatory minimum sentence of eight years in prison up to life imprisonment. The prosecution was led by Crown Counsel Joseph Perez.

Following the sentencing, Nolberto maintained his innocence as he was escorted from the High Court, telling reporters that he refused to cover his face because he believed the conviction was “unjust.”

World.title: Hitman’s appeal denied
World.content:
Simone Campbell-Collymore, whose confessed killer Wade Blackwood had his appeal rejected on Friday.

THE Court of Appeal on Friday upheld the sentence and conviction of killer Wade Blackwood, who in 2021 was sentenced to life in prison after confessing to being the trigger man in the 2018 murder of 32-year-old businesswoman Simone Campbell-Collymore.

The then 24-year-old, in a confession, detailed how he had been subcontracted to kill Campbell-Collymore in a $2-million murder-for-hire plot hatched by her then husband Omar “Best” Collymore.

Thirty-six-year-old taxi driver Winston Walters was also killed during the incident which took place outside Campbell-Collymore’s Forest Ridge apartment in Red Hills, St Andrew, on January 2, 2018.

The two men involved in the shooting that day were identified by the police, from closed-circuit television footage in the vicinity, as Blackwood and a now-deceased Corporate Area don who went by the name Jim.

Blackwood, who had been held by cops in April 2018, had pleaded guilty in January 2021 to two counts of murder and one count of illegal possession of firearm before the Home Circuit Court in downtown Kingston.

He was sentenced to life imprisonment for his role in the murders, ahead of the other individuals involved in the plot, with 35 years on each count of murder before eligibility for parole, and eight years and six months for illegal possession of firearm. Those sentences, however, were to run concurrently, making it so that he would serve 35 years before applying for parole.

Friday, the Appeal Court, which heard the matter over two days, in handing down its decision ruled that based on the fact that Blackwood was resentenced on February 9, 2024, after a plea agreement was reached, the basis of his appeal was obsolete.

Blackwood, through his attorney Shenieka Sparks, in supplemental grounds of appeal filed this year, had contended that a discount for his guilty plea was “unreasoned and inadequate”.

He further argued that the sentencing judge had erred in setting 30 years as a starting point to arrive at his ultimate sentence. According to Blackwood, compared to other similar cases, the discount was “out of parity”.

The Jamaica Observer was told that when Blackwood was advised of the decision of the Appeal Court he accepted that he would not continue challenging his sentence and a notice of abandonment was filed on his behalf.

As such, Blackwood will serve 20 years before he is eligible for parole, as was the sentence imposed on following his plea deal.

In February 2024, Blackwood — who testified against his co-accused following a deal with prosecutors — claimed he was pressured into committing the act by Jim, who was supposedly the leader of a gang his brother had been involved with.

Blackwood claimed that Jim, in levelling death threats at him and his family, told him that he had to carry out the killing to repay his brother’s debt for a firearm that had been seized by the police.

Blackwood, in negotiating with the prosecution, had 15 years shaved off his sentence, which now makes him eligible for parole after 20 years.

At the end of the substantive trial, Collymore, who was slapped with two life sentences, was also sentenced to one year and six months for conspiracy and ordered to serve 46 years and six months before becoming eligible for parole. His co-conspirators Dwayne Pink, Michael Adams, and Shaquille Edwards were also handed life sentences.

In the highly publicised incident, Campbell-Collymore and Walters were ambushed and shot dead outside the apartment complex where she lived with her then husband and children.

The Crown, at the close of its case, established that Collymore ordered the hit to claim his wife’s multimillion-dollar life insurance policies from which their two children were entitled to 15 per cent each while Collymore was entitled to 70 per cent of the benefits.

He was also listed as trustee for the children and their portion. Those policies were taken out by the couple three months before the murders.

Collymore was collared by cops at Norman Manley International Airport while attempting to flee the island a day before his wife’s funeral.

Earlier this month, Collymore, alongside his co-accused Pink, Adams, and Edwards, appeared before the Home Circuit Court again where they are all facing charges of illegal possession of firearm, shooting with intent, and conspiracy to murder with respect to an unnamed woman the businessman was in a relationship with at the time he orchestrated his wife’s death.

A new conspirator, Carey Jonas, is also named on the indictment with respect to the new matter.

On Thursday, Edwards, who had entered into plea negotiations with the prosecution and pleaded guilty to the new charges, was sentenced to six years and nine months for his part in that crime.

Edwards, however, has already spent more than seven years in custody and is set to be released.

World.title: No ease in honey shortage
World.content:
President of the St James Bee Farmers Association Dennis McKay with two bottles of honey, on Tuesday.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — The nation could be facing a severe honey shortage by the end of the year as the long-term effects of last October’s Hurricane Melissa continue to cripple the beekeeping industry, according to president of the St James Bee Farmers’ Association Dennis McKay.

He said even the intense heat now being felt across the country pales in comparison to the lingering effects of the Category 5 storm.

“It’s not so much the heat that is the crisis for the bees. Probably the major problem at this time is the impact of the hurricane and the trees that are missing. The storm turned down all the trees that provide the nectar and the pollen that support the bees. They are unable to get the nectar, so they cannot get enough nectar to store that we can get honey,” McKay told the Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

He explained that this period would ordinarily be the height of the honey-producing season, when beekeepers harvest their largest volumes. However, with many nectar-producing trees destroyed and only now beginning to recover, bees are gathering just enough food to sustain their colonies rather than building honey reserves.

“As the bees get the little nectar, it is only enough to feed them, not enough to store. So that is the major crisis as it relates to where the beekeeping and the honey business is going to go,” he said.

The dramatic decline in production has left many farmers with only a fraction of their usual harvest.

“A man used to get maybe 100 bottles from an apiary, [now] he only gets four bottles,” McKay said, adding that even large commercial operators who previously sold honey by the drum are now only able to provide a few bottles.

“He’s not getting enough that he can be selling by the drum, like before,” he added.

McKay also noted that many beekeepers suffered another devastating blow when they lost entire colonies during the hurricane.

“We are heading into a honey crisis,” he warned.

According to McKay, the dwindling supply has already sent up retail prices.

“Right now, honey used to be selling for $3,000 a bottle. I went into a supermarket and see it for $4,800, before tax added. This is the middle of the honey season; this is a time when everybody get honey,” he said.

McKay predicted that prices could climb even higher by Christmas.

“Going down to December, you might be paying $7,000 per bottle,” he cautioned.

While some damaged trees are beginning to regenerate, McKay said recovery is likely to be gradual and warned that another major weather event could worsen the situation.

“The existing trees now that are coming up, they may blossom next year, or we might have to start talking about importation of honey,” he said.

However, he expressed concern about relying on imported supplies, arguing that consumers cannot always be certain of their authenticity.

“I am seeing online where honey is made without bees. It’s only when you buy your local honey [that] you can have certain confidence that at least it come from bees,” McKay said.

Following the hurricane, the Government distributed sugar to beekeepers to help sustain weakened colonies. McKay said the assistance was useful when nectar was scarce.

“Bees don’t make honey with sugar. They use the sugar syrup to feed their young. As soon as trees start to blossom they don’t want that sugar water anymore,” he underscored.

He also suggested that support programmes should have included replacing lost colonies, noting that while some districts still have flowering trees, many of the bees needed to pollinate them and produce honey were wiped out during the hurricane.

“We have to be concerned because some people depend on that for a living,” McKay said.

World.title: Job scam victims repaid in court but case not closed
World.content:
MONTEGO BAY, St James — Decarlos Christie, who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud, has repaid a total of $200,000 to two women who fell prey to a job scam.

With the payment, part of his case has been resolved but he has been remanded as he still owes one of the women $57,000. There is also a third alleged victim.

Decarlos, who is jointly charged with his brother Bryan Christie, appeared before Judge Kaysha Grant-Pryce in the St James Parish Court on Wednesday. Two of three complainants attended the hearing. One was repaid the full $52,000 she had paid while another received $148,000 of the $205,000 of which she was allegedly defrauded. Judge Grant-Pryce has directed that efforts be made to contact the third complainant

Following Wednesday’s guilty plea Decarlos was admonished and discharged in relation to the matter involving the complainant who received full restitution. He is expected to pay the outstanding balance owed to the second complainant by July 29, when the matter will next be before the court. While he was remanded in custody, his brother’s bail was extended.

During the hearing Decarlos maintained that his brother, Bryan, used his personal information without his knowledge or consent to carry out the transactions while he was in custody in St Ann on unrelated matters. Decarlos insisted that he had no involvement in the alleged scheme.

According to the allegations, in January the first complainant was introduced by telephone to a man identifying himself only as “Mr Campbell”, who claimed to be offering overseas job placement opportunities. She was allegedly instructed to deposit $52,000 into a bank account registered to Decarlos Christie.

Police say a second complainant later deposited $205,000 into the same account for the same purpose, while a third complainant transferred $10,000. Investigators allege the complainants were subsequently assured they would travel to Kingston as part of the overseas employment programme. However, the promised arrangements did not materialise, prompting reports to the police.

During the investigation, police reportedly found that Decarlos’s bank card and account information were in Bryan’s possession, leading to the former being charged. Police further allege that Bryan was the individual who communicated with the complainants while posing as “Mr Campbell” and offering the overseas job opportunities.

World.title: Hill wary of call for ganja amnesty
World.content:
HILL...I have to remind you all that ganja is a Schedule 1 drug. It’s the same thing as fentanyl, the same thing as cocaine

SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — While a key stakeholder in the cannabis industry continues to call for an amnesty to regularise farmers operating outside the regulated sector, Minister of Industry, Investment and Commerce Senator Aubyn Hill has sounded a cautionary note. He pointed to the complex international legal landscape in explaining his stance on the matter.

“I have to remind you all that ganja is a Schedule 1 drug. It’s the same thing as fentanyl, the same thing as cocaine. It’s in the same category as heroin. It is seen as a bad drug,” the minister stressed.

He was addressing a Westmoreland Chamber of Commerce and Industry meeting at the Hotel Commingle in Savanna-la-Mar on Wednesday. He gave a breakdown on the implications for international trade and travel.

“Even today, because it’s a Schedule 1 drug, if you fly in the airspace of the United States, you are illegal. You can be taken out. You see what happened to those guys out there in the sea? That can happen to a ganja plane flying in the airspace of the United States, legally,” warned the minister.

He further emphasised that strict compliance with international drug laws is essential to maintaining Jamaica’s standing in global trade.

Hill was responding to questions posed by Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) board member Verald Vassell, better known as Ras Iyah V. The Westmoreland ganja advocate — who served on the CLA board from 2016 to 2021 and returned in 2024 — has consistently pointed to the need for an amnesty to transition illicit farmers into the legal medical cannabis industry.

During Wednesday night’s meeting Ras Iyah V highlighted what he said was continued harassment farmers face at the hands of the police.

“As the minister in charge of the CLA, what are the plans? Because I know the regulation has been amended recently. But what are the plans, the road map, and if you can explain how this is going to work? Because, as for me, I see a certain approach that creates a glut in the market, and then there is no market… Can you explain what is the road map going forward to bring our ganja farmers from being considered illegal into the legal industry? Because most of these farmers have been out-financed,” stated Ras Iyah V.

Acknowledging the concerns raised by the advocate, Hill outlined recent legislative changes aimed at easing operational restrictions for small-scale cultivators.

“Under my leadership with the permanent secretary and the people in the ministry, we changed the law. Because the very small farmer was constantly complaining of being put upon, [saying] they can’t get their things done. And we said, ‘Alright, you must have a fence of… five feet,” relayed Hill.

The minister pointed out that these regulatory adjustments provide greater flexibility for traditional farmers and workers trying to satisfy compliance requirements.

Addressing the issue of a market glut, Hill attributed the surplus to the initial surge of interest following the decriminalisation of cannabis.

“Understand that the glut that is developing is because when ganja was decriminalised, the euphoria that came around it encouraged people to go into it. Everybody was in it. There was one firm in Canada that seemed to have made a lot of money and then the thing collapsed. But that euphoria took a lot of people in,” the minister said.

Under the Dangerous Drugs Act, which came into effect on April 15, 2015, provisions were implemented for the possession and smoking of ganja; the use of ganja by those of the Rastafarian faith; and the use of ganja for medical, therapeutic, and scientific purposes.

“Our law allows people who use ganja for their religious practices to be exempt. But they have to go through a process,” explained Hill.

Regarding ongoing police enforcement, he noted that while adults are permitted to possess up to two ounces of ganja without criminal charges, the police must act whenever boundaries are breached.

World.title: Market Bag: Soup vendor Bulbie shops for staples as prices fluctuate
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Shoppers at the Coronation Market will encounter a mixed basket in terms of prices this week.

Persistent dry conditions continue to impact farming, pushing up the prices of some produce including tomatoes at $150 per pound, Scotch bonnet peppers at $350 per pound, sweet peppers at $400 per pound, bananas at $1,400 a dozen and lettuce at $700 per head.

Plantains ($700 for three) also continue to be a pricey commodity.

Still, other food items held steady or declined, including onions at $200 per pound.

In this week’s episode of Market Bag, popular soup vendor Nicardo “Bulbie” Sayer joins host Carlysia Ramdeen as he shops for the fresh ingredients behind his signature Bulbie Soups, a favourite among soup lovers.

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: Rajindra Campbell signs with Nike
World.content:
Rajindra Campbell signs with Nike

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica’s 2024 Olympic shot put bronze medallist Rajindra Campbell has signed a contract with Nike.

The 30-year-old Campbell, who has always highlighted the plight of non-track athletes in surviving financially, made the revelation via social media earlier this week.

“The work behind the scenes is paying off, and I’m still building. The season isn’t over yet; the best is still to come. Happy to announce I will be continuing my journey as part of the Nike family, Nike Athlete,” Campbell posted on Instagram.

“From the indoor season to now, 2026 has been all about growth, consistency and progress. Every competition has been another opportunity to improve and compete with the best in the world,” he added.

Campbell was one of four Jamaicans who tried to switch allegiance to Turkey in 2025, citing the lack of financial support from Jamaican athletics administrators.

However, world governing body World Athletics rejected their applications.

In announcing the decision, the panel said approving the applications would undermine the intent of World Athletics’ eligibility and transfer-of-allegiance rules.

It found the requests were part of a coordinated recruitment effort by the Turkish Government, operating through a state-funded club, offering lucrative contracts to attract foreign athletes and enable them to compete for Turkey at major events, including the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.

In 2024, Campbell accused the Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association (JAAA) of not caring about athletes, pointing to an eight-year US$40 million ($6.4 billion) Adidas contract which was turned down when the JAAA extended its contract with longtime sponsors Puma.

“I don’t believe that they really understand that it is challenging. For one, track and field, we are not sprinters, obviously, and as you can see, I am still unsponsored,” he said at the time.

World.title: $1.5-b pothole rescue
World.content:
Water has settled in this pothole on Fairdene Avenue in St Andrew on Thursday.

AS motorists across the island continue to face gaping potholes, minister with responsibility for works Robert Morgan has told the Jamaica Observer that the Cabinet on Monday approved a further $1.5-billion spend for patching and sheeting work on main roads across the island to bring some well-needed relief to drivers.

This brings the money allocated to tackle the persistent pothole problem to $3.1 billion for this fiscal year.

According to Morgan, the additional allocation was necessary based on the scope of the problem. He told the Observer that the money initially allocated for the pothole patching programme is already being spent.

“We are engaged in a $1.6-billion programme patching the roads. It’s really sheeting in many cases. Cabinet just approved another $1.5 billion to do more roads. We are doing the $1.6 billion now and then, before the end of the year, we are going to spend another $1.5 billion on road rehabilitation,” said Morgan.

But even as the minister promised relief, motorists across the Corporate Area were pointing the Observer to several roads where potholes are making driving almost impossible.

In downtown Kingston, where many large potholes pockmark the streets, motorists pointed to one on Orange Street, close to its intersection with Heywood Street, which they said is a source of frustration for many.

While an Observer news team was in the area on Thursday, motorists and pedestrians urged the team to take as many pictures and videos as possible to expose the failure of authorities to maintain roads.

In response, Morgan said that area could be fixed as early as next week as it is schduled for priority repairs.

He underscored that his ministry is responsible for fixing main roads through the National Works Agency, and not streets or lanes.

“Not all the roads are mine. I am strictly responsible for main roads; I am not responsible for avenues, lanes, and I am not responsible for crescents. I am not responsible for any of those community roads. None at all. My roads are roads like Washington Boulevard, Constant Spring and Barbican Road.

“Roads like Liguanea Avenue, Paddington Terrace, roads in Cherry Garden, and a lot of the community roads in downtown Kingston are not mine — they belong to the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation — but I have been getting blamed. Parish councils get a billion dollars a year and they need to fix those roads,” argued Morgan.

However residents of several Corporate Area communities only want their roads fixed, with no concern over which agency will do it.

On Fairdene Avenue in Ackee Walk, St Andrew, residents and passing motorists expressed their displeasure at the state of the road, which is littered with very deep and wide potholes..

“It is treacherous. It is dread. When the rain falls, pedestrians get splashed easily all the time. They need to fix the roads properly and done,” said one motorist.

He was supported by another motorist, who charged that the condition of the roads in Corporate Area forces drivers to make detours into areas where they would rather not drive.

In the meantime, one motorist complained about damage to his vehicle by the potholes.

“The road stay very bad, man. The road need to fix. It a mash up mi front end and we have to drive on the roads every day,” lamented the motorist.

World.title: Grief turns to protest in Troy
World.content:
Placard-bearing residents in Troy, Trelawny, on Thursday protesting againt the arrest of a man in connection with fatal mobbing following murder of 10-year-old Shani Coke.

TROY, Trelawny — Still mourning the murder of 10-year-old Shani “Kaidra” Coke on Tuesday residents of the usually quiet district took to the streets on Thursday after one of their own was reportedly arrested by the police in connection with the mob killing of the man believed to have attacked her.

According to residents the man was taken into custody by the police who are probing the death of Shani and the fatal attack on the suspected child killer Delroy Coke, and the brutal beating of his father.

The placard-bearing residents used debris to block the Troy main road — which links part of south Trelawny to northern Manchester — as they charged that the police had no reason to arrest the man, whose identity has not been released.

The residents also expressed their anger at the murder of Shani.

“We want justice. Protect our children. Children are the future. Let us protect them. The justice system failed us. We want justice for the brutal murder of Shani,” some of the placards read, while other called for the freeing of the man they said had been taken into custody.

Some of the protesters also took to social media platform TikTok to express their frustration and disgust.

“We a protest, because the police lock up a man and we want him to be freed…. We want justice,” one of the protesting residents told the Jamaica Observer.

Shani partially nude body was found with her throat slashed in bushes on Tuesday. Police said following the discovery of the child’s body, there was a mob attack on the father and son in the community.

Residents told the Observer that the two men are Shani’s relatives. They accused the son of raping and killing the child. He was beaten, chopped and stoned to death, while his father was left with major wounds.

When contacted head of the police Area One Assistant Commissioner Glenford Miller said the investigators are seeking those involved in the mob attack.

“I know we are investigating to know who were the persons involved in that mob killing. I cannot say at this time if we have made any arrests,” Miller said mid-morning on Thursday. Subsequent efforts to get a further update were unsuccessful up to press time.

A heavy pall of gloom and anger clouded over Troy on Thursday with one resident telling the

Observer that the community remains grief-stricken.

“The whole of Troy is in mourning. We can’t stop thinking about the little girl and how she died so awful,” said the resident who requested anonymity.

According to a police report, as well as the account of residents, mid-afternoon Tuesday, Shani was walking home from a shop along a roadway near her home when she was abducted.

Later, a farmer, who had gone in search of his cow after hearing strange sounds from bushes, made the grisly discovery and raised an alarm.

On Wednesday relatives remembered the child for her brilliance and radiant smile.

“All last week she got her certificate to show her brilliance. When you look at her you see the next doctor, lawyer, and they just took her life, just cut her off. Right now we are devastated. Right now we don’t know our head from our feet. Last night [Tuesday] we nuh sleep. This is traumatising. Maybe Kaidra was going to come and take her mother out of poverty and they cut her life short and kill her,” her aunt Shawna Williams-Stevens said before breaking down in tears.

World.title: Record-breaking wildfires burned nearly 100,000 hectares in France, interior minister says
World.content:
Nearly 200,000 people have been evacuated because of the fires in southwestern France out of which more than 167,000 are in Gironde, the department of Bordeaux, and around 30,000 in the nearby Landes department.

French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday announced that he requested the activation of an EU emergency mechanism, which has prompted other EU countries including Portugal, Croatia, Slovakia and Sweden to send airplanes and helicopters to help France.

"Europe stands with France and Spain against the devastating wildfires that are hitting them," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote in a social media post on Saturday, stressing that France is already benefitting from five planes and two helicopters provided by other EU countries while four planes will arrive in Spain on Saturday.

France's Nuñez confirmed that Saturday afternoon an Airbus A400 military plane will start throwing a fire retardant product at the wildfires. That is on the top of Canadair and other French and European aircraft.

The wildfires have been the subject of political controversy in France in recent days, with both the hard-left France Unbowed and the far-right National Rally accusing Macron of underinvesting.

Spain has declared the state of emergency in the Madrid and Ávila regions.

"Our priority is to save lives, protect communities, and fight the fires," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Saturday. Around 80,000 people have been evacuated or are confined because of the wildfires, Spanish media report.

World.title: Italy’s defense minister offered adviser job to ousted Ukrainian defense chief
World.content:
The Italian minister said Fedorov was "moved" by the proposal and saw it as "a mark of respect and friendship," but he didn't elaborate on whether Fedorov accepted or not.

Crosetto strongly praised Fedorov, who has been credited with bringing a technology overhaul to Ukraine's military but also clashed with top generals.

“Fedorov embodies innovation; he is one of those who has completely changed the rules of the game on the battlefield, enabling Ukraine first to hold its ground and then to take the initiative,” Crosetto said, adding that Fedorov was faced with "a resistance to change" that is also a problem in Italy, France and Germany.

Fedorov hasn't responded publicly to Crosetto's offer.

Crosetto, who is a top figure in Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's Brothers of Italy party, also made clear that he is in favor of continuing to borrow via EU loans from the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) scheme rather than financing defense spending through national public debt. But he made clear that it was up for the Treasury to make that decision.

Crosetto's comments come as the Italian government is mulling applying for only €5 billion to €7 billion under the SAFE scheme, instead of €15 billion, as initially planned.

World.title: NATO intern arrested over espionage suspicions
World.content:
The Canadian national of Chinese origin is suspected of spying for a third country and being part of a criminal organization.

Belgian police on Friday arrested an intern at NATO's strategic headquarters of the Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE,) suspecting her of "spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization," the Belgian Federal Prosecutor Office wrote in a statement on Saturday.

The intern, a Canadian national of Chinese origins, "had come to the attention" of the security services of SHAPE, NATO’s strategic command for operations in Mons, Belgium.

Belgian authorities searched her home and office on Thursday.

Belgian prosecutors gave no further details on what the woman is suspected of.

Camille Gijs contributed to this report.

World.title: ICC member states remove chief prosecutor over sexual misconduct claims
World.content:
“I have no other way to describe it but an escalation of attempts,” she said in the interview, adding that she feared for her job and hence was afraid to say “no” to Khan’s advances.

Khan has denied any wrongdoing and, according to Reuters, called the Friday vote “unlawful, procedurally unfair and unsupported by evidence.”

The vote to fire Khan comes a week after the U.S. administration announced a campaign to dismantle what it called a “threat posed by the ICC to U.S. sovereignty.” Washington argues that the court should not have the authority to investigate and prosecute U.S. citizens.

Last year, the U.S. sanctioned Khan and other ICC employees after they issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes in Gaza.

World.title: We’ve fallen in love with drones, but they’re not the sole answer
World.content:
They are not. But nor are they mere bit players.

The enthusiasm for drones is understandable. According to the Kyiv Post, on July 9 alone “Ukraine said it struck 14 Russian vessels overnight in the Sea of Azov, including 12 tankers allegedly belonging to Moscow’s sanctioned ‘shadow fleet.’ Ukraine’s drone commander said a total of 35 ships had been hit over the previous 96 hours, while Ukrainian forces also targeted 45 military sites in occupied Crimea and southern Ukraine.”

It’s as if Ukrainian drones are everywhere. And not only is Ukraine using them to hit Russian targets without causing devastating losses to human life the way, say, missiles would; it’s also able to do so at enormous distances.

Drones hit Russian shadow vessels in the Black Sea. They hit Russian shadow vessels in the Mediterranean. They hit Russia’s oil refineries. They hit Russia’s Baltic Sea oil terminals. They’re causing constant problems for the Russian military, and have hit Russia itself. Earlier this month they even struck an oil refinery in Siberia.

In fact, Ukraine’s drones have become such a success that they’re triggering increasingly loud demands for NATO’s European members to shift their focus to these mostly small and cheap weapons. Look at how drones have helped Ukraine shift the course of the war! Look at how much you can achieve at relatively small expense! Drones are the future! Our governments are behind the curve! That’s how the argument goes.

But while drones are indisputably part of the future of warfare, they’re also still experimental and lack clear rules of engagement.

World.title: Russian central bank cuts GDP growth forecast to zero, expects faster inflation
World.content:
The Central Bank of Russia expects inflation at 6–7% in 2026 "due to the significant increase in fuel prices that has already occurred".

 

Previously, the regulator had expected it to slow to 4.5–5.5%.

Inflation expectations among households, businesses and financial market participants have risen. Their persistence at elevated levels may impede a sustained slowdown in inflation, the Bank of Russia said in a press release.

"The fuel situation falls into what is known as supply shocks," admitted Elvira Nabiullina, the head of the Bank of Russia, at a press conference on the same day.

Since mid-May, fuel price growth has accelerated, and in June several Russian regions faced shortages after Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries in Russia in response to the war launched by the Kremlin.

At the same time, some analysts forecast that by the end of the year inflation in Russia could turn out even higher, including as a result of strikes by the Ukrainian Armed Forces on Russian logistics centres.

The forecast for Russian GDP growth in 2026 has been cut from 0.5–1.5% to 0.0–1.0%, including the projection for the fourth quarter (from 1.0–2.0% to 0.0–1.5% year-on-year).

"Companies expect demand to slow, as follows from the real-time data. Taking into account the temporary reduction in capacity in the economy, we have lowered our GDP growth forecast," the head of the Bank of Russia commented.

The Central Bank expects that "fuel production capacity will gradually be restored by the end of the year", but Ukraine continues to use its "long-range sanctions" in response to Russian attacks.

On Saturday, Ukrainian drones struck an oil refinery in Tyumen, a logistics facility in Yekaterinburg and a fuel and lubricants depot in Rostov-on-Don.

World.title: Viktor Orbán calls for new era of 'resistance politics'
World.content:
The time is set for Hungary's Fidesz party to break from opposition politics and establish a new "resistance politics," former PM and party leader Viktor Orbán stressed in a speech on Saturday.

 

Speaking at the Bálványos Summer University, Orbán, who was ousted from government after 16 years following elections in April, said there was no longer time for the party to dwell on the election loss and that it must turn its attention to defending Hungary's freedom, which he claimed was under threat.

Orbán said he believed that those who voted for change in the Hungarian elections in spring "didn't vote to have their trust betrayed."

Most of them, he said, acted in good faith and had simply expected fewer government mistakes and stronger economic performance.

But the ruling Tisza party wants and is beginning to build a new authoritarian system, the Fidesz leader continued, likening the political system being built in Hungary to Venezuela, which he described as a mix of communist thinking, political arbitrariness and economic oppression.

He added that he felt there was also now an effort to eliminate Fidesz altogether by driving its leaders out of politics and using illegitimate means to destroy any viable political alternative.

So instead of pursuing an opposition strategy based on self-reflection, he said, Fidesz must adopt a strategy of "resistance."

In response, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said it was pointless to listen to Orbán.

"It is pointless to deal with an inexorable, disgraced mafia boss," Magyar wrote on Facebook.

"Thank you for your wisdom and trust Hungary," he added.

European Union

Orbán also addressed the European Union in his speech, arguing that "patriots" must take over Brussels if member states are to regain their independence and restore the balance of power within the EU.

He added that the role of European Commission president, currently occupied by Ursula von der Leyen, should be abolished, and that the EU's executive branch should be scaled back.

"Brussels must be occupied by the Patriots," he said.

World.title: UN chief urges global support for Syria during first Damascus visit since 2009
World.content:
In the first visit by a UN Secretary-General to Syria since 2009, António Guterres appealed to the international community to support the country's people as it transitions following the fall of longtime leader Bashar al-Assad.

 

"I have just arrived in Damascus for a visit of solidarity. My message is clear: The UN stands with Syria at this pivotal moment and I appeal to the international community to spare no effort to support the people of Syria as well," Guterres said on X.

Shortly after his arrival, Guterres held talks with Syria’s interim president, Ahmad al-Sharaa, before taking a tour of the old quarter of Damascus and the famous Umayyad Mosque.

His visit comes as Syria recovers from the deadly conflict that broke out in March 2011, which resulted in the deaths of more than half a million people.

Since the five-decade Assad family rule came to an end in December 2024, when forces led by al-Sharaa's fighters stormed Damascus, the nation has been struggling to recover from years of conflict and the effects of crippling Western sanctions.

While the United States and Europe have lifted many of the sanctions imposed during the rule of the Assad dynasty, the impact on the ground has so far been limited.

Since al-Sharaa took power, the international community has urged the new Islamist authorities to build strong and effective institutions and establish a governance system that includes all components of Syria's multi-ethnic, multi-confessional society.

Situation in Golan Heights 'unacceptable'

Guterres is set to meet representatives of Syrian civil society and non-governmental organisations supporting women's issues, and to visit a UN peacekeeping force that has been stationed in south Syria's Israeli-occupied Golan Heights since 1974.

After Assad's overthrow, Israel sent troops into the UN-patrolled buffer zone that separated Israeli and Syrian forces on the Golan, and has carried out strikes and repeated incursions deeper into Syrian territory.

Israeli officials have said they intend to keep forces in a "security zone" in southern Syria, where they seek a broader demilitarised zone.

"What is happening in the region around the Golan Heights is totally unacceptable," Guterres told a press conference alongside Syria's Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani, who called for an "immediate and unconditional Israeli withdrawal" from the area where they had advanced.

Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa walks with United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres, at the Syrian presidential palace in Damascus, Syria, Saturday, July 25, 2026. AP Photo/Omar Albam

Despite tensions between the neighbours, Israel and Syria's new authorities have held several rounds of direct talks and have agreed to establish an intelligence-sharing mechanism, though the move has failed to halt Israeli military activity.

Since al-Assad's ousting, some 1.9 million internally displaced people and 1.7 million refugees from abroad have returned, according to the UN, while around 5.5 million people remain displaced inside the country and another six million overseas.

With many Syrians living in poverty, an estimated 15.6 million people require humanitarian assistance.

World.title: German teacher ill for 17 years fights in court for full salary
World.content:
For years, the case of a teacher from North Rhine-Westphalia has been making headlines across Germany. The 62-year-old has been on long-term sick leavesince 2009, but throughout this period she has continued to receive her full salary as a civil servant teacher. She is now taking legal action against being forced into retirement – because that would mean she would only receive her pension in the future.

 

Most recently, the teacher worked at a vocational college in Wesel. According to WDR and Spiegel, she submitted medical certificates over many years citing a psychological condition. An official medical assessment was not initially ordered. It was only this year that a public health officer concluded that a return to teaching within the next six months could not be expected.

The Düsseldorf district government then ordered at the end of May that the civil servant be placed into retirement. The 62-year-old has since filed a lawsuit against this decision with the Düsseldorf Administrative Court, the court has confirmed.

Until a ruling is made on the lawsuit, she will receive payments equivalent to her pension. According to the district government, any amount exceeding her pension entitlement are currently being withheld. If the teacher succeeds with her claim, these payments would have to be paid out retrospectively.

Suspected fraud and disciplinary proceedings

At the same time, the case is also occupying the law enforcement authorities. The Duisburg public prosecutor's office is investigating on suspicion of commercial fraud. There is suspicion that the teacher at least temporarilyfalsely claimed to be unfit for dutyand worked as an alternative health practitioner while on sick leave.

Back in March, investigators searched her home and seized documents and digital storage devices. According to Spiegel, potentially relevant evidence was found, which is currently being analysed. The investigations cover a period of four years, as any older alleged offences may now be time-barred.

Disciplinary proceedings are also under way against the teacher and against an employee of the Düsseldorf district government. He is accused of having failed for years to initiate a proper review of the alleged permanent incapacity for service.

The case has sparked a nationwide debate on checks on civil servants who are on long-term sick leave. North Rhine-Westphalia's education minister Dorothee Feller (CDU) described the events as "inexcusable" and "incomprehensible in its scale" as long ago as last year.

World.title: Israel's move to recognise Armenian genocide stalls under regional pressure
World.content:
The Israeli parliament's decision to postpone a vote on recognising the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey is being seen as a triumph for regional diplomacy, as Azerbaijan in particular seeks to avert a further escalation in tensions between its close allies.

Advertising

The Israeli government gave no official reason for postponing the vote to formally recognise the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey during World War I, which would have ratified a motion approved by the cabinet last month.

Ankara strongly denies the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Armenians constitute genocide.

While the motion's architect, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, called recognition a “moral duty”, critics say the move took aim at Turkey amidst rising tensions.

Based in Tbilisi, Israeli defence and security expert Eugene Kogan claims Israel badly miscalculated. “Foreign Minister Sa'ar could have waited and not just dropped a bomb that led to different repercussions coming from different sides,” he said.

Armenia, which is seeking to normalise ties with Turkey, reacted coolly, with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan saying he saw no need to comment. Meanwhile, Israel’s close ally Azerbaijan reportedly lobbied Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to drop the motion.

“At the end of the day, it might be either dropped or dismissed, and it will not come again to the new parliament agenda,” predicted Kogan.

The Knesset dissolved on 17 July and won't reconvene until after elections scheduled for 27 October.

Israel's recognition of the Armenian genocide unsettles Turkey and Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan's influence

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that pressure from Azerbaijan tipped the scales, though officials deny it.

Azerbaijan supplies nearly 40 percent of Israel’s oil and is a major customer for Israeli arms. The two countries’ partnership involves frequent Israeli ministerial visits and strong military cooperation, especially crucial for Israel given Azerbaijan’s border with Iran.

Baku also maintains a deep alliance with Ankara, summed up in the phrase “one nation, two states”. As Israeli-Turkish tensions flare over the Gaza conflict and Ankara’s support for Hamas, Azerbaijan is walking a diplomatic tightrope.

Zaur Gasimov, a Caucasus expert at Istanbul’s Turkish-German University, believes Baku viewed the Israeli genocide motion as a direct threat to its difficult balancing act.

“I can imagine that there were negotiations and talks on various levels between political elites of both countries,” he said. “For Israel, Azerbaijan is still of paramount importance. I would even say it's much more significant than it used to be with regard to the situation in and around Iran. So Baku was and is maybe the key intermediary between Israel and the Republic of Turkey.”

In what may be a calculated move to turn up the heat on Israel, Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev welcomed Palestinian Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa this month. It was the first visit by a Palestinian leader since 2011.

“They [Israel] perceive it with a great sense of caution,” claimed analyst Kogan. “They don't know exactly what came out of this particular meeting between Aliyev and the Palestinian prime minister. And so there is a lot of guessing games right now taking place in both Tel Aviv and Jerusalem about the outcome.”

Such ambiguity over Baku’s intentions could strengthen its diplomatic hand, he suggested: “If Aliyev is involved in this Palestinian issue directly and no longer indirectly, it makes the situation very different for the Israelis.”

Turkey warns it could be Israel's 'next enemy' as tensions escalate

Syrian precedent

Baku is already leveraging its strong relationships with both Israel and Turkey to cool tempers.

“We have organised meetings between Turkey and Israel in Baku, specifically at the very beginning of the change of the Assad regime in Syria, where both parties had their own legitimate concerns,” said Hikmet Hajiyev, chief foreign policy adviser to the Azerbaijani president.

Syria is viewed as a potential flashpoint, with Israel and Turkey having a military presence. One tangible outcome of Azeri-brokered talks was the establishment last year of a military hotline in Syria, providing a rare glimmer of hope as tensions continue to mount.

“It's not unavoidable that Israel and Turkey will reach confrontation. I think we can stop this process,” argued Gallia Lindenstrauss, a specialist in Turkish foreign policy at Tel Aviv University's Institute for National Security Studies.

“They have a hotline between the Israeli Air Force and the Turkish Air Force, making sure that we will not have a collision in the skies of Syria, because we know both air forces are operating there. And the hotline has managed to keep the situation quiet. If I'm trying to find some anchor of reassurance that Turkish-Israeli relations can be controlled, it's Syria.”

As Israel approaches elections, a temporary lull in Turkish-Israeli tensions is anticipated. Still, since the main opposition shares the government’s concerns over Turkey, relations are set to remain fraught.

World.title: Germany news: Industry hemorrhaging 15,000 jobs a month
World.content:
07/24/2026 July 24, 2026 Foreign Minister Wadephul draws international law and traffic offense analogy in satire show interview

The show airs as Wadephul returns from a trip to Africa this week Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has taken the bold but risky move of appearing in a feature interview on public television's premiere weekly satirical comedy the "heute-show," roughly like the US "Daily Show."

Wadephul speaks at some length to young anchor Fabian Köster in an elevator in a playful interview that's nevertheless focused on entirely serious topics. It spans NATO relations and Donald Trump and Greenland, Russia's war against Ukraine, the low popularity of government he serves in, the war in Iran and Nicolas Maduro's abduction from Venezuela.

"We're not conducting some kind of foreign policy interview here," Wadephul said at one point with a chuckle after a trickier question, only for Köster to immediately reply "doch!" or roughly "oh, but we are!"

When the topic turned to the US military operation to kidnap Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, Wadephul was asked whether "international law can rub up against the boundaries of Realpolitik."

"Yes, if you're honest, yes, that's the case," Wadephul said. "But to be honest, we're familiar with this in the rule of law. If you think of yourself in road traffic, for instance, have you always kept to everything 100%?"

Köster said he liked the analogy but noted that "a stop sign is something slightly different" than the abduction of a head of state.

"In the law it's written that you can't drive faster than 50 km/h in a built-up area, but nevertheless sometimes people drive faster. And it's the same, fundamentally, in international law. And you have to deal with that. The laws are there to provide an orientation, but they are never dogmatically upheld 100%," Wadephul said.

Asked whether it was "embarrassing" for Germany to only speak up against breaches of international law if "the right countries" are offenders, Wadephul said it was important to note that there were gradations of color.

"There are differences," he said. "If you, like [Russian President Vladimir] Putin, have been waging five years of war against Ukraine and killing thousands upon thousands of people — including your own people — or if you took this one step against a person in power in Venezuela, who did not exactly keep to international law himself: There really is a difference."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz had faced criticism amid the US operations in both Venezuela and Iran for comments suggesting the situations were "complex." Wadephul expanded on this saying they were politically complex but perhaps simpler from a purely legal perspective, still without explicitly saying they were breaches of the law.

The show airs on Friday evening .

World.title: Could 'mesh networks' help overcome authoritarians' internet blocks?
World.content:
In authoritarian countries, the state is often either monitoring online communications or has the ability to shut them down in a political crisis. But there are other ways that activists can keep in touch.

Iran, January 2026: During some of the country's largest protests in decades, the Iranian government shut down the internet.

US-based internet monitor, IODA — short for Internet Outage Detection and Analysis — registered almost no data traffic at all and US internet infrastructure analyst Doug Madory described it as "one of the largest government-directed communication shutdowns in history."

During that time, the Iranian government killed and arrested thousands of people but to this day, nobody knows exactly how many. Estimates of the death toll have been anywhere between 7,000 and 40,000, though many observers suspect its closer to the higher number. The lack of clarity is partially because the internet blackout meant that communication with the outside world was all but impossible.

The Iranian government's behavior is not unusual. In Russia, Belarus, Myanmar and Sudan, particularly when governments fear resistance, the internet has become a weapon — because those who cannot communicate cannot organize.

Radio-powered networks

One solution for these sorts of communications crises could be what is known as a "LoRa mesh network."

Mobile phones may not function if the system overloads in crises or concerts; mesh networks don't overload like that Image: Laurent Zabulon/ABACA/picture alliance

LoRa, which is short for "long range," is based on a simple principle invented for industrial purposes. Small radio modules, also known as LoRa transmitters, have regularly been embedded into physical silicon chips that are used for industrial devices that connect to the internet, things such as smoke alarms, smart water or power meters and environmental sensors — basically any device that requires long battery life and long-range data transmission but only for small amounts of data.

To transmit information, these devices use license-free radio frequencies of the sort available for civilian use, the same frequencies used by weather stations and garage door openers.

To form an internet-free communications network, users first need to purchase a transmitting device that uses LoRa; these can cost anything from about €30 ($35) to €80 ($91). Then users can connect their phone to the device using special software.

The LoRa devices transmit encrypted data packets over a distance of several kilometers. Each device automatically forwards messages to the next one, like a baton being passed through a crowd. If any single device fails, the message finds the next nearby device, via a different route. This means the communications network that is formed can repair itself.

The result of all of the above is what is known as a "LoRa mesh network."

The different transmitting devices are called "nodes" in the network and because there is no central node, there's no way the communications network can be shut down. The radio modules can be kept hidden and powered either by batteries or a small solar panel.

Iran reconnects — but can everyone browse freely? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Only smaller messages, no pictures

The major disadvantage of a network like this is that, unlike the ordinary internet, users can only exchange smaller messages, with a maximum size of around 237 bytes, equivalent to a short text message.

On the other hand, the less data transmitted, the longer the distance it can travel, the less power it consumes, and the less likelihood the radio transmission could be tracked.

Two of the best-known platforms that enable this type of communication are Meshtastic and MeshCore, both of which are free to use and open source.

Both place emphasis on data protection. The transmitting devices merely forward messages and cannot read the content. Third parties, including the police or government agencies, cannot intercept the messages either.

MeshCore's motto is "your communications, your keys, your control."

That the concept works, even under extreme conditions, has been demonstrated by users in Ukraine. Meshtastic-UA offers a real-time network map that shows active nodes throughout the country; there are a lot of nodes near the front lines.

MeshCore has a similar map showing the global distribution of nodes. But there are also many other users who conceal their locations.

This MeshCore map lists the locations of mesh nodes Image: meshcore.co.uk

It's not possible to censor information sent on LoRa mesh networks. When governments halt the internet, they do things like block internet addresses and domains, scrutinize data packets and legally compel providers to cooperate.

For example, Russian security agencies require locally operating telecommunications companies to grant them direct access to communications data. Those who don't comply lose their license. This works mainly if communication takes place over the internet.

That is something that doesn't happen with LoRa mesh networks. The messages travel via radio waves, bypassing firewalls and surveillance systems.

Mesh networks imperfect

There are still risks to this kind of communication, however. For one thing, transmitters can be tracked as encryption protects the content of a message, but not the sender's location. Authorities with the right equipment can triangulate the radio signals, meaning they can physically locate the transmitter to within a certain distance.

Additionally, in some countries, operating unauthorized radio equipment is a criminal offense. In Iran or Russia, being found to be in possession of such devices can have serious legal consequences.

Starlink and the fight for Internet access in Iran To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With any other mesh network — such as those that use mobile phones as transmitters — a LoRa mesh network can only work if enough people participate. If there are not enough nodes, then the distance messages can travel is limited. Building up a network like this takes time, something that isn't possible in crisis situations.

It is unclear whether anti-government activists in authoritarian states are using LoRa mesh networks at all. For good reason, anyone taking part in such a network would prefer not to reveal it.

However Ukraine has demonstrated that the concept can work in the real world. The hardware and required software is freely available worldwide and the technology is mature enough that even people without a lot of technical expertise can set it up themselves .

In a world where more and more governments are using the internet as an instrument of power, and where companies such as Apple are increasingly subject to government pressure, what options are left for safe communication? A network of small radio modules could be the answer for some.

This story was originally published in German.

World.title: Niger still seeking stability after 3 years of military rule
World.content:
The military government in Niger promised social, security, and economic improvements when it took power in 2023. Three years down the line, there are mixed reviews on its performance.

The military seized power in Niger on July 26, 2023. General Abdourahamane Tchiani , who became head of state, justified the coup by citing the poor security situation, which he said persisted despite international support.

In the weeks that followed, the military government announced a transitional period that was to last a maximum of three years.

However, the political promises made upon taking office have not been fulfilled. The transitional government continues to hold all the reins of power, and the security situation in the Sahel country remains fragile.

In the Tillabery region in southwestern Niger, attacks by jihadists are on the rise. Thousands of people have been forced to flee their villages, plunging the region into a severe humanitarian crisis.

Niger's military government has struggled to end an Islamist insurgency despite promises to do so Image: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images

"Today, attacks on the armed forces and the civilian population are significantly more frequent and violent than they were three years ago," Maiga, who lives in the city of Tera, which has a population of 30,000, told DW. Maiga wished to remain anonymous for security reasons.

"Life used to be better despite the insecurity; the weekly markets operated normally and supplies arrived regularly," he said, adding that at the moment entire villages had fled and schools are closed.

The independent conflict monitor ACLED has also said the the security situation has deteriorated since the 2023 coup.

According to the organization, the Tillaberi region remains the main hot spot for clashes between two rival Islamist groups, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin and the so-called Islamic State in the Sahel Province (formerly ISGS). This rivalry has resulted in numerous casualties among soldiers and civilians.

In 2025, nearly 1,200 deaths were recorded in the region. For Heni Nsaibia, a staff member at ACLED, these figures attest to the scale of the security crisis affecting Niger.

The most recent major attack, on July 17, claimed the lives of at least 16 soldiers and 15 terrorists, according to Niger's state media, ANP.

"The situation in Niger has worsened, particularly in the Tillaberi region, where the death toll is the highest in the central Sahel," Nsaibia told DW.

Insecurity taking a toll on civilians

"We live in makeshift shelters and are defenseless against the elements; we take on small odd jobs to survive," a woman told DW.

"I used to be able to live with dignity from my work, but right now it's very difficult; even drinking water is a problem for us," added a local herder.

Young Nigeriens are torn between disappointment and optimism: In the youth assemblies, known as "Fadas," the topic continues to spark discussion. Some — like Fadila — believe that the situation is gradually stabilizing after the turmoil of the first few years.

There was much optimism in Niger after the military took over power three years ago Image: AFP/Getty Images

"For a while, it wasn't easy at all: Salaries weren't paid on time, food supplies… that wasn't easy. But for some time now, things have been going pretty well overall," Fadila told DW.

General Tchiani has emphasized that young people can once again participate in politics. "Before the coup, young people were excluded from decision-making bodies." But in the meantime, he said, an advisory commission has been established that includes young people. "So that means the concerns of young people are now being taken into account in decision-making bodies."

Just two days after the ouster of President Mohamed Bazoumin 2023, junta leader Tchiani announced plans to combat corruption and boost the economy.

But three years later, the people of Niger are no better off, noted Tahirou Garka, a close ally of Bazoum, and spokesperson for the G25, a movement advocating for a return to constitutional order in Niger.

"They have failed economically and socially," he said, referring to the military government. "People are struggling to find drinking water; there is no water, no electricity, no fuel."

What is the Alliance of Democrats for the Sahel? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, Hamani Oumarou of LASDEL, a social sciences research institute based in Niamey, takes a different view. According to him, the socioeconomic situation has improved for a large portion of Niger's population, especially for those who are not part of the middle class or the elite.

"Households with low incomes have more money left over to feed their families," Oumarou told DW. However, Niger is also forced to import food at certain times of the year, which leads to a sharp rise in prices.

Rebuilding ties with ECOWAS

Along with Mali and Burkina Faso, Niger is a founding member of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), formed in 2023 after all three countries withdrew from the West African regional organization ECOWAS.

The AES has distanced itself from Western partners and is seeking closer ties with Russia.

Pape Ibrahima Kane, an expert on international organizations, now hopes for a rapprochement between the AES member states and their longtime allies in West Africa.

The military leaders of the Sahel Alliance support one another militarily and economically, but still face political sanctions by the African Union Image: Mahamadou Hamidou/REUTERS

He sees a positive sign in the fact that former Guinean Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate was elected chief negotiator for ECOWAS a few days ago. According to Kane, Kouyate seems to have been accepted by the AES.

"We are at the beginning of a promising process, as both sides are truly on the same page when it comes to starting talks," he told DW.

For him, economic negotiations should also play a role. Niger depends on access to the port of Benin and on its electricity supply from Nigeria and Benin, both of which are ECOWAS member states.

Reliou Koubakin and Ali Abdou contributed to this article, which was originally written in German.

Correction, July 24, 2026: A previous version of this article stated that Lansana Kouyate is Guinea's current prime minister. This has been corrected.

World.title: Europe wildfires rage on, forcing 200,000 from homes
World.content:
Hot, arid weather and strong winds have continued to fuel wildfires in France, Spain and Italy, devastating huge swaths of land and forcing mass evacuations. As national emergencies are declared, the danger remains.

As wildfires continue to engulf massive stretches of western France and central Spain, some 200,000 people have been forced to flee, with flames devouring forests and homes near Bordeaux and Madrid.

Firefighters have said that the blazes, the largest recorded in both countries in recent years, are so massive that they cannot be tackled head on.

On France's Atlantic coast, 44,000 people were removed from the Cap Ferret peninsula, many by boat.

Towns near Bordeaux, the famed winemaking town popular with tourists, were evacuated "as a precaution" as strong winds fueled approaching flames.

On Saturday morning, regional authorities further ordered the evacuation of three of the city's western suburbs "to ensure residents' safety."

In all, French authorities say more than 140,000 people have been evacuated in France's western Gironde and Landes departments.

In Spain, the Interior Ministry said 60,000 have been forced to flee.

Wildfires in southern Europe cause mass evacuations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU sending firefighting aircraft to France and Spain

Authorities in France say the country's two main blazes were sparked accidentally, however, as summers become drier and hotter the magnitude of such fires has increased exponentially.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who said the government would do everything possible to protect citizens, warned that a wind shift had transformed the Cap Ferret blaze into "a large, self-sustaining fire that is extremely difficult to bring under control."

"It is now moving east, toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area," added Nunez, who pledged, "We are going to reorganize our response so we can fight it from the ground and prevent it from advancing toward Bordeaux."

French President Emmanuel Macron called for European Union assistance on Friday as well as the mobilization of the French army to halt fires that have so far destroyed 22,000 hectares (54,000 acres) of land.

The European Commission announced that it is sending three firefighting aircraft to France and four to Spain in an effort to gain the upper hand.

This week's fires have injured dozens of firefighters and killed three of them — two in western France and one in Sicily, Italy, which is now also battling blazes.

Heat waves fuel wildfires across southern Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Spain declares national emergency

In Spain, the government has declared a national emergency as two of the country's three current fires, all burning near the capital Madrid, merge into one.

Madrid's regional emergency management services said the massive blaze has now reached "its peak and is currently beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain."

The largest active fire in the region, in Guadalajara province, has already laid waste to some 32,000 hectares.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is scheduled to visit affected areas west of the capital on Saturday, as temperatures in the region are expected to top 39 degrees Celsius (102 Fahrenheit).

High winds are also in the forecast, which will make things even more difficult for firefighters.

NASA abandons comms facility amid Spain's summer of fire

The US space agency NASA on Saturday reported that it had been forced to evacuate its Madrid Deep Space Communications Complex (MDSCC), which is located in the region. The facility is one of three worldwide that allow the agency to communicate with spacecraft in distant parts of the galaxy — the others are located in Australia and the US.

"The safety and well being of our personnel is our highest priority and our thoughts are with the families and neighbors who are also experiencing the impact of the wildfires in the surrounding communities," said a statement released by the agency.

Wildfires raging near the Spanish capital Madrid forced the evacuation of a NASA deep space communications center Image: Gabri Solera/Europa Press/IMAGO

Spain, which regularly sees wildfires, has experienced an especially devastating summer. Earlier this month, fires in the south of the country killed 13 people.

Environmental officials say that 1,140 square kilometers (440 square miles) have already been lost to flames this year, more than five times the area burnt throughout the first half of 2025.
