World.title: Polish president renews bid for referendum on EU climate policy
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has submitted a second request to parliament for a nationwide referendum on whether Poland should continue implementing the European Union’s climate policies, which he argues are too costly. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, first proposed a referendum in May. But it was rejected by the Senate, the upper house of parliament, where the more liberal government has a majority. Senators argued that the proposed referendum question was “absurd”. The president has now submitted a revised proposal featuring a simplified question and again proposed holding the referendum on 27 September this year. Nawrocki’s originally proposed question was: “Are you in favour of implementing EU climate policy, which has led to an increase in citizens’ cost of living, energy prices and the cost of running business and agricultural activity?” However, following criticism in the Senate that the question was clearly intended to elicit a specific answer, this time he has proposed a more neutral one: “Are you in favour of Poland implementing the European Union’s climate policy?” “I’m looking for compromises, looking for solutions,” said Nawrocki on Thursday while announcing the new referendum bid. “The Senate wasn’t satisfied with the [previous] question”, so “we prepared a different one…[that] does not suggest anything”. However, the president has also proposed that the ballot paper would include information on what answering “yes” or “no” would mean in practice. Voters would be told, for example, that maintaining EU climate policy would result in, among other things, “Poland bearing costs estimated at 3.5 trillion zloty by 2040”, “burdens on agriculture”, “increasing costs for industry” and “obligations for owners of buildings”. By contrast, voting “no” would mean “negotiating exceptions and exemptions for Poland with the relevant EU bodies that will protect Polish industry and citizens from the burdens of climate policy”. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Under Poland’s constitution, the president may call a referendum with the approval of a majority of senators in a vote where at least half of all members of the 100-seat chamber are present. The ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk controls 63 seats in the Senate, making approval of proposals brought forward by Nawrocki, who often clashes with the government and regularly vetoes its bills, unlikely. While the government is generally pro-EU, it has also been critical of Brussels’ green policies, arguing that they place too great a burden on Poland. After the European Commission last Friday unveiled changes intended to soften the impact of the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS), the EU’s flagship climate policy, they were welcomed by the Polish government as a step in the right direction. Dzisiaj robimy milowy krok w zmianie systemu ETS. Po raz pierwszy Komisja Europejska proponuje rozwiązania, które łagodzą, a nie zaostrzają wpływ systemu na gospodarkę i obywateli. To efekt konsekwentnych działań Polski i zbudowania silnej koalicji państw w UE. Dzisiejsza… pic.twitter.com/5AMd9KCBVa — Ministerstwo Klimatu i Środowiska (@MKiS_GOV_PL) July 17, 2026 However, in his written justification for the new referendum proposal, Nawrocki wrote that, while he had “given the government time” in its push for ETS reform, the final result was simply “technical adjustments” that postpone some elements but do “not change the direction” or ultimate outcome. “ETS will remain an increasingly expensive, increasingly extensive system, and increasingly burdensome for the Polish economy,” wrote the president. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), which is the main opposition and supported Nawrocki’s bid for the presidency last year, wants Poland to unilaterally withdraw from ETS. Government figures warn, however, that there is no way to do so without either accruing enormous fines or leaving the EU entirely. When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Nawrocki’s new referendum proposal was met with criticism by figures from the ruling coalition. “There is no possibility of one country suspending part of EU law,” wrote Stanisław Gawłowski, a senator from Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO) party. “This referendum is pure fraud.” Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, also from KO, wrote that, “as the Brits have learned, the Europhobe’s dream world, in which one enjoys all the privileges of EU membership without any obligations, does not exist”. However, Nawrocki’s initiative was welcomed by Przemysław Czarnek, deputy leader of PiS, who wrote that, “on such fundamental matters as climate policy, Poles should decide, not Brussels bureaucrats”. Zaproponowane przez @NawrockiKn pytanie referendalne jest wybiórcze. Kontrpropozycja: „Czy jesteś za likwidacją unijnych dopłat do inwestycji i dla rolników?” Jak przekonali się Brytyjczycy, świat eurofoba, w którym ma się same przywileje członkostwa w UE, nie istnieje. — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) July 23, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland appoints new human rights commissioner
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government’s majority in parliament has chosen Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram as Poland’s new human rights commissioner. She will take office after the five-year term of the incumbent, Marcin Wiącek, expires today. Gregorczyk-Abram is a prominent lawyer and activist, who is particularly well known for opposing the overhaul of the judiciary by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. PiS, which is now the main opposition party, strongly opposed her election, arguing that she is politically aligned with the current, more liberal government. Gregorczyk-Abram herself, however, has pledged to “put all my beliefs and views aside” when she takes up the new role. Senat wyraził zgodę na powołanie Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram na Rzecznika Praw Obywatelskich. pic.twitter.com/gz3rwGy3hi — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) July 22, 2026 The commissioner for human rights (widely known by its Polish initials, RPO) is appointed by a resolution of the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, with the consent of the upper-house Senate. Candidates must meet certain requirements, including not belonging to any political party and having legal expertise and relevant experience. As well as acting as a watchdog for human rights, the RPO also has the power to submit motions to the Constitutional Tribunal to assess the constitutionality of laws and to file so-called cassation appeals to the Supreme Court and Supreme Administrative Court against rulings by lower courts. Poland’s human rights commissioner has written to the government expressing concern that a "temporary" ban on asylum claims by most migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus remains in place after more than a year https://t.co/9SA2TypQdK — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Gregorczyk-Abram was last month nominated as a candidate to be the new RPO by the main ruling party, Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO), along with one of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica). PiS proposed a rival candidate, Adam Borowski, a veteran of Poland’s anti-communist struggle in the 1980s. However, critics argued that Borowski, an activist and former PiS election candidate, does not appear to have the requisite legal knowledge and experience. In a Sejm vote last Friday, the ruling coalition supported Gregorczyk-Abram, who won 233 votes to Borowski’s 177. On Wednesday, her candidacy was also supported by the Senate, with 59 votes in favour and 25 against, confirming that she will become the new RPO. Gregorczyk-Abram is best known as one of the founders and leaders of the Free Courts (Wolne Sądy) initiative launched in 2017 amid a wave of protests against the then-PiS government’s efforts to take greater control over the judiciary. Free Courts was prominent in efforts to defend the rule of law. Many of its leading figures are now associated with the current ruling coalition: Maria Ejchart is a deputy justice minister, while Michał Wawrykiewicz is a member of the European Parliament representing KO. In April last year, Gregorczyk-Abram was made chairwoman of a commission established by the current government to look into cases of abuse of power against civil society under the former PiS administration. In September, her commission published its first findings, in which it said that public media outlets under PiS control had “carried out systematic repressive and defamatory actions against activists, non-governmental organisations, and civil society”. Poland's public media “carried out systematic repressive actions against activists, NGOs and civil society” during the rule of the former PiS government, a report commissioned by the new government has found https://t.co/S2MO9KGssC — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 26, 2025 PiS argues that Gregorczyk-Abram’s previous activity makes her unsuitable as a suitable candidate for RPO, which is meant to be a non-partisan role. They also point to claims that she was involved in a group of legal figures that discussed the Tusk government’s controversial takeover of public media in December 2023. “[She] is a discredited and extremely politicised person who should be brought to justice, and not receive the laurels of the commissioner for human rights,” former PiS justice minister Marcin Warchoł told the Do Rzeczy weekly last month. After a Sejm committee hearing on Gregorczyk-Abram’s candidacy earlier this month, former PiS deputy justice minister Sebastian Kaleta criticised her for ignoring questions over her alleged “role in the illegal takeover of public media”. Zadałem Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram serię pytań o jej działania i możliwe spotkania z Ewą Wrzosek w sprawie przejęcia TVP, w tym możliwego tworzenia dokumentów prokuratorskich w prywatnej kancelarii. Kandydatka ostentacyjnie zdecydowała się ignorować te pytania. Ma bardzo dużo do… — Sebastian Kaleta (@sjkaleta) July 15, 2026 Speaking to state broadcaster TVP on Wednesday after her appointment was confirmed by the Senate, Gregorczyk-Abram declared that, “from the moment I take the oath and assume the position of commissioner, I will be independent and sovereign”. She pledged to “put all my beliefs and views – because each of us has them – aside and become an advocate for all citizens, regardless of what they believe in, how they live, or who they vote for”. Gregorczyk-Abram said that among her priorities as RPO would be the justice system, supporting the rights of disabled people and their carers, protecting older people, and fighting hate speech. With regard to the last of these issues, she noted that certain politicians present some groups as “enemies”, pointing to how this previously happened with LGBT+ people and judges, and is now being directed towards Ukrainians. Those are all groups who have at various stages been targeted by PiS and other right-wing parties. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. World.title: President to swear in new judge to Poland’s disputed constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has agreed to swear in a new judge to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), ending weeks of doubt as to whether the opposition-aligned president would accept the judge appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority. Although Sławomir Patyra will now be accepted onto the court, four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year continue to be excluded after Nawrocki refused to receive their oaths and the TK’s chief justice, also aligned with the opposition, blocked them from taking office. W najbliższy wtorek 28 lipca Prezydent Karol Nawrocki działając na postawie art. 4 ust. 1 ustawy o statusie sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, przyjmie ślubowanie od prof. Sławomira Patyry i tego samego dnia wręczy powołania czterem nowym sędziom Sądu Najwyższego. W przyszłym… — Zbigniew Bogucki🇵🇱 (@BoguckiZbigniew) July 22, 2026 Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK – for example when a judge’s nine-year term expires – the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again this week, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. Patyra himself has also made clear on which side of the dispute he stands. In an interview with news website Onet in May, he accused Nawrocki and Święczkowski of “blatantly unlawful actions” in deciding which TK judges can and cannot take office and suggested that the police should intervene. Sędzia TK prof. Patyra po raz kolejny zaapelował do Prezydenta o wyznaczenie mu terminu na złożenie przysięgi. Ignorowanie sędziego TK przez Prezydenta jest kolejnym przykładem psucia państwa. To pokazuje, jak bardzo siły anty-demokratyczne boją się odbudowy niezależnego TK.… — Dariusz Mazur (@_Dariusz_Mazur) July 21, 2026 Finally, on Wednesday this week, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, announced that Nawrocki had invited Patyra to the presidential palace on Tuesday next week to take his oath. Speaking to Polsat News, Bogucki said that, in the case of Patyra, initially “there were some doubts, but the president dispelled them”, without specifying what they were. In the end, they concluded that “we had a fundamentally clean situation here” and Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”, unlike the six new judges chosen by the Sejm in March to fill longstanding vacancies. “It was not President Nawrocki or the current opposition who destroyed and are destroying the tribunal; it is the government that is doing it,” he added. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. World.title: Germany deploys soldiers to Poland to help reinforce eastern borders
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Germany has deployed soldiers to Poland to help reinforce defences on NATO’s eastern flank in response to the threat of Russia. While Poland already hosts various allied forces, the presence of German troops is particularly symbolic given the two countries’ difficult history. “United, we will prevail,” wrote the General Staff of the Polish Armed Forces (SGWP), announcing the deployment. “This is what allied cooperation looks like in practice, which translates into greater military readiness and strengthens NATO’s defensive potential.” Polscy i niemieccy żołnierze razem wzmacniają granicę z Rosją. Takie rzeczy możliwe tylko za Tuska ☺️ pic.twitter.com/oNBME2gBsv — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 22, 2026 Last December, the Polish and German defence ministries revealed that a “mid-double-digit number” of German troops would be deployed from mid-2026 until the end of 2027 to support implementation of Poland’s East Shield operation, which seeks to bolster defences along the borders with Belarus and Russia. They said that the German personnel would mainly engage in engineering work, such as digging trenches, laying barbed wire and constructing anti-tank barriers. Today, Poland’s SGWP confirmed that “several dozen” German troops, including “highly specialised engineering forces” along with their equipment, had since June been temporarily deployed to “support the Polish armed forces in expanding defence infrastructure on NATO’s northeastern flank”. It emphasised that the East Shield project is “purely defensive in nature” and comes in “response to threats stemming from, among others, Russian aggression against Ukraine”. While the armed forces did not reveal the location of the deployment, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated in a social media post that it was on the Russian border. Poland has a 210-km frontier with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. German public broadcaster Deutsche Welle reports that the activities of the German sappers are focused in particular on improving defences around the so-called Suwałki Gap, a strategically important stretch of land around the Polish-Lithuanian border between Belarus and Kaliningrad. “Together, we are ensuring Europe’s security,” said Lieutenant General Alexander Sollfrank, the Bundeswehr’s operational commander, announcing the deployment today. “Through our engagement in Poland, we are strengthening NATO’s defence capabilities and underscoring the alliance’s unwavering commitment to ensuring peace through unity and credible deterrence.” Poland and Germany have signed a bilateral security agreement that will see the two neighbours and NATO allies increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity https://t.co/6BPX2WxvxH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 SGWP, which shared footage of Polish and German forces installing anti-tank barriers, said the work aims to “hinder and delay an aggressor’s actions in the event of a threat”, thereby “increasing the time for a response from the Polish armed forces and the entire [NATO] alliance”. It also seeks to “create conditions for the efficient reception, deployment and use of NATO forces on Polish territory”. SGWP welcomed “the involvement of the German contingent as a practical expression of allied solidarity and the result of consistently developing military cooperation between Poland and Germany”. It also noted that the cooperation would help the two sides improve their ability to operate jointly, including “developing the competencies necessary for conducting a joint defence operation”. However, it emphasised that the current deployment is focused on training and engineering, with no combat component, and that the German troops are unarmed. SGWP also emphasised that the East Shield operation remains entirely a Polish national programme. The leaders of eight countries on the EU's eastern flank have met in the first summit of its kind to discuss closer security cooperation. Finland and Poland announced that they would jointly lead an initiative, Eastern Flank Watch, to bolster defences https://t.co/fxRHpkM6w9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 The deployment of German troops to Poland comes shortly after the two countries signed a defence cooperation agreement in which they pledged to increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity. The agreement is a sign that the two countries now stand “shoulder to shoulder, as equals”, declared German defence minister Boris Pistorius. Poland is also currently seeking a new permanent US military base on its territory, after President Donald Trump recently pledged to boost American troop numbers. Last week, Tusk also announced that Poland will host military exercises involving France and the UK this autumn. Poland will host military exercises later this year with France and the UK to prepare for providing future security guarantees to Ukraine, says PM @donaldtusk. World.title: Prague Compared to 11 European Cities: Housing, Jobs, Transport,
World.content:
A new report from the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR) compares life in Prague with 11 other European cities, following a typical resident’s day—from housing and commuting to work, education, and leisure.

Based on verified data collected directly from partner cities, the study highlights both Prague’s strengths and its biggest challenges.

Prague Has Some of Europe’s Least Affordable Housing

The report found that Prague has the least affordable owner-occupied housing among the cities compared.

Buying an apartment requires more than 13 years of gross salary, placing Prague alongside cities such as Barcelona, Munich, and Amsterdam. Unlike many Western European cities, Prague also lacks relatively affordable rental housing.

Renting a 60-square-meter apartment costs around 40% of the average salary in Prague. By comparison, the same apartment would consume about 28% of average income in Munich and just 14% in Vienna.

Strong Job Market, But Lower Incomes

Prague continues to have one of the lowest unemployment rates in Europe, making it relatively easy to find work.

However, real incomes remain below those of most Western European capitals. Workers in Munich earn roughly 50% more than those in Prague, while wages in cities such as Copenhagen have grown steadily over the past decade.

Although Prague residents now work fewer hours than they did ten years ago—less than 39 hours per week on average—they still work around three hours more each week than people in many Western European cities.

Public Transport Is One of Prague’s Biggest Strengths

Prague ranks among Europe’s top cities for public transport.

Around 70% of residents use public transport regularly, while 87% report being satisfied with the service. The city’s extensive tram, metro, and rail networks make commuting easy, and the system stands out for its reliability, dense coverage, and affordability.

A monthly public transport pass costs less than 1% of the average monthly income, making Prague one of the most affordable cities for public transport after Barcelona.

Car Ownership Continues to Rise

Despite having one of Europe’s best public transport systems, Prague continues to see a steady increase in car ownership.

Together with Warsaw and Bucharest, Prague is one of the few cities in the study where the number of registered cars is still growing significantly. By contrast, cities such as Stockholm, Copenhagen, and Vienna have between one-third and one-half fewer cars per capita and a much higher share of electric and hybrid vehicles.

The report warns that increasing car ownership contributes to traffic congestion, road accidents, poorer air quality, and greater pressure on public space.

World.title: Meet the Four Prague Pizzerias Recognized in 50 Top Pizza Europa 2026
World.content:
Prague’s growing pizza scene gained international attention after four local restaurants were recognized in the 50 Top Pizza Europa 2026 guide.

The biggest success went to Pizza Nuova, which secured 30th place among the best pizzerias in Europe outside Italy. While the restaurant slipped a few places compared with last year’s ranking, it remains the only Czech establishment to appear in the guide’s main European list.

Located near Prague’s Kotva department store, Pizza Nuova has built its reputation on authentic Neapolitan pizza made with premium Italian ingredients. The restaurant also holds certification from the Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana, an organization that promotes traditional Neapolitan pizza-making standards.

Prague’s recognition extended beyond a single restaurant. Three additional venues received the guide’s Excellent Pizzerias distinction, awarded to restaurants that consistently demonstrate outstanding quality.

This year’s recipients are Da Pietro, Sasy The Original, and Diskotéka in Prague’s Dejvice district.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pizzeria Da Pietro Praha (@dapietropraha)

Diskotéka is one of this year’s notable newcomers. Shortly after opening, the restaurant attracted attention for its distinctive interior, centered around a large silver pizza oven designed to resemble a disco ball.

Alongside its food, the venue hosts DJ nights and combines a traditional pizzeria with a relaxed social gathering space.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Diskotéka Pizza (@diskoteka.pizza)

The annual 50 Top Pizza rankings are compiled by anonymous inspectors who visit restaurants without prior notice. Their assessments go well beyond the pizza itself, taking into account ingredient quality, dough preparation, baking technique, service, beverage selection, atmosphere, and the overall dining experience.

World.title: Czech Women Earn About CZK 109,000 Less Per Year Than Men
World.content:
Czech women earn significantly less than men on average, with the annual difference estimated at CZK 109,000.

New figures based on Eurostat data show the country’s gender pay gap remains above the EU average.

Across the EU, employed women earn an estimated CZK 93,800 less annually than men on average. The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC), which converted the hourly wage gap into annual earnings, estimates that the combined difference across the bloc amounts to more than CZK 8.65 trillion every year.

Czech Republic exceeds the EU average

According to Eurostat, women across the European Union earned 11.1% less per hour than men in 2024. In practical terms, women received CZK 88.90 for every CZK 100 earned by men. The figures cover companies with at least ten employees.

Applying that methodology, the ETUC estimates that women in the Czech Republic earn roughly CZK 108,700 less per year than men, placing the country above the EU average.

Only a handful of member states recorded larger estimated annual gaps. Finland ranked highest at around CZK 183,500, followed by Austria (CZK 165,600), Germany (CZK 146,200) and Sweden (CZK 123,600).

At the opposite end of the scale, Luxembourg was the only EU country where women earned slightly more than men on average. There, women’s hourly earnings exceeded men’s by 0.8%, equivalent to roughly CZK 11,500 annually in their favor under the ETUC model. Estonia recorded the largest percentage gap in the bloc, at 18.8%.

Different methods produce different figures

National Czech statistics paint a somewhat different picture because they rely on a different methodology.

Data from the Czech Statistical Office shows that in 2025 the median gross monthly wage reached CZK 41,068 for women and CZK 47,648 for men. That represents a monthly difference of CZK 6,580, or just under CZK 79,000 over a full year.

The discrepancy does not mean either calculation is incorrect. Eurostat measures average gross hourly earnings, while the Czech Statistical Office compares median monthly wages. Because the indicators measure different aspects of income, the results cannot be directly compared.

Eurostat uses an unadjusted gender pay gap, which reflects a range of labor market factors, including differences in occupations, industries, management roles, work experience, career interruptions, age and the balance between public and private sector employment.

World.title: Spicy, Not Spicy: How This Chef Is Bringing Authentic Chinese Street Food to Prague
World.content:
At Manifesto Market, the aroma of Sichuan peppercorns and chili oil stands out among the usual mix of street food and drinks.

It comes from Lá Bù Lá Street, the more casual sibling of the restaurant Lá Bù Lá, both founded by Wen, a Chongqing native who wants to introduce Prague diners to the real flavors of her hometown.

Wen arrived in Prague in 2019 after being accepted into a Master’s program at the Prague University of Economics and Business. But studying was only part of the reason she moved. At 22, she wanted a new beginning and the chance to discover a different version of herself.

“There was something about Prague that attracted me immediately,” she says. “The architecture, the pace of life, the atmosphere of the city —

it all felt very charming. I wanted to see what kind of person I could become here.”

That decision eventually led her into the restaurant business, with four concepts launched over the years — two that closed and two that continue today.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Lá Bù Lá Street (@labula_street)

Beyond the Stereotypes

For Wen, opening a Chinese restaurant in Prague was never only about selling food. It was also about showing people that Chinese cuisine is far more diverse than many stereotypes suggest.

“China is a huge country, and every region has its own culture and food traditions,” she says. Through her restaurants, she hopes guests become more curious about where dishes come from, how ingredients are used, and how different regions eat.

She also wants Chinese food to be seen as something connected to special occasions, not only a quick meal.

“Chinese food can create beautiful memories too,” she says. One example is Chongqing chili, which is often associated only with heat. Wen says there is much more to it.

“Many people think Chongqing chili is only about being spicy. But it is also about aroma,” she explains. The same applies to Sichuan peppercorns, where the famous numbing sensation is only part of the experience.

Learning the Hard Way

Wen’s path has not been simple. Her first two projects, Chi Xiao Mian and Mi I’m, did not succeed as she had hoped, but she sees them as important lessons.

“They taught me how to work with people, how to manage a team, and how important communication is,” she says.

The experience also taught her to stay focused on her original vision. Running a restaurant requires listening to others, but also knowing when to trust your own ideas.

“Building something meaningful always requires finding a balance between dreams and reality,” she says.

A Restaurant, and Then a Street

Today, Wen runs two concepts: Lá Bù Lá and Lá Bù Lá Street. The name, meaning “spicy, not spicy,” reflects the idea that Chongqing cuisine is about much more than just heat.

The original restaurant offers a deeper introduction to traditional Chongqing dishes, while Lá Bù Lá Street at Manifesto Market has a more relaxed atmosphere.

“It is more spontaneous and more social,” Wen says. The concept is inspired by street food culture in Chongqing, where people gather, share dishes, and spend time together.

At Manifesto, surrounded by music, travelers, and international crowds, the idea has naturally evolved. Some dishes work better for sharing, while others simply encourage people to stay longer.

“For us, food tastes better when shared,” Wen says. “Passed around a table. Offered to a friend. Or quietly stolen from someone else’s plate.”

Growing Step by Step

Like many restaurant owners, Wen faces daily challenges, from managing a team to introducing unfamiliar flavors to new customers. Building a group of people who share her values has been one of the most difficult parts.

When asked about opening more locations in Prague, she says the ambition is there — but there is no rush.

“Of course, I would love for more people to discover the food of my hometown,” she says. “But I am not in a hurry.”

For now, Wen is focused on improving the restaurants she already has and building a stronger team.

“When my team and I are truly ready, we can always begin the next journey,” she says. “For now, we are happy to keep growing step by step.”

World.title: Prague and Stockholm Launch Cross-Border Public Art Project
World.content:
Visitors in Prague and Stockholm will soon be able to communicate across borders through a pair of interactive public art installations designed to exchange anonymous messages between the two cities.

The linked installations, created by the Czech initiative Praho! project and its Swedish partner Stockholm! project, will open in Stockholm on August 20 and in Prague on August 31.

The installations are designed as private spaces intended for one visitor at a time.

After entering, participants answer a series of questions before listening to an authentic audio recording left by someone in the other city. They are then invited to record their own message, creating an ongoing exchange between residents and visitors in Prague and Stockholm.

According to the project team, the concept explores what happens when anonymous thoughts become personal through the human voice.

“The installation creates a space where you first listen to someone else—and only then can you speak,” the organizers said. “We want to explore how connecting two different cities through shared experiences can foster understanding.”

The initiative is part of Art & Design Without Borders, an international collaboration supported by the Erasmus+ programme. The project brings together organizations from the Czech Republic and Sweden to promote participatory art, community engagement and new approaches to public space.

Although they work closely together, Praho! project and Stockholm! project operate as independent non-profit organizations. Their partnership reflects a shared history rather than a branch structure.

Praho! project was founded in 2021 and focuses on participatory art in public and digital spaces. Through text-based interventions and an online platform, it has collected more than 30,000 anonymous responses addressing personal experiences and broader social issues. Those contributions have since been transformed into publications, exhibitions and artistic installations.

The concept, however, began even earlier. Founder Annamarie Čermáková first developed the idea in 2019 while studying at Stockholm University of the Arts. Returning to Sweden inspired the creation of Stockholm! project in 2025.

The project extends beyond the installations themselves. Organizers will also host workshops, educational programmes, international internships and prepare a methodology guide documenting best practices in participatory public art across different European settings.

World.title: BAY55: 114 Luxury Apartments Planned for Prague’s Riverfront in Smíchov
World.content:
One of the last undeveloped riverfront plots in central Prague is set to become home to a new luxury residential project.

Developer Daramis has unveiled plans for BAY55, a development featuring 114 high-end apartments on Hořejší nábřeží in Smíchov, just steps from the railway bridge and within walking distance of the city center.

According to Daramis, BAY55 is designed to compete with premium residential developments in leading European and North American cities. The company says the project will emphasize architecture, technology, privacy and resident services alongside its prime location.

The residence will include a wellness and fitness center covering roughly 600 square meters, a private residents’ lounge and hospitality facilities.

A restaurant or café is also planned on the ground floor, serving both residents and visitors. The developer says the level of amenities is intended to match those found in luxury hotels.

Designers have also focused on balancing density with comfort. Every apartment is planned to include either a spacious balcony or terrace, complemented by integrated shading systems intended to provide greater privacy despite the urban setting.

Before construction of the residential complex can begin, significant work will be carried out along the riverfront.

The existing Smíchov embankment will be extended, creating additional public space and improving pedestrian access along the Vltava. The infrastructure upgrades are expected to become part of the wider transformation of one of Prague’s fastest-growing neighborhoods.

Daramis acquired the land from BPD Development in 2024. Although the developer has not disclosed the value of the investment, it says BAY55 represents the largest and most expensive project in the company’s history.

Costs are driven not only by the location and construction standards, but also by flood protection measures, advanced building technologies and architectural features planned for the shared spaces.

The project is currently progressing through the permitting process. If approvals proceed as expected, construction of the new embankment will begin first, followed by the residential development itself.

Completion is currently scheduled for around 2030.

World.title: From Müller to Krispy Kreme, Global Chains Are Coming to Czechia
World.content:
International drugstores, fashion retailers, discount chains and restaurant concepts are preparing to open their first locations in Czechia, adding new competition for established players.

Here are some of the biggest brands expected to enter the Czech market.

Müller

German retailer Müller is preparing to launch in the Czech Republic. The company has already established a Czech branch and website, although it has not yet announced the opening date of its first store.

Unlike traditional drugstores, Müller combines cosmetics and personal care products with toys, stationery, household goods, pet supplies and organic food.

The chain operates nearly 1,000 stores across nine European countries and will compete with established Czech market leaders such as dm, Rossmann and Teta.

Krispy Kreme

American doughnut chain Krispy Kreme is reportedly searching for a location in central Prague and could open its first Czech store soon.

Founded in North Carolina in 1937, the company became famous worldwide for its Original Glazed doughnuts and stores where customers can watch the production process.

Ochnik

Polish fashion brand Ochnik plans an ambitious expansion in the Czech Republic, with 15 to 20 stores expected by the end of 2026.

The company specializes in leather jackets, footwear, luggage and accessories. It previously considered acquiring Czech brand Kara but decided to build its own network instead.

OVS

Italian fashion retailer OVS is also preparing its Czech debut.

The company focuses on affordable clothing for the whole family and is particularly strong in children’s fashion. It is positioned between discount retailers and mainstream brands such as H&M, C&A and Reserved.

Normal

Danish discount chain Normal is preparing to enter the Czech market after establishing a local company.

The retailer sells cosmetics, household products, snacks and everyday goods at permanently low prices. Its stores are designed to encourage impulse shopping, with customers walking through a changing selection of products.

MR. D.I.Y.

Malaysian discount retailer MR. D.I.Y. has some of the biggest expansion plans among new arrivals.

The company plans to open around 20 stores in Prague and eventually grow to more than 100 locations across the Czech Republic. Its first Czech store is expected to open at Forum Nová Karolina in Ostrava.

MR. D.I.Y. sells household equipment, DIY products, electronics and stationery.

Burgermeister

Berlin burger chain Burgermeister will enter the Czech Republic as part of its European expansion.

The brand started in 2006 inside a converted toilet building near Berlin’s Schlesisches Tor station before growing into a chain with more than 30 restaurants.

It focuses on its own production, including burgers made with Irish beef and ingredients prepared in Berlin.

Dave’s Hot Chicken

American fast-food chain Dave’s Hot Chicken is preparing to compete with KFC and Popeyes in the Czech market.

The brand specializes in Nashville-style spicy fried chicken, offering chicken tenders and sandwiches with different levels of heat.

Founded in Los Angeles in 2017, the chain has expanded to more than 400 locations worldwide.

Arthur Gelato

Slovak premium ice cream brand Arthur Gelato has already opened its first Prague location on Francouzská Street.

The company focuses on handmade ice cream, fresh ingredients and unusual flavors. It plans further expansion through franchising.

Sticks’n’Sushi

Danish restaurant group Sticks’n’Sushi will open its first Prague location this autumn.

The concept combines Japanese sushi with grilled skewers and will operate a three-story restaurant on Jungmann Square with around 160 seats.

World.title: Five Things to Know Before Flying From Prague Airport This Summer
World.content:
Passengers departing from Prague Airport this summer are being advised to plan ahead as the airport prepares for its busiest travel season in years.

To help travelers avoid unnecessary delays, the airport has released a list of practical recommendations covering transport, security screening, travel documents and baggage rules.

Leave Extra Time to Reach the Airport

The biggest challenge this summer is expected to be road access to the terminals. Construction at the Aviatická–Lipská intersection may cause traffic congestion on routes leading to the airport.

Airport officials recommend using public transport whenever possible, as buses are not affected by the roadworks. Travelers arriving by car should allow extra time to reach the terminals, particularly during peak holiday periods.

Self-Service Check-In Can Save Time

Passengers can speed up the departure process by using the airport’s self-service facilities. Prague Airport now offers 31 check-in kiosks and 32 self-service baggage drop counters, available for flights operated by 18 participating airlines.

Before heading to the airport, travelers should also verify the entry requirements for their destination. Those flying to the United Kingdom, for example, now need an Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) before departure.

Bring Physical Travel Documents

Although many travelers rely on digital wallets and electronic documents, Prague Airport reminds passengers that electronic IDs and passports cannot be used during passport control.

Travelers should carry a valid physical passport or national identity card, depending on the requirements of their destination.

Security Rules Depend on the Terminal

Passengers departing from Terminal 2 will notice a faster security process thanks to newly installed CT scanners.

The new technology allows travelers to leave electronics and liquids inside their cabin baggage during screening. In addition to the standard one-liter transparent bag containing containers of up to 100 milliliters each, passengers may also carry one extra liquid container with a capacity of up to two liters.

These updated rules currently apply only in Terminal 2. Security procedures in Terminal 1 remain unchanged.

Pack Power Banks Correctly

The airport is also reminding travelers about one of the most common packing mistakes.

Power banks, laptops and tablets must always be transported in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage. In addition, lithium batteries must not exceed 100 Wh unless specifically approved by the airline. Ignoring these rules can lead to delays during security checks or, in some cases, passengers being refused boarding.

World.title: Two centuries of history: Why the Hungarian Grand Prix trophy is so iconic
World.content:
Fans hardly need to be told just how much drivers long to get their hands on the Hungarian Grand Prix trophies. For many years now, the top three finishers have been rewarded with creations from the Herend Porcelain Manufactory, which rank among the most exceptional pieces of the entire season. Crafting these awards, however, involves a tremendous amount of work, and it’s no coincidence that they are so valuable.

Author: Tamás Szikora

A 200-year-old tradition comes to life at the 40-year-old Hungaroring

While the racetrack in Mogyoród has been home to the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix and numerous prestigious international races for exactly four decades, the Herend Porcelain Manufactory is celebrating its 200th anniversary. Founded in 1826, the manufactory is now not only synonymous with handcrafted porcelain but has also become part of Hungary’s cultural heritage. This is one of the reasons why the trophies they create are such a perfect fit for the Hungarian Grand Prix. Just as teams strive for perfection on the racetrack and drivers must demonstrate tremendous precision, these values are also reflected in the products of this iconic brand.

Although there were periods when various sponsors awarded trophies to the winner and podium finishers, the histories of Herend and the Hungarian Grand Prix have long been intertwined. It was Jenson Button who, in 2006, won one of the Grand Prix’s most memorable races and received this special porcelain trophy as a reward for his first career victory. Since then, with a few brief interruptions, the Herend Porcelain Manufactory has generally produced the trophies for the podium finishers, which the drivers themselves consider among the most special. This is no coincidence, as it is not only the appearance of these trophies that makes them special.

Photo: Hungaroring Média

Their value stems, among other things, from the fact that they are handmade, taking several months to achieve their final form and appearance, while drawing inspiration from elements of Hungarian folk art. Not to mention that every phase of the production process was carried out using the Herend Porcelain Manufactory’s traditional artisanal techniques. Each piece is a one-of-a-kind work of art, including the trophies set to be awarded in 2026, which are all distinct from one another. The trophies’ rankings were highlighted in a unique way.

The trophy for first place is gold, the second-place award is platinum, and the one for third place is accented with bronze tones. According to the manufactory’s announcement, the piece created for the winner is 53 centimetres tall and weighs 3 kilograms, with its decoration based on Herend’s iconic Hungarian-style gold ornamentation. Of course, the winning design team was not forgotten either; the top team receives an openwork porcelain bowl measuring 520 millimetres in diameter and weighing 4 kilograms. Interestingly, the trophy for the runner-up is made of platinum rather than silver because, unlike silver, platinum does not oxidise.

The special relationship between Herend and F1

Several events over the past decade or so have further boosted the reputation of the Herend Porcelain Manufactory. Sebastian Vettel triumphed in the 2015 Hungarian Grand Prix driving a Ferrari, but the simpler metal trophy did not really win his approval. His complaints quickly made their way through the global press, but in the end, he was surprised with a smaller Herend trophy. This clearly demonstrated that there is a demand for legendary works of art, a sentiment further reinforced when, later on, many others spoke out about the sponsor-provided trophies used in several countries and the often unremarkable awards.

However, this is just one of the stories that highlighted the connection between the manufactory and the sport. In 2023, Max Verstappen won the race held at the Hungaroring, but while celebrating with champagne on the podium, Lando Norris, who had finished in second place, accidentally shattered the Dutch driver’s one-of-a-kind porcelain trophy with a clumsy move. Everyone could see how a trophy worth 15 million forints—which had been crafted by roughly thirty artisans over the course of about half a year—was shattered. In the end, the story concluded with the fact that, since Herend offers a lifetime replacement guarantee for these pieces and the trophy’s design was still available, a new one was produced within a few weeks. They personally delivered it to Verstappen at the time, and Norris was also present at the handover, which made the footage of the event even more widely shared.

Partly as a result of this, the idea arose for Norris to race in Hungary in 2024 wearing a hand-painted Herend-style helmet created in collaboration with the manufactory. Through these stories, in response to a question from Totalcar in early July of this year, it was revealed that both Sebastian Vettel and Lando Norris had been elected honorary members of the Herend Porcelain Manufactory; moreover, a few years ago, the McLaren driver even spent a short time at the painting tables. We eagerly await seeing how the unique story of F1, the Hungarian Grand Prix, and Herend porcelain will unfold starting in 2026.

World.title: Warning: Hungary to be the hottest in Central Europe as the biggest heatwave creeps closer to the country
World.content:
Hungary has just seen an unusual early-morning cold record fall, with 4.6°C measured in Lénárddaróc at 5 AM, according to the meteorological service. But the relief will be short-lived, because a new and intense heatwave is expected to build quickly over the coming days.

Sunday should still bring relatively fresh mornings, though daytime temperatures will already rise above 30°C across a wide area. By the second half of next week, much hotter air is forecast to arrive.

Heatwave builds again from next week

The outlook suggests that from the first days of August, temperatures above 35°C are likely to return. HungaroMet has also shown a forecast indicating that in Szeged there is a more than 20 per cent chance of temperatures climbing above 40°C during the first week of August.

The current pattern points to no clear end to the hot spell yet. That means Hungary could be heading into a prolonged period of extreme summer weather rather than a brief burst of heat.

Hungary may be the hottest in the region

Medium-range forecasts suggest that a longer-lasting heatwave will reach the country again within days. Rain and thunderstorms are still possible in isolated places on Sunday and Monday, but from Tuesday the airflow is expected to turn south-westerly and temperatures should rise day by day.

By 3 August, Hungary may be the biggest victim of the heatwave in Central Europe, with the highest chance of exceeding 35°C concentrated over the middle of the Carpathian Basin. Forecast averages currently point to daytime highs of around 36°C to 39°C, although that figure may still increase as the forecast becomes more refined, writes Időkép.

What to expect

The main message is straightforward: the brief cool spell is over, and much hotter weather is coming back fast. Even if the exact peak shifts slightly, the overall direction is clear, with Hungary once again likely to sit near the top of the European temperature charts.

For readers, that means the next few days are the time to prepare for extreme heat rather than enjoy a long-lasting break from it.

World.title: Youngest Indian diplomat Dr. Mukesh Kumar Srivastava’s Hungarian farewell message draws widespread public appreciation
World.content:
In a heartfelt gesture reflecting the close cultural ties between India and Hungary, youngest Indian diplomat Dr. Mukesh Kumar Srivastava concluded his tenure as Director of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre (ASCC), Embassy of India in Budapest, by sharing a farewell video message in the Hungarian language.

Photo: Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre

The video, accompanied by a Hungarian-language social media post, received an overwhelming response from Hungarians, members of the Indian community, artists, academics, journalists, and cultural personalities. Many praised the gesture as a reflection of Mukesh’s sincere respect for Hungary and his efforts to build meaningful relationships beyond the traditional framework of diplomacy.

In his farewell message, Mukesh expressed gratitude to the Government and people of Hungary, the Indian community, cultural and academic partners, media, and friends for their support in strengthening the longstanding cultural ties between the two countries.

Reflecting on his tenure, he described Hungary as a country that would always hold a special place in his heart, saying that his three-year in Budapest had left him with unforgettable memories, lasting friendships, and invaluable experiences.

During his tenure, the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre significantly expanded its activities, organising and supporting a wide range of cultural, literary, educational, yoga, Ayurveda, music, dance, and artistic programmes that strengthened people-to-people connections between India and Hungary. Under his leadership, the Centre organised, on average, more than 100 programmes annually.

Among the major initiatives introduced during his tenure was the “India Knowledge Series”, which brought together Hungarian experts from diverse fields to promote a deeper understanding of India. He also significantly expanded yoga activities across Hungary, with the Centre organising more than 100 yoga events this year—the highest number in its history. Another key initiative was strengthening partnerships with schools, colleges, and universities across Hungary through lectures, cultural presentations, workshops, and academic outreach programmes, further enhancing educational cooperation and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries.

Mukesh became widely known for his humility, accessibility, and genuine personal engagement. His commitment to learning the Hungarian language was particularly appreciated and was widely seen as a sign of his respect for Hungarian culture and his desire to connect more deeply with local communities. He regularly incorporated Hungarian into his public speeches, a gesture that many viewed as both meaningful and uncommon for a foreign diplomat.

His farewell message prompted an outpouring of appreciation from across Hungary. Many described him as an inspiring and compassionate leader who encouraged artists, supported young talent, and promoted Indian culture with warmth, professionalism, and sincerity. Others praised his openness, kindness, and ability to build lasting friendships that extended well beyond official diplomatic responsibilities.

Have you read this? Hungary celebrates Diwali 2025 at the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre – photo report

In a comment on the farewell post, Amar Kumar Sinha, a senior member of the Indian community who has lived in Hungary for more than five decades, described Mukesh’s tenure as unprecedented. He noted that the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre organised, on average, more than 100 cultural programmes annually under his leadership, attributing this achievement to his dedication, enthusiasm, and unwavering commitment to promoting Indian culture.

Many farewell messages on social media also highlighted that Mukesh’s leadership had created numerous opportunities for cultural exchange, education, yoga, music, dance, and artistic collaboration, while strengthening mutual understanding between the people of India and Hungary. Several described him not only as an accomplished diplomat but also as a mentor, a trusted friend, and an exceptional human being whose kindness and respect left a lasting impression.

If you missed it: Rhythms that unite cultures: ASCC celebrates International Dance Day in Budapest – photos

The overwhelming response to Mukesh’s farewell illustrates the deep personal and cultural connections forged during his years in Hungary and reflects the enduring friendship between the people of India and Hungary, strengthened through cultural exchange, mutual respect, and lasting human relationships.

World.title: Orbán changes tone at Tusványos: Fidesz recast its role as “resistance politics” shifts into gear
World.content:
Viktor Orbán used his address at the Bálványos Summer University in Baile Tusnad (Tusnádfürdő) to argue that Fidesz must move away from traditional opposition politics and adopt what he called “resistance politics”.

He said the party’s immediate task is no longer mainly self-criticism after defeat, but defending what he described as Hungary’s freedom. Orbán said he did not believe voters who backed change in the spring had done so in bad faith. In his telling, many had simply expected fewer government mistakes and stronger economic performance.

Freedom, not party politics

According to Orbán, freedom in Hungary is “not a party issue”, and Fidesz should act as a broad umbrella for everyone who values it. He said the party should not behave like a normal party organisation, but more like a “service centre” and “incubator” for freedom-minded groups and organisations.

He also said the movement should stand by its 2.5 million voters, but insisted that would not be enough on its own for a majority. He argued that the missing support would come from “political waves created by reality” and from what he called a broader coalition for freedom.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Péter Magyar quoted Závecz Research Institute’s latest survey, which claims that the governing Tisza Party is more popular than ever, and that Fidesz’s popularity is around 19% in the latest polls, whereas at the time of April’s parliamentary election, they received the aforementioned 2.5 million votes, which was more than 38 percent.

Economic message and campaign line

Orbán linked the political message to economics, suggesting that the current governing side lacked solid economic foundations and would eventually lose support. He said the ratio from April, when 53 percent voted for Tisza and 47 percent against it, would reverse sooner than many expect.

He was also not afraid to use big metaphors and adjectives. In his view, a South American-style dictatorship is on the loose in Hungary, which has “become like Venezuela without oil wealth.” He referred to the Tisza-style system as “new-age communism.” But he also thinks the majority of voters are unlikely to understand this, so he is sticking with the term “autocracy.”

He also framed the coming period as one in which Fidesz should learn from its mistakes while “proudly” standing by its achievements. That combination of self-reflection and defiance is central to the new messaging he outlined in Tusványos.

Stay up-to-date: Hungarian lawyers’ circle head: says former PM Orbán may soon become a suspect – can he be arrested?

Dull: Orbán avoided facing his defeat

According to investigative journalist Szabolcs Dull’s Facebook post, Orbán avoided facing up to his defeat and only apologised because of Magyar. “The leader of Fidesz spent an hour expounding on how Hungary has turned into Venezuela—a place where arbitrary rule and “New Age communism” run rampant,” and added that Orbán sought to explain to his base why resistance is called for instead of self-criticism.

According to Dull, with his speech, Orbán signalled that he would change the way Fidesz operates, but not its substance.

Why it matters

The speech is significant because it shows Fidesz repositioning itself after losing power, but without adopting the language of a normal parliamentary opposition. Instead, Orbán is trying to turn political setback into a broader mobilisation narrative built around national resistance, freedom and continuity.

That approach could shape how Fidesz speaks to supporters in the coming months, especially if the party wants to keep its base while reaching beyond it.

World.title: Easier after dark: Budapest expands night transport to a lot more suburbs
World.content:
From 1 August, getting home from Budapest at night will become significantly easier, as Hungary rolls out the next phase of its expanded suburban night transport network.

Announced by Transport Minister Dávid Vitézy, the development builds on July’s timetable overhaul and aims to connect even more towns and villages to the capital after midnight. The new services are synchronised with the last metro, HÉV, and train departures, ensuring smoother transfers and reducing waiting times for passengers travelling beyond Budapest’s city limits.

New direct routes from key hubs

A major highlight is the introduction of direct night connections from Kelenföld. These buses will serve Biatorbágy and continue to Sóskút, Pusztazámor and Etyek. From 11 August, additional routes from Kelenföld will reach Szigethalom, Halásztelek and Tököl, linking up with Metro Line M4.

In northern Budapest, a new night route will run from Újpest Városkapu all the way to Visegrád, passing through popular riverside settlements such as Szentendre, Leányfalu, Tahitótfalu and Dunabogdány.

The M4 metro line. Photo: BKK

North-west and north-east areas better connected

Transport links in the north-west will also improve. From Solymár, early-morning and night buses will connect to Pilisszentiván and Pilisszántó, timed to rail services. Meanwhile, from Pomáz, new connections will serve Pilisszentkereszt and Csobánka following the last H5 HÉV.

In the north-east, passengers travelling from the Stadion transport hub will gain access to Veresegyház and surrounding settlements, including Szada, Erdőkertes, Őrbottyán and Csomád. Services from Örs vezér tere will also run more frequently towards Csömör and Nagytarcsa.

Southern expansion reaches as far as Dabas

The southern agglomeration will see some of the most extensive upgrades. Night buses from Népliget will now run as far as Dabas, stopping at Alsónémedi, Ócsa, Inárcs, Kakucs and Újhartyán along the way.

A brand-new direct connection will also link Budapest with the Kiskunlacháza area. Until the Budapest–Belgrade railway line opens, buses will serve Dunaharaszti, Taksony, Dunavarsány and Délegyháza, continuing to Kiskunlacháza and even Dömsöd. Once the rail line is operational, the route will be adjusted to pass through Bugyi instead.

Stay up-to-date: Budapest public transport explained: Tickets, passes, fines and airport connections

A realistic alternative to driving

According to Vitézy, the expanded system is designed to be simple, predictable and competitive with car travel, even at night. With tens of thousands of commuters expected to benefit, the multi-phase rollout could transform how residents of the Budapest agglomeration travel after dark.

The minister emphasised that the long-term goal is a reliable, safe, and comprehensive night-time network that serves the needs of the region’s growing population.

World.title: 40 years without a break: Remarkable statistics from the Hungarian Grand Prix
World.content:
Very few countries can claim to have hosted more than 40 consecutive races at the same track and under the same name. The Hungaroring and the Hungarian Grand Prix are among them, and over four decades, they have produced some remarkable statistics. Several of the drivers currently on the starting grid secured their first victory here, and that’s just one of many interesting facts.

Author: Tamás Szikora

The first one is always special

Six drivers have celebrated their first Formula 1 victory at the Hungaroring, and three of them have since become world champions. Damon Hill triumphed in 1993 driving for Williams and went on to win the world championship three years later. Fernando Alonso, who competed as a Renault driver in 2003, started from pole position and crossed the finish line first; he then claimed his first world championship title in 2005, followed by another in 2006.

Jenson Button followed a similar path in this regard, though he had to wait quite a while for his first victory. He achieved this in 2006 while driving for Honda; surprisingly, this was the first rain-soaked race at the Hungaroring, and the British driver emerged from the chaos as the clear winner. Three years later, in 2009, Button finally became world champion with Brawn GP; to this day, he remains the last driver to win the world championship two or three years after his victory at the Hungaroring. In 2008, Heikki Kovalainen claimed his first and only F1 victory. In that race, Felipe Massa held a comfortable lead, but a few laps before the checkered flag, his Ferrari suffered a mechanical failure, allowing Kovalainen to inherit the victory.

In 2021, Esteban Ocon won a race that was particularly memorable and full of twists and turns due to the rain—this victory remains his only one to date. Then, in 2024, Oscar Piastri won the Hungarian Grand Prix. That race was no less memorable, as although Piastri was in the lead, McLaren’s strategy left him at a disadvantage compared to his teammate after the pit stops. The team eventually asked Lando Norris to let Piastri back in front of him, but the British driver was only willing to do so a few laps before the end of the race. This created a rather tense situation, but at the same time wrote another memorable chapter in Hungary’s racing history.

The track was completed in eight months

The Hungaroring was built in just eight months. Construction officially began in October 1985 and was fully completed by May 1986. This was a record at the time, and the track has undergone several renovations since then. One of the most significant renovations took place in 2003, when the Hungaroring was extended to 4,381 meters; the same track layout has been in use ever since, and major infrastructure improvements were completed this year. The main elements of these improvements were already in place by 2025, but the work was not fully completed until this year.

The Grand Prix held most frequently on the same circuit

If we consider only those races that have been held continuously from the very beginning, under the same name, and on a single circuit, the Hungaroring ranks first. Although the Hungarian Grand Prix ranks 11th on the list of the most frequently held races (as of Sunday) with 41 editions, the races ahead of it were often held at different tracks or with breaks in between. The Brazilian Grand Prix, for example, has so far been held at two different tracks and under two different names, but the British and Italian Grand Prix—which have been held every year since 1950—have also been held at multiple tracks. The Hungarian races, however, have always been held at the Mogyoród circuit, and fortunately, not a single year has been missed since 1986.

If you missed it: Three soccer players based in Hungary at the World Cup: everything you need to know

The record for the most pole positions at a single track

This record is also tied to the Hungaroring. Ahead of the 2026 race weekend, Lewis Hamilton has secured pole position a total of nine times in Hungary. Tied for second place in the rankings—each with eight pole positions—are Hamilton in Australia, Michael Schumacher in Japan, and Ayrton Senna at the San Marino Grand Prix. It is not impossible that the record for the most wins at a single track will also be set in Hungary in the future. Hamilton has won here eight times so far; the British seven-time world champion has achieved even greater success at a single venue, having won the British Grand Prix nine times.

World.title: Brace for another heatwave: Only a few cooler days left before extreme heat returns to Hungary
World.content:
Hungary has only a few days of relatively comfortable summer weather left before another long-lasting heatwave arrives, according to medium-range weather forecasts.

Forecasters say temperatures will begin rising steadily from next Tuesday, with early August expected to bring widespread highs above 35°C, while some areas could once again see temperatures close to 40°C. According to weather portal Időkép, current forecast models indicate that the hot spell could continue until at least 7 August, with no significant cooling in sight.

Pleasant weekend before the heat returns

Saturday is expected to be mostly sunny across Hungary, with only occasional thin and fair-weather clouds. No rainfall is forecast, and afternoon temperatures should reach 25–30°C, offering ideal conditions for outdoor activities.

Sunday will start with another relatively cool morning, with temperatures between 9°C and 19°C. During the afternoon, cloud cover will increase from the west, bringing scattered showers and thunderstorms first to western Hungary before spreading towards central and eastern parts of the country later in the day.

Strong southerly and south-westerly winds are expected in many areas, particularly across Transdanubia and central Hungary, while thunderstorms may produce locally severe gusts. Afternoon highs will range between 29°C and 34°C.

Heat builds rapidly next week

A cold front passing through on Monday may still trigger isolated showers and thunderstorms. However, meteorologists expect weather patterns to change quickly afterwards.

From Tuesday onwards, south-westerly airflows are forecast to bring increasingly hot air into the Carpathian Basin, causing temperatures to climb day by day.

According to Időkép, the first days of August are expected to bring persistent daytime temperatures well above 35°C across most of Hungary, with some locations potentially reaching or even exceeding 40°C.

Tropical nights expected to return

The heat will not be limited to daytime hours. Forecasters also expect nights to become progressively warmer, making restful sleep increasingly difficult. From the second half of next week,

temperatures in many parts of the country may remain above 20°C overnight, meeting the definition of so-called tropical nights.

Drought conditions likely to worsen

The returning heatwave is also expected to intensify Hungary’s ongoing drought. With scorching sunshine and little or no rainfall forecast for several consecutive days, soil moisture levels are likely to deteriorate further.

As Daily News Hungary reported, according to the latest data from HungaroMet, 90.2% of Hungary is currently experiencing at least moderate agricultural drought, highlighting the growing pressure on crops and water resources after an already exceptionally dry summer.

World.title: Shocking details emerge of Gáspár Orbán’s Chadian military mission: could many have died at immense cost?
World.content:
Fresh revelations have surfaced about one of the Hungarian state’s most opaque ventures in Africa’s Sahel region. Citing multiple independent sources, Magyar Hang reports that Gáspár Orbán was not merely a participant in the Chadian deployment but, from the outset, served as its commander in the rank of captain—despite the Orbán government having sought to deny the very existence of the intervention. Fellow soldiers reportedly described the “prince” as behaving like “a philosopher who had wandered onto a battlefield”.

Gáspár Orbán was to be reported to by all

According to Magyar Hang, on 20 September 2023, aboard a Hungarian Defence Forces Airbus departing from Kecskemét air base, Brigadier General Gábor Sánta announced after take-off that he would hand over command to “the Captain”, naming Gáspár Orbán as head of the Chadian mission. Accounts suggest members of the delegation reported directly to him.

This sharply contradicts earlier official communications. Kristóf Szalay-Bobrovniczky, then defence minister, had described Orbán merely as a “liaison” in an interview with Index, while former Chief of the General Staff Gábor Böröndi later said the Prime Minister’s son had participated for a time in a governmental planning group, adding that it was a “gross exaggeration” to claim he had led the mission. In parliament, Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi declined to comment on the new reports, stating only that an investigation is under way.

Magyar Hang reports that Gáspár Orbán spent extended periods in Chad, mostly in civilian dress, though at times in military uniform. One source said he behaved “like a philosopher straying into a military exercise”, frequently using his Iridium satellite phone, while some members of the team referred to him behind his back as “the prince”. The paper also claims that another captain’s insignia was removed to ensure no Hungarian of equal rank served alongside him.

Villa and accidents

A series of unusual incidents reportedly surrounded the mission. The Hungarian side, for instance, leased a villa on a long-term basis, intended to serve as a future embassy. Its furnishings were described by one source as “as if Győzike had been the interior designer”. Following refurbishment overseen by the security firm Inrimas, part of the team moved in; however, during the first evening’s showers, one Hungarian reportedly suffered an electric shock from stray current, prompting everyone to return to the hotel the following day.

PM Orbán and the Chadian President in Budapest in 2024. Photo: Facebook / Viktor Orbán

According to the paper, Inrimas—employing former soldiers and ex-Foreign Legion personnel—arrived in Chad before the Hungarian military to protect staff of the Hungary Helps humanitarian programme. Hungary Helps received 817 million forints in funding to open its Chadian office even before any official decision had been taken. Magyar Hang further reports that in 2024, ahead of presidential elections, local intelligence services searched the Hungarian delegation’s hotel rooms and seized small arms, bulletproof vests, a drone, thermal imaging equipment and other devices. This did not affect Hungarian soldiers, who were by then stationed at a French military base; however, the security firm has reportedly not had its equipment returned.

Hungarian universities linked to the mission

The mission, according to the paper, rested on four pillars: military, humanitarian, agricultural and investment cooperation. Óbuda University confirmed that, at the government’s request, it launched an English-language Humanitarian Response Manager course for Chadian participants over two academic years, receiving a total of 40.8 million forints in support. The Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences also acknowledged a presence in Chad but has yet to provide further details.

Parliament approved the Chadian military mission in November 2023. The government said it had been requested by the Chadian president, although the letter of request was not presented to the defence committee and was later obtained by Telex. While the official justification cited training Chadian forces, counter-terrorism efforts and curbing illegal migration towards Europe, the mission ultimately did not proceed.

Gáspár Orbán (l). Photo: PrtScr/Youtube/RTL

Hungary’s military mission to Chad leaked: “direct combat operations” were in plans

Did Gáspár Orbán anticipate half the force being lost?

A defence submission from November 2025, as reported by Magyar Hang, projected mission costs of more than 4 billion forints for 2026, alongside approximately 1.15 billion forints in national security spending and 21.8 billion forints in logistical expenditure. Earlier, Captain Szilveszter Pálinkás claimed that during their university years in London, Gáspár Orbán had told him the mission was calculated with a 50 per cent loss of combat effectiveness—in other words, the loss of half the Hungarian troops. Yet ahead of elections, the government also sought to deny that any Chadian mission had been planned at all.

Hungarian Defence Forces officer Captain Szilveszter Pálinkás. Screenshot: Telex/YouTube

Gáspár Orbán is the only son of Viktor Orbán, the former prime minister. He was previously a footballer and later led a charismatic Christian youth movement known as Felház. In the summer of 2019 he joined the military, and in 2020 was promptly sent on a state scholarship to the prestigious Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, alma mater of, among others, the heir to the British throne.
