World.title: China’s Study Abroad Boom Finds a New Generation: Retirees
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018818/China’s Study Abroad Boom Finds a New Generation: Retirees
World.content:
After decades spent working, raising families, and putting personal ambitions on hold, two Chinese women in their 50s returned to school thousands of kilometers from home.

In Athens, 58-year-old Ella Wang found a new sense of purpose at university, studying Greek archaeology, history, and literature. While in New Zealand, 54-year-old Zhao found herself overwhelmed by an English program that was far beyond her level.

Both studied alongside classmates young enough to be their children, but their experiences could hardly have been more different. Yet both are part of a growing number of Chinese retirees looking overseas for education.

Having spent their working lives during China’s reform era, many now have greater financial security, more control over their time, and familiarity with overseas education after sending their own children abroad.

China already has about 105,000 universities for older adults, but overseas programs that combine learning with international travel have a particular appeal for retirees seeking cultural experiences beyond the classroom. EF Education First, one of the world’s largest international education providers, estimates that China’s broader overseas education market for older adults will reach 1.2 trillion yuan ($167 billion) by 2030.

Yet for those entering education systems designed around younger students, the challenge is finding a classroom that fits.

Lesson learned

Zhao discovered that within days of arriving in New Zealand.

She had enrolled in what she believed was a beginner English program. EF had assessed her at A1, the lowest level, and shown her an A1 textbook before she left China. But when lessons began, every available course was beyond her level, and teachers spoke only English.

“It was completely incomprehensible,” Zhao told Sixth Tone.

After one lesson, she returned to the same room for the next class, only to find it empty. The class had moved, but she had not understood the instructions. On another occasion, a teacher called on her, and she did not understand the question.

Zhao had paid about 160,000 yuan for tuition and an eight-month homestay. After retiring from Shanghai’s flower industry, she hoped the program would teach her enough English to travel while she was still healthy. EF’s promotional videos had shown students studying, immersing themselves in local culture, and traveling around New Zealand.

She soon considered quitting. The experience, she felt, had been “overly romanticized” by overseas education providers. “I completely broke down and burst into tears,” Zhao said. “I couldn’t tell my family how miserable it was. I only said I missed them.”

Zhang, 56, had enrolled in a six-week program at the same school and found the pace equally punishing. “It was like I hadn’t even learned to stand, and they were already asking me to run,” she said.

Both had hoped to learn practical English: how to read a menu, take a bus, ask for directions, and order food. Instead, their classes focused on subjects such as history, biology, and mathematics. Another Chinese retiree in the same course quit after three days.

Zhang began to question what she was struggling for. “Do I really need to learn history, biology, and math at this age?”

That mismatch has led some Chinese education providers to design programs specifically for retirees. Yao Xiaoqiong, head of private education provider New Oriental’s Global Campus Center, told Sixth Tone that one- to three-year courses remain difficult for many older students. Instead, the company offers two- to four-week overseas programs, including art courses in the UK and culinary courses in France.

The programs require no prior language skills and include 10 hours of preparation before departure, as well as interpreters and coordinators during the trip. Yao said older clients generally seek cultural immersion and hands-on learning rather than degrees.

Zhang encountered some of that outside the classroom. When she got lost or struggled to understand bus announcements, strangers stepped in to help.

But keeping up with the course consumed her. Zhang studied until 11 p.m. and woke at 4 a.m. to prepare. In class, she relied on a translation app but still “couldn’t keep pace with everyone else.” Younger students often avoided partnering with her for group work.

By the end of the program, she was physically and mentally exhausted. She still hoped to return to New Zealand one day as a tourist. “But this time, I just don’t have the mood to travel,” she said.

Zhang said the program did not match how it was promoted, and planned to file a complaint with EF. The company did not respond to Sixth Tone’s requests for comment.

Zhao’s longer course gave her more time to adjust. Gradually, she learned to manage the classes, grew more confident, found time to hike, and made local friends through a church.

“Now I’ve made it through,” Zhao said. “I’m mentally much stronger.”

Second chance

At the University of Athens, 58-year-old Wang found her way back to an undergraduate thesis she had never considered complete.

Titled “God, Humanity, and Their Destiny,” the thesis at the time fell short of the university’s highest assessment. At her defense, a professor told her she would need “at least another 30 years of life experience” before she could fully develop its argument.

In 2023, while staying at her family’s holiday home in Athens, Wang came across an English-taught undergraduate program in Greek archaeology, history, and literature. More than 30 years had passed since her professor’s remark. “If I finish the archaeology and literature courses here,” she recalled thinking, “maybe I can write the essay better.”

Born in northwestern China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, Wang had worked as a Chinese teacher, an advertising executive, and later in publishing before retiring. With one child in college and the other already working, she was free to spend part of the year in Athens.

Most of her classmates were born around 2006. “The last students I taught were born in 1983 and 1984,” she said. “Now, their children are my classmates.”

Keeping up with them meant learning more than history. Wang typed with two index fingers and struggled to navigate the university’s online systems.

During her first semester, Wang’s daughter arranged to work remotely from Athens, helping her practice English and navigate campus life. Reading textbooks on a screen made Wang “dizzy,” so she ordered printed copies and asked her husband to bring them to Greece.

The effort showed. While many students skipped lectures, Wang rarely missed one. She sat in the front row, stayed after class to ask questions even when she could not fully follow the answers, and spent weekends catching up on coursework. Before long, she was using AI to review her exams and identify mistakes.

She even won over classmates by showing them photos of her cats. “No one can resist kittens,” she said. She also discovered that gray hair was no obstacle to using her student ID for a 10% discount at KFC.

Studying the Peloponnesian War changed how Wang thought about conflict. She began to see the same struggle playing out beyond ancient Greece. “One side wants to preserve the existing order, while the other wants to change it,” she said. “That’s how many conflicts in the world work.”

She came to see traditional expectations around family and marriage as part of that same order. She wanted to break away from them, while her husband, who benefited from the arrangement, was more comfortable preserving it.

“My life used to be a multiple-choice question with only one correct answer,” Wang said. “Work, love, marriage. There was always something I was supposed to do at each stage, and I was carried along by society. People were always defining me: whose daughter I was, whose student I was, whose wife I was, whose mother I was.”

“Now my definition comes from myself,” she said. “I no longer care about those labels. I even have a new name: Ella. I’m Ella.”

Wang has thought about becoming a museum guide or writing a memoir after graduation. But she said those plans matter less than what she has already discovered. “The biggest thing I’ve gained over the past two years is realizing that learning itself is the goal, not a means to something else. I just enjoy learning.”

Sometimes, Wang still thinks of her hometown’s long winters in Xinjiang. As the eldest of four daughters, she helped her parents prepare vegetables for the cold months ahead. Surrounded by piles of produce, she longed to play with other children but could not leave.

“My body was confined by labor, but my thoughts were free. They had already traveled thousands of miles around the world,” she said.

Decades later, Wang feels she has finally caught up with those childhood dreams.

“Now I am standing in the open field of life,” Wang said. “I am lonely, but I am free. It is the solitude of freedom.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Ella Wang in Athens. Courtesy of Wang)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018814/China-Developed ALS Therapy Shows Early Trial Promise
World.title: China-Developed ALS Therapy Shows Early Trial Promise
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018814/China-Developed ALS Therapy Shows Early Trial Promise
World.content:
Chinese researchers have reported encouraging early results for a domestically developed experimental therapy targeting a genetic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. In a six-patient trial published this month in Nature Medicine, the drug was generally well tolerated and reduced key disease-related biomarkers.

Called RAG-17, the therapy uses small interfering RNA, or siRNA, to suppress SOD1, a gene whose mutations can cause ALS. By reducing production of the harmful protein associated with the mutation, the drug is designed to target a biological driver of the disease.

ALS is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that destroys the nerve cells controlling voluntary movement, gradually impairing a patient’s ability to move, speak, swallow, and breathe. The disease gained wider public attention through campaigns such as the Ice Bucket Challenge, but it remains incurable.

China has an estimated 60,000 to 100,000 people living with ALS, with about 23,000 new cases diagnosed each year. Around 2% of patients carry SOD1 mutations, the only genetic form of ALS with an approved targeted treatment. Tofersen, the first approved therapy targeting SOD1-related ALS, received U.S. approval in April 2023 and was approved in China in September 2024.

RAG-17 was jointly developed by a team led by Wang Yilong at Beijing Tiantan Hospital and researchers led by Li Longcheng at biotech company Ractigen Therapeutics.

In the trial, six patients with SOD1-related ALS received repeated injections of the drug into the fluid surrounding the spinal cord over several months. Researchers reported no serious adverse events. Two participants experienced mild muscle tremors that later resolved.

The treatment produced substantial reductions in two disease-related biomarkers. SOD1 protein levels in cerebrospinal fluid fell by more than half, while plasma levels of neurofilament light chain, a marker of nerve-cell damage, also declined.

The changes indicate that RAG-17 reached its intended target.

In preclinical studies, RAG-17 delayed disease progression, preserved motor function, and extended survival in rodent models of SOD1-related ALS. Tests in macaques also found sustained suppression of the SOD1 gene in the central nervous system.

The Chinese research team said a larger clinical trial of RAG-17 is now underway.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Shijue Focus/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018808/Game Changers: China’s Female Football Commentators Take Their Shot
World.title: Game Changers: China’s Female Football Commentators Take Their Shot
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018808/Game Changers: China’s Female Football Commentators Take Their Shot
World.content:
Editor’s note: Once confined by gender stereotypes to largely decorative, in-studio roles, China’s women are breaking down barriers in the male-dominated world of live football commentary — and at the forefront is Liu Chang. With nearly a decade of experience, the 34-year-old was part of the commentary team formed for the 2026 FIFA World Cup by the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote. Here, Liu talks about her passion for the “beautiful game,” her online critics, and her unforgettable farewell to the former France and Real Madrid star Karim Benzema.

For two days before the 2026 FIFA World Cup final, football fans could finally take a break. I couldn’t.

After England’s semifinal defeat to Argentina on July 16, I had to continue livestreaming, reviewing the match in detail, and chatting with viewers online. That day, I still had a program to record. During a major tournament like the World Cup, commentators work around the clock. We can only really rest after the final game.

In China, most matches this time started in the early hours of the morning. For a 3 a.m. kickoff, we usually arrived at the studio around 11 p.m. or midnight to prepare, and we wouldn’t finish work until after 5 a.m. the next day. Once I got home, I would record a post-match analysis video, edit and publish it, then sleep until the afternoon. After waking up, I would immediately begin preparing for the next match. Sometimes I slept only two or three hours a day.

As I began commentating on bigger matches, I knew my voice was reaching a larger audience. But that also brought more criticism. I often saw comments on social media saying they weren’t used to a female commentator, that the voice was too shrill or overly emotional.

I don’t shy away from this feedback. I want to hear genuine reactions from viewers, even though it might be painful.

As for the harsher comments, you have to look at them case by case. Take the criticism about shrill voices — there are historical reasons behind that perception. Honestly, growing up, I hardly ever heard a woman cover a football match. We were used to female commentary for figure skating, synchronized swimming, or diving — sports associated with graceful and delicate imagery, where a softer voice seemed a natural fit.

But football is intense, full of passion, and constantly changing. The drama of the game is inseparable from emotion. So I completely understand why some viewers initially felt uncomfortable hearing a female voice. That’s why I adjusted my vocal technique, shifting to a deeper, fuller tone by relying less on head resonance and more on chest resonance. When emotions run high, I can use professional methods to control my pitch.

Of all the comments, what I care about most is how people evaluate my accuracy. My colleague Wu Tong (another female commentator who covered the 2026 World Cup) and I genuinely want to provide fans with an accurate and reliable reading of the game.

Some viewers noted that our commentary felt even-keeled and impartial — a compliment that, to me, reveals a double standard. If a female commentator shows visible emotion or a hint of bias, viewers are far quicker to mark it down to a lack of professionalism.

There’s been a noticeable change in public perceptions of female football commentators in recent years, though. Today, Chinese fans have a far richer array of ways to engage with a match. Once, they simply stared at the screen. Now they travel to the games, share updates on social media, and create highlight videos on players and teams. Given how much modern sports coverage has evolved, it was only natural that audiences would begin expecting something different from the commentary box.

That means commentators can no longer present themselves as distant authorities. If you want to connect with viewers, you need to be on their wavelength.

When I watched football as a kid, the commentators seemed unreachable — they represented a kind of solemn authority. But expectations have changed. Today, fans prefer commentary with personality, someone who understands internet culture and knows how to weave memes into a broadcast.

This is where my generation has an advantage. I’m a fan first, so I naturally approach the game from a fan’s perspective. When I’m not commentating, I spend much of my time scrolling through sports forums, hunting for hilarious memes and the wildest hot takes.

Over the line

The 2010 FIFA World Cup in South Africa was the first major tournament I followed from start to finish.

My interest in the Spanish national team began in 2008, when gathering information wasn’t nearly as convenient as it is today. Many overseas Chinese fans would share updates from Spain online, and we would meet to discuss the matches and the players. It was a lively community built around a shared passion.

That tournament became the starting point of my connection with other fans. I had only recently left school, had little money, and couldn’t afford many forms of entertainment. Football became one of the few joys that didn’t cost a thing. The game felt pure: there was no script, only the unpredictability of competition and the possibility of victory or defeat.

We were full of curiosity, and football was a window into a world I longed to understand.

I’ve always loved sports, but after graduating from Beijing’s Communication University of China, I initially worked for nine years at CCTV-7 (a China Central Television channel that, at the time, focused on agriculture and military affairs).

Choosing a career in sports media was not an easy decision. My family did not support it at first. By then, I had been taking on more football-related freelance work, often staying up late, while my regular job also required lots of business trips. It became difficult to balance my health, energy, and workload. I kept asking myself: Could I make a living from football?

I decided to take the leap. In 2017, I joined (Chinese tech giant) Tencent, working in the football media. It was a risk, but working in football brought me real joy. It allowed me to fulfill a long-held dream to attend matches, meet players, and share my insights with fans.

During my years at Tencent, I tried almost every kind of role: interviewing players, interacting with guests before and during matches, and working on the front lines of major tournaments. I found all these experiences fascinating.

But after trying so many roles, I realized that what I loved most was still the game itself. Whenever I watched a match, I felt an overwhelming urge to give it a voice — to capture what was happening on the pitch. And there was only one role that could satisfy that impulse.

Calling the shots

My first commentary assignment came by accident. It happened during an English Premier League match between Chelsea and Everton seven or eight years ago. I was supposed to only host the coverage, but just before kickoff the production team got word that one of the commentators would not arrive in time. It was a late-night broadcast, and the studio had only me and one guest. So I stepped in.

If it happened today, with my understanding of the profession and the entire workflow, I probably wouldn’t have dared go on air at such short notice. But I didn’t think much about it at the time. I was just excited — ridiculously so. I had no real grasp of how to share the microphone or coordinate with a partner. I just said whatever came to mind. Fortunately, my partner was highly experienced. Knowing I had been drafted in at the last minute, he didn’t put any pressure on me. It also helped that I’d followed the Premier League for years and knew both teams well.

After the match, I went home to sleep, feeling pleased. The next day, I watched the recording to see where I could improve, only to discover that all my commentary had been cut. It was probably because the platform didn’t want anyone to notice that its scheduled guest hadn’t shown up. Plus, female football commentators were then still a rarity.

My commentary that first time wasn’t preserved, but I had impressed both the production crew and my co-commentator, and the response in the live chat was encouraging. It showed me that commentary was perhaps something I could pursue.

That experience didn’t immediately make me a commentator, but it gave me confidence that I could handle a full match. When my next opportunity came, I put myself forward.

And so, in 2019, I “transferred” to PP Sports (one of the first Chinese platforms to livestream sporting events). The platform broadcast a wide range of competitions at different levels, which gave me invaluable opportunities to practice. There’s a “10,000-hour rule” behind mastering a craft, and in my industry, people can’t deliver a confident, insightful commentary without having handled hundreds of games. After every assignment, I would listen back, reviewing my performance, identifying mistakes, and thinking about improvements.

For late-night matches, platforms often rely on younger commentators. I did my share of games that attracted little attention, where information on the teams and players was scarce. I had to research everything myself. That, too, was part of the learning curve. I still take on many lower-profile matches now. Yet for commentators, each game deserves the same preparation and professionalism.

From my first assignment to where I am today, it took at least six or seven years.

The final whistle

The commentary box is a place of “magic” for me. I’m naturally a low-energy person, but when that countdown to kickoff begins — “five, four, three, two, one” — it feels as if a switch inside me suddenly flips. It doesn’t matter whether you have prepared for years or just days;, the moment has arrived, and you need to deliver.

The commentary box becomes my creative space, and for the next 90 minutes or so, I’m given the power to tell a story.

It is where storytelling meets the unpredictability of professional football. I look forward to every match because the game has no script. No matter how much analysis and prediction you do, you can never know how the action will unfold.

Of all the matches I’ve covered, one of the most unforgettable was (former France international striker) Karim Benzema’s final match for Real Madrid on June 4, 2023. About an hour or two before kickoff, we received the news that Benzema would be leaving the club (after 14 years). Both my partner and I found it hard to process emotionally. We had watched him develop at Madrid, and an entire generation of fans had grown with him.

As I quickly gathered all the memories I had of Benzema, a line from the song “Da Er Wen” (by Singaporean singer Tanya Chua) came to mind. So, when the match finally ended and the camera lingered on Benzema, I read out the lyrics: “My youth was not without its scars / There was rivalry, there was sacrifice / I learned to be earnest, learned to be loyal, and only those who adapt survive.”

It was a broadcast that could never be replicated. After that, I never had another opportunity to weave song lyrics into my commentary.

At the 2026 World Cup, the match that stayed with me most was defending champion Argentina’s knockout-stage encounter with Cabo Verde.

Before the tournament began, I didn’t know much about Cabo Verde. It was only after they emerged as an exciting newcomer that I started doing my homework. Their three group-stage matches showed a team defined by remarkable discipline and collective spirit. But even then, I never expected them to produce such an extraordinary performance against Argentina in the Round of 32. They denied Lionel Messi a goal, scored, and pushed their opponents to the brink. Even in the final minutes, the Cabo Verde players continued pushing forward, forcing the Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez into a spectacular save.

Judging by the viewers in our livestream, many Chinese fans likely only logged on to check the score after waking up that morning. But when they saw the match was still going — that it had gone into extra time — they rushed to the livestream, eager to find out how the drama would play out.

It was a match and feeling I will remember for the rest of my life.

That, to me, is the magic of football. It can be incredibly distant — many matches are played thousands of miles away, and most fans may never have the chance to watch them in person. Yet at the same time, it can feel incredibly close. It moves you emotionally, making your heart rise and fall with every moment. And when the people around you support the same team, a sense of intimacy emerges almost instantly. That sense of kinship transcends language and borders, creating a shared emotional bond among people who may otherwise have nothing in common.

My greatest lesson from football has been that nothing is truly decided until that final whistle is blown. Life is the same — until the end, everything is possible.

As told to reporter Li Yiming.

A version of this article originally appeared in Fir Record. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Chen Yue; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image): Liu Chang (center) commentates alongside Chinese referee Ma Ning (right) and commentator Yu Xinmiao (left) during the 2026 FIFA World Cup final, July 2026. From Liu’s Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018813/China’s Bank Wealth Products Face Scrutiny Over Yield Displays
World.title: China’s Bank Wealth Products Face Scrutiny Over Yield Displays
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018813/China’s Bank Wealth Products Face Scrutiny Over Yield Displays
World.content:
One wealth management product advertised annualized returns above 3% but delivered a loss. A “stable, low-volatility” investment began declining the day after purchase. Other wealth management offerings highlighted their strongest short-term yields, making it harder for investors to assess their actual performance.

The cases were among those highlighted in a recent investigation by Chinese state news agency Xinhua, which found that some institutions continue to showcase selective short-term returns despite tighter regulatory scrutiny.

By the end of the first quarter this year, the number of bank wealth management investors in China had reached 148 million, while 48,000 products were available on the market, up 18.23% from a year earlier.

According to Xinhua, while regulators have curbed overt “ranking chasing” — the practice of inflating yields to improve performance rankings — some wealth management institutions continue to rely on selective performance displays.

The probe found that even products from the same bank may use different periods to calculate annualized returns, with some showing one-month figures and others three-month figures, making comparisons difficult for investors.

Lin Xiaoyuan told Xinhua that she bought a three-month holding-period product advertised with an annualized return above 3%. When it matured, the investment had posted a loss.

Another investor, surnamed Chen, said a bank wealth manager promoted a six-month “low-volatility” product as a “stellar performer.” But the investment began losing value on the day his purchase was confirmed and continued declining for the following month.

Xinhua also reviewed product pages on bank apps and found discrepancies between promotional displays and recent performance figures. One product page highlighted a “positive annual return since inception” and a cumulative return of 10.18%, while further data showed annualized losses over both the previous three-month and one-month periods.

An insider at a bank wealth management firm told Xinhua, “If everyone else is showing 4% or 5%, how can we sell ours if we show the real number?”

The probe also found that some banks use inconsistent metrics to display yields, with products from the same institution sometimes showing annualized returns calculated over different periods.

“This kind of selective disclosure is a key reason investors are being misled,” said Wang Pengbo, a senior analyst at market consultancy Botong Analysys. He added that banks often highlight their strongest short-term figures on homepages and pop-ups, making it difficult for ordinary investors to assess a product’s actual risk and return without digging through the fine print.

In December 2025, the National Financial Regulatory Administration issued rules aimed at curbing misleading performance disclosures, including selective reporting and inconsistent presentation of returns.

Such practices violate both net-value management requirements under China’s asset management regulations and the principle of fair market pricing, Wang added.

Regulators have also targeted wealth management products that use short-term returns to influence performance rankings and attract investors. Xinhua reported that selective yield presentation remains an issue despite the regulatory focus.

Experts advised investors to look beyond short-term rankings, examine longer-term performance, compare returns with benchmarks, and consider volatility alongside headline yields.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: TotalImage/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018804/China’s Changing Climate May Be Why Your Garlic Is Moldy
World.title: China’s Changing Climate May Be Why Your Garlic Is Moldy
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018804/China’s Changing Climate May Be Why Your Garlic Is Moldy
World.content:
You may have had this experience. It’s dinnertime. You peel a clove of garlic and notice a small greenish-gray patch. Do you cut it away or toss the clove and reach for another? It’s a small annoyance that won’t derail your dinner, but, if social media posts are any indication, it’s an annoyance that is happening across the world, with users saying they are noticing it more and more.

It is also a reminder that food quality is shaped long before an ingredient reaches the cutting board. Garlic’s journey often begins in China, the world’s largest garlic producer and exporter, accounting for more than 70% of global production. When the kind of extreme or unusual weather made more common by climate change affects China’s garlic-growing regions, the consequences can travel well beyond the field, reaching processors, warehouses, supermarkets, and kitchens around the world.

In the garlic-producing provinces of Shandong and Jiangsu in the east, and Henan in central China, garlic is planted in the fall. Farmers will break up the soil to create crop rows, separate and select cloves, then press them, one by one, pointy-side up, into the soil. Then, after the cloves are covered with more dirt, watered, and mulched with plastic, they embark on several months of exposure to changing temperatures and moisture conditions.

The timing for this process needs to be exact. Plant too early, and the young sprouts might overdevelop, draining energy. Too late, and the plant doesn’t develop enough. In both cases, it might not be able to defend itself against diseases and the winter cold.

After planting, garlic must undergo a period of cold to initiate a process called vernalization. Only after prolonged exposure to low temperatures will the plants successfully develop bulbs — the cluster of garlic cloves. Vernalization typically requires a temperature range of 0 to 10 degrees Celsius for at least three weeks. Too much cold will harm the garlic; too little will disrupt the plant’s maturation.

Weather extremes can upset this process. In the fall of 2025, for example, excessive rainfall across northern China delayed garlic planting by about three to six weeks. The winter that followed was mild, and as a result, government data show, the garlic harvested in Shandong continued to grow during a period when no growth should have occurred.

Though this period of extra growth, in some ways, made up for the season’s late planting, this additional early-stage growth may have affected resource allocation within the plant. For example, it can cause the bulbs’ side buds — which later become cloves — to develop their own leaves instead of growing in size.

When the seasons change to spring and the world begins to bloom, a slender flower stalk begins to bolt from the center of the garlic plant. This flower stalk, known as a garlic scape, is a beloved vegetable in Chinese cuisine, often stir-fried with meat, eggs, or tofu. For the farmers, garlic scapes are a lifeline, as they represent the first opportunity to turn a profit in the garlic farming season. Large, high-quality garlic scapes can provide needed revenue to cover the costs of seasonal workers, farm supplies, and farm management for the rest of the season. Harvesting scapes also leaves more resources for the developing bulb.

However, the harvest window for garlic scapes is extremely short, often lasting for only one or two weeks. If the scapes are not harvested in time, they become old and lose much of their market value, and harvesting them relies heavily on human labor. Usually, different regions reach their harvesting season at different dates, allowing workers to move from one area to the next.

In many garlic-growing regions, this year’s spring was warmer than usual. When that happens, harvesting timelines start to overlap, tightening the labor market and placing additional strain on procurement and distribution. At this point, the farmers face the difficult decision of whether to pay more to harvest their garlic scapes or let them continue to grow, potentially affecting the quality of their bulb harvest later in the season. News stories about the pressures Chinese garlic farmers faced earlier this year spawned the social media meme, “Got garlic scapes, any takers?”

In early summer, the aboveground structures of the garlic plant begin to shrivel, while the belowground bulbs enter their prime harvest period. In northern China, farmers will bind harvested garlic into bunches and lay them out to dry in the sun. The dried skin encasing the bulb acts as a jacket, protecting it from damage, moisture fluctuations, and mold during sorting, storage, and shipping.

Global warming has caused China’s rain belt to shift northward, leading to record rainfall in northern China. If the main harvest period is hit by persistent rain, the garlic skin can get damaged, and both soil moisture and air humidity rise. Bulbs may not fully dry, and damaged outer skins can both cause garlic to sprout more leaves and make it more vulnerable to fungal growth. While a moldy bulb at the supermarket can also result from mistakes during storage and transport, a rainy harvest amplifies those risks.

The China Meteorological Administration’s Bluebook on Climate Change in China, published last year, states that, as warming continues, China is experiencing changes in precipitation patterns and extreme weather risks. This doesn’t mean climate change can be cited as the direct cause of every heavy rainfall event or every below-standard bulb of garlic; it means farmers, traders, and meteorological services must plan for more unstable combinations of heat, rain, humidity, drought, and winter warmth.

Given the large areas used to grow garlic, it’s not feasible to use greenhouses to shield it from the elements. The real test of adaptation will come from recognizing risks earlier, forecasting with more accuracy, and responding more quickly. Accurate and precise weather reporting is of the utmost importance. According to the China Meteorological Administration, Shandong’s garlic-growing Jinxiang County has created a specialized garlic meteorological service team to provide weather support throughout the production cycle.

The fate of a single bulb of garlic may seem inconsequential — but in reality, it is a signal of something larger. Climate change doesn’t just affect the far-off polar ice caps, and it isn’t just the stories of climate disasters filling our televisions. It may already be sitting on our dinner tables. These changes will not stop at the garlic bulb, but with each accurate forecast, each planting decision, and each decision to harvest, we are gradually building our ability to respond. Viewed in this way, this single bulb of garlic is a microcosm of the ongoing negotiations between humans and our climate.

Translator: Cynthia Lin.

(Header image: A farmer sorts garlic harvested from a field in Yongji, Shanxi province, May 24, 2026. Liu Baocheng/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018801/China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.title: China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018801/China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.content:
Before they were immortals, they were scammers.

That’s the irreverent premise behind “All Wishes Come True!,” a new Chinese animated comedy that has turned a band of mythological figures from Taoist legend into a summer box-office hit.

Released July 18, the film recasts the Eight Immortals — traditionally symbols of people from all walks of life — as con artists who impersonate gods and deceive worshippers before achieving immortality themselves.

In less than a week, the film has grossed more than 370 million yuan ($51 million), becoming the second highest-grossing domestic animated film of 2026 behind “Boonie Bears: The Hidden Protector.” It also holds an 8.3 rating on Chinese review site Douban, the highest among this summer’s new releases.

The film’s biggest twist unfolds in Penglai, a fairyland where gods and humans coexist under a surprisingly modern bureaucracy governed by an immortals management bureau. Deities are assigned temples, evaluated on performance targets, and ranked on giant leaderboards based on the incense offerings they receive.

Unlike traditional tales of the Eight Immortals’ journey toward enlightenment, the film gives the legendary figures a new beginning: they first appear as schemers targeting the riches of Fu, Lu, and Shou, the three deities of fortune, prosperity, and longevity.

Zhongli Quan, traditionally portrayed as a general who became a Taoist immortal, is reimagined as a con artist who leads the group in impersonating deities. Cao Guojiu, traditionally linked to the Song dynasty (960–1279) imperial court, appears as an official in the immortals management bureau.

After taking over a temple, the group finds itself responsible for granting wishes — and eventually becomes known for catching thieves. Their journey later leads to a clash with the war god Yang Jian.

Director Mu Zhengyang said he designed Penglai as a “first-tier megacity,” where gods and humans operate within a modern social system. “At first, audiences should feel that they’re entering a traditional Eastern fairyland. But once inside, it becomes much more like an amusement park,” he told domestic media.

The film’s character-driven approach also extends to its voice performances. Voice director Chen Hao, who worked on the popular “Ne Zha” films, voices Zhongli Quan, while Tieguai Li’s Chongqing dialect adds regional flavor to the character.

The film’s cultural references have also fueled online discussion. On streaming platform Bilibili, videos decoding more than 100 Easter eggs and hidden details have each attracted nearly one million views.

One widely discussed clue is the Eight Immortals’ temple number — 1350, the same number associated with Sun Wukong, better known as the Monkey King, in the “Book of Life and Death,” a mythical register of the underworld in “Journey to the West,” hinting at his possible appearance later in the story.

The same reinterpretation has also drawn criticism from some viewers, who argue that the film alters the identities and values associated with traditional mythology.

Yang Jian, for example, traditionally portrayed as a righteous war god who protects ordinary people, is reimagined as a figure willing to sacrifice heaven and humanity to save his mother. The film’s other redesigns have also drawn attention, including Cao Guojiu’s portrayal as an overweight, flamboyant official and Lan Caihe’s depiction as a toddler.

The debate also extends to the film’s portrayal of immortality. Through the line, “Only immortals can do good deeds,” it offers a new interpretation that some viewers praised, while others argued it differs from traditional Taoist ideas of attaining eternal life.

The production team, based in southwestern China’s Sichuan province, said the Eight Immortals offer creative space for reinterpretation because many audiences know their famous stories but are less familiar with their broader legends. The filmmakers said they hoped to introduce the figures to a new generation through a fresh retelling.

“We didn’t want to simply bring the Eight Immortals in front of young audiences and tell the same story again,” producer Ying Xujun told domestic media. “We had to create something new for a new generation.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A poster for “All Wishes Come True!” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.title: At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.content:
This year’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai was larger, more crowded, and more politically prominent than in previous editions.

President Xi Jinping attended the event for the first time, while more than 1,100 companies showcased computing systems, AI agents, robots, and other products aimed at workplaces, factories, and consumers. In-person visits topped 400,000, and tickets were reportedly resold for more than 1,000 yuan.

Xi called for wider access to open-source AI, and China launched a 29-country AI cooperation body, placing issues of governance, access, and international coordination alongside the usual displays of commercial technology.

Beyond the speeches and packed exhibition halls, the most revealing conversations were practical: lowering computing costs, putting AI agents to work, managing new safety risks, and building businesses that can last.

Here are four takeaways from this year’s WAIC.

Computing power gets practical

Computing power was one of the most discussed topics at this year’s WAIC, second only to AI applications by number of related forums. But the focus moved beyond building more data centers or training ever-larger models.

Two questions dominated: what the next generation of computing power might look like, and how to make today’s resources cheaper and more efficient.

At one flagship forum on the future of computing, scientists discussed emerging approaches including quantum computing and space-based computing. Among the speakers was Pan Jianwei, a leading quantum physicist and recent recipient of a top United Nations science award, who outlined recent advances in the field.

Pan also urged caution. Although the field has reached a series of important milestones, he said, building a general-purpose quantum computer capable of quickly solving problems with clear practical value will still require years of sustained research. The academic community, he added, has a responsibility to help the public assess the technology realistically and guard against an industry bubble.

Companies also seemed more focused on improving the efficiency of existing computing resources and reducing the cost of each AI query.

Some were working to improve the performance of models trained mainly on Nvidia chips when deployed on Chinese chips. Others focused on allocating and managing computing resources more efficiently.

Rather than chasing only the most powerful and expensive models, many Chinese AI companies appeared more concerned with making AI cheaper to run.

AI Governance and Safety

AI governance and safety were prominent throughout this year’s WAIC, from high-level forums to the opening ceremony and President Xi Jinping’s speech.

Brian Tse, an AI safety expert and founder and CEO of Concordia AI, said he has seen more discussion in China around cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure, especially the risks posed by frontier AI models.

“The threat landscape is evolving rapidly,” Tse said. “Many experts at the forums expressed concern that threats and potential misuse are developing faster than society’s current defenses.”

The concerns also appeared to be shifting beyond large language models and the harmful content they can generate. More attention was paid this year to the risks posed by autonomous AI agents, which can plan tasks, make decisions, and interact with other tools.

On July 15, just before WAIC, China’s new rules on AI anthropomorphic interaction took effect, targeting services that simulate human personalities and sustained emotional interaction. The rules prohibit providers from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors and bar services from inducing emotional dependence or addiction.

In May, regulators also released guidance on the standardized application and development of AI agents, including plans to explore digital identity management for them.

“China is positioning itself as an architect of multilateral AI governance,” Tse said.

AI lands at work

One phrase heard often at this year’s WAIC was AI’s real-world “landing” — the push to move the technology out of demos and into everyday work. Companies ranging from Tencent and Alibaba to smaller startups showed AI products aimed at offices, factories, and consumer services. AI agents were among the most visible examples.

At booths run by major tech firms, exhibitors demonstrated how agents could be built into corporate workflows, from searching internal documents to generating reports and coordinating routine tasks.

The impact could be broad because many of these companies’ software systems are already embedded in Chinese workplaces. Adding AI agents to existing platforms may prove easier than persuading companies to adopt entirely new tools.

Still, genuinely effective applications appeared limited. Office productivity remained the most obvious use case, while other areas were less developed.

Robotics and embodied AI occupied an entire floor at this year’s WAIC. Visitors could still see robots performing awkward dances or taking six minutes to make a cup of tea. But some companies were beginning to move beyond staged demonstrations, showing robots designed for inspection, manufacturing, logistics, and other industrial uses.

The founder rush

Some of the most revealing conversations at this year’s WAIC took place after the official sessions ended.

Across after-hours gatherings, private meetups, and open-mic sessions, young founders and industry professionals swapped ideas on AI agents, robotics, and productivity tools. Some gatherings ran late into the night, with almost any topic open for discussion.

Many entrepreneurs seemed eager to absorb every new idea, experiment, business opportunity, and professional connection they could find.

But that urgency also carried risks. Some founders said their AI ventures were burning through years of savings. Many still lacked a convincing answer to a basic question: how their projects would generate lasting value and revenue.

That tension ran through WAIC: crowded halls, founders eager to share projects and failures, and a palpable fear of moving too slowly and missing the AI wave. The mood mixed optimism with anxiety, much of it fueled by the speed of the technology and the sheer volume of information surrounding it.

The conversations also suggested a maturing industry. More speakers and founders were asking not only what AI could do, but where it could be useful, how it could be governed, and which businesses could survive once the initial excitement fades.

(Header image: A humanoid robot from a Chinese robotics firm waves Chinese national flags during the 2026 WAIC in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP Photo via VCG)

World.title: The Soybean That Built Northeast China
World.content:
In 2020, I traveled to Kaishantun, a town in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture near the China-North Korea border. It fit every stereotype of the deindustrialized Northeast. Young people had left. The government had built two rows of barracks-style apartment blocks for the elderly residents who remained. Kaishantun railway station had long been abandoned. On the station sign, the space for the next stop was blank. North Korea lay only a few hundred meters away.

On the walk back, I wandered into a derelict movie theater and discovered several reels of old film. Later restored, they revealed something astonishing: clips of a symphony orchestra and a traditional folk orchestra.

What kind of small town could support two orchestras of its own?

As I dug deeper into the history of my home region, Northeast China, I found that part of the answer lay in a crop that today frequently appears in international headlines: soybeans. A century before China became a major importer of American soybeans, it was the world’s leading producer.

In August 1872, three Japanese army officers, disguised as merchants and acting on the orders of General Saigō Takamori, traveled through “Manchuria,” the term they used for Northeast China. Saigō was studying relations between Japan, Korea, and China as he prepared a future campaign against Korea. A year later, the officers submitted their “Report on an Inspection of Manchuria,” one of Japan’s earliest intelligence briefings on China. The report includes a detailed discussion of soybeans:

“From winter through spring, soybeans are continuously transported by inland waterways. Regardless of the cold, day and night, dozens of horse-drawn carts move in a single direction. Large merchants purchase the beans and pile them into circular mountains more than two rooms across and over 6 meters high … The quantity stored is beyond counting.”

In 1885, another Japanese military officer, Kikuchi Setsuzō, passed through Northeast China on his return from the Russian Empire. Along the way, he studied how Qing forces fed their military horses, which he regarded as superior to those of Japan and Russia. Qing troops processed the residue left after soybean oil extraction into pressed soybean cakes for animal feed. Each cake weighed about 12.5 kilograms and could feed three horses for a day. Kikuchi even claimed such soybean resources would be “indispensable” for training military horses.

In the 19th century, Kikuchi was among the few who grasped soybeans’ strategic significance. The crop had reached Europe and North America in the 18th century but remained largely a botanical curiosity. A handful of enthusiasts, such as the Austro-Hungarian agronomist Friedrich Haberlandt, sought to introduce soybeans into Western diets. Yet while they imported the crop, they did not import the culinary traditions that had made it a staple across Asia.

In East Asia, by contrast, people had accumulated more than a thousand years of experience cooking and consuming soybeans. They also recognized the crop’s value as animal feed. After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Japanese rice farmers gradually abandoned traditional fish-based fertilizers in favor of soybean cake. Between 1882 and 1902, Japan’s soybean imports increased four-hundredfold.

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 finally alerted the world to soybeans’ importance. European military observers noted that both sides relied heavily on the crop. Japanese forces consumed soybeans directly and used them in military logistics. Russian forces fed them to cavalry horses. Soybean oil served as a raw material for soap and as a lubricant for artillery equipment and wagon axles.

The soybean trade expanded rapidly. A 1911 report from the Customs Service in Shanghai observed that “It is only in the last three years that soya beans have become important in intercontinental commerce,” calling their rapid emergence from obscurity “one of the most remarkable commercial events of recent times.” In the same year, the U.S. ambassador in Beijing told the State Department that Northeast China had until recently been largely unknown for its commercial potential, despite supplying soybeans to global markets. He observed that its economic trajectory was now drawing attention in major cities including New York, London, Hamburg, and Seattle, and attributed this shift to soybeans, whose rapidly growing demand he characterized as “phenomenal in trade annals.”

Estimates suggest that Northeast China accounted for between 16% and 42% of global soybean production between 1908 and 1930, shipping soybeans, soybean oil, and soybean cakes to the rest of China, Japan, and Europe. Until the eve of World War II, China produced more than 80% of the world’s soybeans. The crop became widely known as the “Manchurian bean.”

Soybeans were also among the most important exports of a then largely impoverished China. After World War I, their importance grew rapidly, and by the 1920s they had overtaken tea and silk to become China’s leading export, accounting for more than 20% of export earnings.

As trade expanded, so did Japan’s territorial ambitions. In the run-up to Japan's formal annexation of Korea in 1910, Yanbian became a frontier along the China-Korea border where Chinese and Japanese spheres of influence met directly. Japanese strategists viewed the wider Yanbian area as a gateway to the interior of Northeast China and sought to build a railway linking the Korean port of Chongjin with China’s inland Northeast. General Hasegawa Yoshimichi, commander of Japanese forces in Korea, regarded Yanbian as a vital supply corridor for sustaining colonial rule on the peninsula. He advocated occupying the region to secure access to strategic commodities such as soybeans.

Over the following three decades, Japan steadily expanded its influence in Northeast China. In 1931, Japanese forces seized the region and took control of its economic resources. This expansion, justified in the name of protecting economic “lifelines,” would later extend across Asia during the Pacific War to the oil fields of Burma, Sumatra, and Borneo; the rubber plantations of Malaya; and the chromium and iron deposits of the Philippines.

In Yanbian, war and colonial rule only reinforced the region’s economic importance. Beyond soybeans, Japanese authorities coveted the region’s timber. In Kaishantun they established the Eastern Manchuria Rayon Pulp Company, whose output eventually surpassed that of most producers in Japan. After the Chinese Communist Party won the civil war and founded the People’s Republic of China in 1949, the new state’s flagship pulp and paper enterprise was established in the same town.

Factories brought more than jobs. They brought hospitals, movie theaters, and even symphony orchestras.

Yet by then Northeast China was no longer the sole center of the global soybean trade. By the early 20th century, American farmers were already familiar with soybeans, using them to replenish soil and support other crops. After the Russo-Japanese War, however, the crop’s industrial potential attracted growing attention.

One unlikely champion was Henry Ford. He used soybean protein and soybean-oil derivatives in automotive components and in 1941 unveiled a prototype car with body panels made largely from soybean-based plastic. To demonstrate its strength, he famously struck it with an axe.

Ford’s soybean car was hardly a commercial success, but it generated publicity for the crop. When Japan severed America’s access to Asian supply routes during the Pacific War, soybeans were transformed from an industrial curiosity into a strategic resource. Combined harvesters and advances in plant breeding helped American farmers scale up production.

By the 1950s, the center of gravity in soybean production had shifted decisively to the Americas.

One final piece was still missing from the modern soybean map: Brazil. In the early 1970s, a major El Niño event, a climate pattern that warms the Pacific Ocean, devastated the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, a key source of animal feed, driving demand for soybean meal. Prices surged, and in 1973 the Nixon administration imposed restrictions on soybean exports.

History then took an ironic turn. Japan, heavily dependent on imported American soybeans, increased its investment in South American agriculture, while Brazil’s agricultural research agency, Embrapa, developed soybean varieties suited to tropical conditions. The result was a dramatic expansion of Brazilian production.

In 2024, more than 70% of China’s soybean imports came from Brazil. When trade tensions between China and the United States intensified in 2025, Brazil became China’s principal alternative for former U.S. suppliers.

Northeast China remains the country’s most important soybean-growing region, producing the beans that become tofu and soy milk on Chinese tables. But it no longer supplies the world with soybean oil and soybean meal. Once-thriving industrial towns have been swept up in the tide of deindustrialization, leaving behind abandoned railway stations and empty movie theaters.

From an unassuming plant in Northeast China to one of the world’s most traded agricultural commodities, the soybean’s history is ultimately a story of globalization. A soybean harvested in Paraguay may be processed in Argentina, sold to China by a trading house in Geneva, and eventually find its way into milk, cakes, or meat products. It shapes what we eat, how we farm, and how nations interact with one another. It also shapes the fate of countless small towns, including places like Kaishantun.

(Header image: A soybean field in Xingkai Lake Farm, Heilongjiang province, 2023. VCG)

World.title: Rhymes and resilience: Illest Morena raps her truth
World.content:
As she enters her fifth year, rapper Illest Morena now carries herself differently, molded by countless experiences that only a woman in a largely male-dominated space could have

Since 2021, female emcee Illest Morena has fought tirelessly for a seat at the table in the local hip-hop scene.

Back when she first started, she could only count the number of active Filipina rappers on one hand. But even when it appeared that the less competition there was, the better, it remained a big challenge for her and her fellow “femcees” to actually get people to listen.

It was Illest’s hunger (and outright audacity) as a newcomer that powered her through that — and it was precisely how she lured new listeners into her craft in the first place. There was a fearlessness that came with putting out every new song, and an intense desire to prove herself to the public early on.

“I wasn’t scared when I started. Ibang-iba ang gigil ng isang rookie. Kapag rookie ka (The grit of a rookie is totally different. When you’re a rookie), you don’t think about the consequences of what’s gonna happen. You don’t think about the outcome. You only think about the possibilities of the things you wanna do,” she told Rappler.

Now, she’s entering her fifth year in the industry with her head held high. She carries herself differently this time — with the consolation of knowing who she truly is despite what those around her may say, and a new air of confidence she got from towering over all the noise.

Silver linings

When it comes to public perception, rappers are often thought to have a steady sense of self-assurance. Many of them are seen as headstrong individuals who are unfiltered, and are able to easily tune out the hate they may get in return.

Illest is as outspoken as ever. It shows not just in her autobiographical approach to music, but in the views she expresses as a human being.

At the end of the day, however, she is a human being before anything else.

“A lot of people think that I don’t get hurt by the words they say kasi kita mo naman wala din silang preno magsalita sa akin eh. Feeling siguro nila hindi naman ako masasaktan or hindi ko naman mapapansin yun. But I internalized a lot of those words that they said about me and that they said to me. It took a lot of self-healing for me to get to the point where I kind of got immune na nga sa mga sinsasabi nila,” she confessed.

(A lot of people think I don’t get hurt by the words they say because they have no filter when they speak to me. They probably think I won’t get hurt or I won’t pay attention to what they say. But I internalized a lot of those words that they said about me and that they said to me. It took a lot of self-healing for me to get to the point where I kind of became immune to what they say.)

Now wise beyond her years, the Illest we see now was molded by countless experiences that only a woman in a largely male-dominated space could have.

There was a time when the Illest who was unafraid to pour out her deepest thoughts for everyone else to see appeared to have faltered.

“Later on in my career, when I reached some kind of traction, doon pumasok ‘yung pressure (that’s when the pressure came in) and being afraid to speak out, and being afraid of detractors. [There was] this pressure to look and seem perfect all the time. That was one of the fears I developed as I went on in the industry,” she admitted.

For a year, she had stopped releasing solo tracks, her public performances became limited, and her once steady social media presence dwindled, too.

“I wasn’t posting that much on social media because I gained weight. And being a female artist, part of your currency is your looks. And it hurt me because that time I realized that you guys were kind of just objectifying me. Are you guys really listening to my songs? Do you guys really like me for my talent? Or is it just because I look like this? Is it because I present myself this way?” she explained.

It was then an uphill battle for Illest to come to terms with loving herself no matter what form she came in — even if it meant having to fight hard to convince herself that she liked what she saw whenever she stood in front of the mirror.

“I’m still writing the same songs, the same message. What just changed was how I looked, and it hurt me. It offended me. But when I look in the mirror now, I can say to myself, ‘I’m proud of you no matter how you look. With your bed hair, kahit kakagising mo lang or wala kang ligo (even if you just woke up or haven’t showered), I am proud of myself no matter what happens.’”

It was tough, and Illest will be the first to admit that. Still, like the fighter she is, she learned to use it to her advantage. Instead of retreating and boxing herself in, she stood firmly and peeled her mask off for good.

“I think now, kaya lumalabas na lalo ‘yung personality ko sa (the reason why my personality comes out more on) social media and I’m being more active, is because I’ve kind of learned that lesson and I gained this newfound confidence that I never would’ve found if I didn’t gain weight or if I didn’t get these bashers on social media. No matter what they say, or no matter what I look like, this is me. I’m a baddie,” she added.

Two sides to Illest

When she’s not on stage, Illest Morena is Angelica Layague. Angelica is quiet, enjoys her own company, and appears to be a bit more reserved than the fierce performer that struts around the platform like she owns it.

“[There’s] this private version of me where I love journaling. I love scrapbooking. People don’t know that about me because they think that when they see me, I’m like a fighter. That’s what they see but they don’t know I love to do affirmations: ‘I am beautiful. I am great.’ And I like talking to myself sometimes. And they don’t see that. But when I go to TikTok, you guys see a little bit of that version of myself. I’m kind of funny and crazy.”

But when it comes time to get behind the mic, Illest Morena goes through a complete transformation. Once she’s surrounded by a crowd waiting to hear her spit bars, she emanates a sort of aura that can’t seem to be shaken. She attests that she gets it all from her fans.

“Masaya ako kapag nakikita ko talaga ‘yung mga fans. Sila ‘yung nagbibigay sa akin nung extra extroverted version of myself kasi nga ‘di ba, medyo mahiyain ako in real life, as Angelica, not as Illest Morena,” she told Rappler.

(I’m really happy when I see my fans. They bring out the extra extroverted version of myself because I’m quite shy as Angelica, not as Illest Morena.)

“But when I see their faces, it makes me wanna show out and show off so that they get their money’s worth when they pay for tickets.”

For five years and counting now, fans have come to love Illest’s signature flavor R&B and hip-hop — catchy, and deeply rooted in what’s personal to the artist. Her music has always been autobiographical, in the sense that it captures Illest in all her seasons, even the ones she’s long outgrown.

Play Video

The core of Illest’s artistry was what remained unchanged all these years. This time, though, her catalogue has taken on a new form, one that’s even more raw and vulnerable.

And in doing that, Illest has no regrets.

“I’d rather have people see me as I am than see me as something I’m not, and then they expect something from that version of me or that mask that I have or put me on a pedestal. I don’t like that,” Illest told Rappler.

Fueled by delusion

In year five, Illest is on a roll. She’s more grounded in her sense of self, and she’s achieving milestone after milestone to boot.

The 24-year-old “femcee” already has a long list of joint bangers to her name (think “Lagabog” feat. Skusta Clee and “Quickie” feat. Hev Abi to name a few) — and she’s determined to keep it coming.

She just never would have thought her next collaborator would be Apl.de.Ap, who not only knew her by name when they first met, but was well aware of Illest’s impact in the local music scene. When the Black Eyed Peas star reached out for a potential feature on an upcoming song, it was an instant “yes” for Illest.

“It felt like I had to live up to the first impression because he said he heard I was one of the best here. I don’t want him to think otherwise,” Illest shared in a mix of English and Filipino.

Then came “Wind It,” a summery, reggaeton-inspired track featuring Apl.de.Ap, Fana, and Illest herself.

Play Video

These opportunities don’t just get handed to Illest, though. They all come as a result of years of grit and — cliche as it sounds — unapologetic belief in yourself.

Illest, then, has this to say: “Be very delusional with your self-belief. And also, never let one mistake or a challenge bring you down. Because it’s just part of learning, part of growing, and part of upgrading into this better version of you.”

That’s Illest Morena for you. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s SONA 2026
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is set to deliver his State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Monday, July 27, 4 pm, at the Batasang Pambansa in Quezon City.

The situation is markedly different from last year, when Marcos’ erstwhile ally, Vice President Sara Duterte, avoided an impeachment trial after the Supreme Court ruled that the complaint against her was unconstitutional as it is barred by the one-year rule.

This year, as Marcos delivers his fifth SONA, the impeachment trial against the Vice President is in full swing. Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez, the President’s cousin, is no longer House speaker following his resignation after he was implicated in flood control corruption. Marcos himself had announced a crackdown on those involved in the scandal in his SONA last year.

How will Marcos set the tone for the last two years of his presidency? What promises will he declare as fulfilled, and what remains to be done? What will be his new marching order a year since he called for crackdown on flood control corruption?
