World.title: Kazakhstan Advances as Regional Education Hub With Rise in Student Cities Ranking
World.content:
143076

ALMATY – Kazakhstan continued to strengthen its position as Central Asia’s leading higher education hub as Almaty reached its highest-ever position in the QS Best Student Cities 2027 ranking and the country recorded another year of growth in international student enrollment.

Astana also improved its position, rising eight places to 119th, reinforcing Kazakhstan’s growing role as a regional higher education hub, reported the Ministry of Science and Higher Education’s press service.

Published by international higher education analytical agency QS Quacquarelli Symonds, the ranking assesses 150 cities worldwide that meet population and university criteria based on the QS World University Rankings 2027. Cities are evaluated across six indicators: university rankings, student mix, employer activity, affordability, desirability and student views.

University ecosystem and affordability

One of Almaty’s strongest advantages remains its concentration of higher education institutions. The city is home to nine universities included in the QS World University Rankings 2027, placing it 50th globally in the university rankings indicator, which measures the overall strength of a city’s university ecosystem.

Kazakhstan also continues to rank highly for affordability. Astana placed ninth in the world for the cost of studying and living, while Almaty ranked 24th, making both cities among the most affordable destinations for international students.

The rankings also recorded improvements in the student diversity indicator for both cities, reflecting the increasing international composition of Kazakhstan’s university communities and the growing attractiveness of the country’s higher education sector to students from abroad.

International student enrollment

The improved rankings coincide with rising international enrollment. During the 2025-2026 academic year, 35,075 international students from 88 countries studied at Kazakhstan’s universities, an 11% increase compared with the previous academic year.

The government has identified the internationalization of higher education as one of the priorities of the Concept for the Development of Higher Education and Science for 2023-2029. According to the ministry, Kazakhstan aims to increase the number of international students to 100,000 by 2029.

Officials attribute the growth in international enrollment to Kazakhstan’s competitive tuition and living costs, strategic geographic location, expanding number of English-language degree programs and increasing demand for education in medicine, engineering and information technology.

Foreign university branches

Kazakhstan has also expanded cooperation with leading international universities. More than 30 branches of foreign universities now operate in the country, including Cardiff University, Coventry University, and universities from the United States, South Korea, Italy, Russia, China and France.

Science and Higher Education Minister Sayasat Nurbek told The Astana Times in an interview that expanding branches of leading foreign universities is central to achieving the goal of transforming Kazakhstan into a global education hub.

“Branches of foreign universities allow our students to pursue an international education without leaving Kazakhstan. This greatly reduces the financial burden on families and opens world-class programs to a much wider range of young people,” he said.

According to the ministry, these partnerships contribute to improving the quality of higher education, expanding academic cooperation and strengthening the international integration of Kazakhstan’s university system.

Nurbek also mentioned that quality assurance has become a cornerstone of the national strategy to expand foreign university branches. To reinforce credibility, Kazakhstan has officially recognized the UK’s Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education (QAA) as an accreditation body. This allows local and international campuses to be evaluated against the same rigorous standards applied in Europe and worldwide, strengthening confidence in degrees earned in the local schools.

To achieve its target of attracting 100,000 international students by 2029, the country plans to continue expanding English-language programs, modernizing university infrastructure, increasing the number of student dormitories, and creating comfortable and safe conditions for international students.

Officials said these measures are part of broader efforts to strengthen Kazakhstan’s position in the global higher education market and establish the country as one of the leading academic centers in Central Asia.

World.title: Another activist in Georgia convicted over insulting Facebook post: doctor Giorgi Akhobadze
World.content:
Georgia: activist Giorgi Akhobadze sentenced over FB post

On July 24, another person in Georgia was sentenced to administrative detention over a Facebook post containing profanity. Giorgi Akhobadze, a doctor and active participant in the country’s pro-European protests, was sentenced to 25 days in detention.

Giorgi Akhobadze

The ruling was issued by Tbilisi City Court. Giorgi Akhobadze did not attend the hearing.

He was represented by his lawyer, Mikheil Zakareishvili.

A few hours after the ruling, Akhobadze was arrested during a special police operation at his home.

Administrative proceedings against Giorgi Akhobadze were initiated following a complaint by the Interior Ministry’s recently established Department for Monitoring Hate Speech.

Akhobadze was sentenced over a Facebook post in which he used profanity to insult police officers who had testified against him in an earlier criminal case.

In December 2024, Akhobadze was returning home from a pro-European protest (which has continued in Georgia for nearly two years) when he was detained by police. He was searched and charged with purchasing and possessing drugs.

Akhobadze and his lawyers maintained that the drugs had been planted on him during the arrest. After an eight-month trial, he was acquitted and released from the courtroom in August 2025.

The Facebook post that led to his current administrative sentence referred specifically to the police officers whom Akhobadze accuses of planting the drugs.

“I stand by every word of that post,” Akhobadze told TV Pirveli after learning of the court’s decision, repeating the profane insult directed at the police officers.

“I’ll spend 25 days in a cell, get some rest, and if they think I’ll come out thinking differently, they’re very much mistaken,” Akhobadze said before his arrest.

On fines and detention for offensive social media posts

Giorgi Akhobadze is the second person to receive a jail sentence over comments posted on social media.

A few days earlier, on July 22, Tbilisi City Court sentenced well-known journalist and Formula TV host Vakho Sanaia to 14 days of administrative detention.

Sanaia had published a Facebook post containing profane and insulting language directed at senior officials of the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Administrative cases over opinions expressed in public are being initiated on the basis of reports filed by the Interior Ministry’s new Department for Monitoring Hate Speech, which began operating on June 1.

The department’s mandate is to monitor and proactively identify statements that violate human dignity, are insulting, or incite hatred, where they may constitute an administrative offence.

According to the Georgian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, between June 1 and July 2 the department identified 170 alleged administrative offences and referred 150 cases to court.

Courts have already ruled on 33 of those cases: 31 people were fined and two received verbal warnings. Most of those fined are activists taking part in the mass protests demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenian police see rise in domestic violence reports: Data and analysis
World.content:
Domestic violence reports in Armenia

In the first half of 2026, Armenia‘s police received 1,375 reports of domestic and family violence. That is 78 more cases than during the same period last year.

Police say that for many years incidents of domestic violence went unreported because families kept them hidden. Now, however, many victims are choosing to contact the police. Law enforcement officials attribute this to people’s growing confidence that “their voices will be heard and their safety and rights will be protected.”

Representatives of civil society have also noticed a change in people’s behaviour. Nare Hayrapetyan, head of the Kotayk regional NGO Women’s Empowerment Resource Centre, describes it as a “victory” that even people who previously categorically rejected the idea are now turning to law enforcement for help.

“Trust in both the state and the institutions responsible for providing protection has increased,” she says.

Police register 1,155 perpetrators

In the first six months of 2026, Armenian police registered 1,155 people who committed violence against family members, up from 1,011 during the same period last year.

In response to the identified cases of domestic violence, police took the following measures:

325 perpetrators received an official warning (compared with 304 last year);

961 emergency intervention orders were issued (up from 833 last year).

Civil society’s role in preventing domestic violence

The Interior Ministry says cooperation between civil society organisations and the police is key to preventing domestic violence. To strengthen that cooperation, regular meetings are held in Yerevan and the regions to assess the effectiveness of joint efforts and identify existing challenges.

“Our cooperation with the police is at a very high level,” says Anahit Abgaryan, head of the NGO Talin-Huys.

According to her, many more people are now turning to the police, which she also sees as a result of growing trust in the system.

“In the past, we encouraged victims to go to the police. We explained that we could not guarantee their safety in the same way the police could. But they refused,” Abgaryan says.

Protecting victims is the priority

According to Georgy Khachatryan, head of the Police Department for Professional Methodological Support, police respond promptly to every report of domestic violence.

“For a police officer working in the community, protecting victims of violence is the priority,” he says.

He outlined the police’s main responsibilities:

identifying and preventing all forms of violence;

protecting every person subjected to violence;

taking the necessary measures to reduce the risk of repeat violence.

Khachatryan argues that the increase in domestic violence reports should not be viewed as a negative indicator.

“Domestic violence is, in fact, a hidden crime. Therefore, the increase in detected cases does not necessarily mean there are more incidents of violence. Rather, these crimes are now coming to the attention of law enforcement authorities,” he says.

To improve the speed of emergency responses, the SAFE YOU app has been operating since 2025 as part of a partnership between the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) and the Armenian police.

“When an alert is triggered, it ensures the simultaneous involvement of all relevant state agencies. This is crucial both for a rapid response and for organising protection measures,” Khachatryan said.

World.title: Landslide hits village in Georgia, leaving two families worst affected
World.content:
Major landslide hits Georgian village

A landslide struck the mountainous village of Gomaro in Georgia’s Adigeni municipality. Rocks and debris swept down the mountainside, damaging residents’ homes and cars. No injuries were reported.

The incident occurred late on 23 July. The first photos and videos from the scene were published by local outlet TOK TV.

Footage from the scene shows that the debris that crashed into one of the houses piled up to nearly half the height of the building.

A pickup truck parked beside the house was completely buried under rocks and mud.

The homeowner told TOK TV that the debris reached the level of the windows. A surge of water smashed a window and flooded the rooms.

“A torrent suddenly came rushing through and swept everything away. The whole house is flooded. The fridge, the gas supply—everything has been damaged,” the young man said.

The Siradze family’s home was among the hardest hit. Its owners told the reporter that the house had also been damaged by a landslide in the same area last year.

Local residents say last year’s landslide was less severe. This time, a much larger torrent of water and rocks came crashing down from the forest, damaging more homes than in the previous landslide.

Another local outlet, Samkhretis Karibche, reported that the family was not at home when the landslide struck.

“My father is ill, and we had gone to Batumi to visit him. Our neighbours called and told me to come back. When I arrived, I saw they were using pumps to drain water from the houses and had torn down walls… I have nothing left. The fridge, the gas supply, all the household appliances—everything that could be plugged into the electricity… The beds and the floor have been ripped out. Nothing is left.”

According to a local resident, officials at the mayor’s office said it would take time to resolve the problems in Gomaro. Geologists from Tbilisi first need to assess the situation. After that, “it will take millions to build bridges and retaining walls.”

“If we try to repair the bridges and retaining walls ourselves, we’ll be the ones held responsible. We’ve already been waiting for a year,” the young woman said.

Heavy machinery was brought into Gomaro on Thursday evening, and part of the affected area has already been cleared. Cleanup operations are set to continue the following day.

Flooded home in the village of Gomaro. Photo: Sknews

Flooded home in the village of Gomaro. Photo: Sknews

The village of Gomaro on the second day after the landslide. Photo: Sknews

The village of Gomaro on the second day after the landslide. Photo: Sknews

Statement from the authorities

The Adigeni Municipality administration released an official statement on the second day after the disaster.

According to the statement, heavy rainfall across the region caused damage in three villages: Gomaro, Kvemo Enteli and Shoka.

The administration said the landslide in Gomaro damaged two residential homes, while a car was buried under debris. In Kvemo Enteli, agricultural land was damaged, while in Shoka both road infrastructure and farmland were affected.

“As a result of the emergency response, the riverbed in the village of Gomaro has been restored to its original course, while road clearance operations are continuing in the village of Shoka. At the same time, a special commission established by the municipal administration continues to assess the extent of the damage,” the administration said in its statement.

Major landslide hits Georgian village

World.title: Georgian Foreign Ministry expresses ‘regret’ over EU sanctions on Kulevi plant
World.content:
Georgia on EU’s 21st sanctions package

In an official statement, Georgia‘s Foreign Ministry expressed regret over the inclusion of the Kulevi oil terminal in the EU’s 21st sanctions package. The ministry said that “there are neither factual nor legal grounds for placing the Kulevi oil terminal on the sanctions list.”

On 23 July, the European Union’s 21st sanctions package against Russia was announced. It includes the Kulevi oil terminal in Georgia and several cryptocurrency platforms.

The ban on transactions with the Kulevi oil terminal will take effect in six months unless the facility changes its operating practices.

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry said the country fully takes into account the EU sanctions regime, “the context of that regime”, and is taking all necessary measures to ensure that Georgian territory is not used to circumvent sanctions.

The statement also stresses that cooperation with the EU in this area is based on transparency and openness. Georgian authorities, it says, consistently provide EU institutions with all necessary information and clarifications in a timely manner.

The ministry also said that, to date, authorities have not recorded any cases of EU sanctions being circumvented through Georgian territory.

“During preparations for the EU’s 21st sanctions package, the Georgian side provided the European Commission with comprehensive information and supporting documentation clearly demonstrating that there are neither factual nor legal grounds for placing the Kulevi oil terminal on the sanctions list,” the statement says.

The Foreign Ministry also expressed hope that the relevant departments of the European Commission and EU member states “will be guided by the principle of fairness and review the decision” within the next six months.

A brief overview of the new sanctions package

The EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia, which is due to take effect shortly, received final approval from the permanent representatives of the EU member states on 23 July 2026.

The sanctions are expected to enter into force on 23 July following approval by EU leaders and their official publication.

The measures target sectors of the Russian economy that provide the greatest financial support for the war in Ukraine, including energy, financial services and the cryptocurrency sector.

The package also imposes sanctions on more than 50 companies and organisations that supply military equipment and weapons to Russia.

It also includes the largest set of individual sanctions to date, targeting a total of 218 entities: 48 individuals and 170 legal entities.

It marks one of the largest expansions of EU sanctions over the past four years.

Georgia on EU’s 21st sanctions package

World.title: Armenia’s labour market trends: Social media replaces employment agencies as jobs and wages grow
World.content:
Analysis of labour market trends in Armenia

Armenia‘s unemployment rate fell only slightly in 2025, declining to 11.8% from 13.3% in 2024. At the same time, according to the country’s Statistical Committee, wages continued to rise, with the average monthly salary increasing by 5.6% over the same period to 303,140 drams ($828).

Compared with 2021, the average nominal monthly salary has increased by 48.6%, the number of employees has grown by 22.4%, and the unemployment rate has fallen by 2.7 percentage points.

Employment remains highest in the wholesale and retail trade sectors, as well as in education and manufacturing. By contrast, employment is lower in the arts and culture, scientific research, and real estate sectors.

An analysis of online job platforms shows that employers are currently seeking couriers, waiters, accountants, assistants, sales and marketing specialists, and fundraising professionals.

At the same time, job seekers are increasingly drawn to international, foreign, and joint ventures, attracted by both higher salaries and better working environments.

“The labour market has become more coordinated”

Until 2016, Naira Piloyan ran an employment agency that helped many people find jobs and earned a reputation as a reliable partner for local organisations. Over the past decade, however, she says the labour market has changed. Employers now search for candidates through online platforms, using their own social media pages and job websites. As a result, she had to close her agency. She now works as a human resources specialist at a pharmaceutical company.

She says every medium-sized and large company in Armenia now employs HR specialists. They use online platforms and professional networks to find qualified candidates.

“I closely follow developments in the labour market. From my own experience, I can say that local professionals have become much better at presenting themselves during the hiring process. Employers have also become more selective when recruiting staff. The whole process is now far more streamlined and coordinated,” she says.

At the same time, she notes that personal connections and recommendations from friends or acquaintances still influence hiring decisions.

However, serious companies have realised that hiring unqualified staff creates a “time bomb” for their future development.

Instead, they rely on candidates’ experience, references from previous employers and personal interviews.

“Over the past few years, salaries at our company have increased by around 30% on average. Higher levels of professionalism among staff have largely driven that increase. Every employee takes professional development courses or retrains in a new field. As people gain knowledge and experience, they expect higher pay. If they don’t receive the salary they believe they deserve, they start looking for another job. That staff turnover has become a major challenge for large companies,” the HR specialist explains.

She says employers have also started investing more in their employees’ skills. Many companies now pay for foreign language courses, mainly English, as well as training abroad in manufacturing, technology and other fields.

She believes this growing coordination has improved the quality of Armenia’s labour market. When someone from another company applies for a job with her employer, she can now openly discuss the candidate’s abilities and professional qualities with HR managers at their previous workplace.

“In the past, asking someone for an opinion about a job applicant felt awkward. Now I simply send an email and receive a reply within a few days. The only real difficulty today is finding highly specialised professionals and technical staff. Problems usually arise when we urgently need to hire someone like a driver, security guard or cleaner. Candidates for these jobs tend to be very conservative. For example, if they need to stay just 10 minutes beyond the end of their shift, they often show little flexibility. Some may even leave work during the day without informing anyone.”

According to her, wages for these positions have risen by a larger percentage than salaries for many higher-skilled professions, including finance specialists and translators.

Working conditions are more attractive at foreign companies

Ilona Khachatryan is a logistics specialist. She now works for an American company and earns four times more than she did two years ago in the same role at a local firm. But salary is only part of the reason she left. She says unhealthy relations with management at her former company also played a major role. More broadly, she is critical of hiring practices and personnel management at many local organisations.

“At the company where I worked, it was extremely difficult to receive the bonuses that management itself had promised. To avoid paying them, they would even falsify hourly timesheets.

I applied for jobs at other local companies as well. I attended interviews and then waited for months without hearing back. Even if they decide not to hire you, shouldn’t they at least tell you? After all, you invest your time and effort preparing for those interviews. Foreign companies treat candidates much more fairly. They make transparent hiring decisions. If they decide not to hire someone, they explain in detail why they cannot move forward with the candidate.”

Ilona says her current employer hired her after the first interview. The company immediately explained the salary, holiday entitlement, employment rights and job responsibilities.

“Hearing the words ‘thank you for your work’ genuinely motivates me. It gives me energy and makes me work with greater enthusiasm and commitment. And when your employer also recognises your achievements, you realise just how undervalued professionals are in the local labour market.”

Analysis of labour market trends in Armenia

World.title: Azerbaijan changes status of internally displaced people: What do new rules provide?
World.content:
The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

On 23 July, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed into law amendments to the Law on the Status of Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons and the Law on the Social Protection of Internally Displaced Persons and Persons Equated with Them.

The amendments to the Housing Code provide for the creation of a Permanent Resettlement Fund in the territories liberated from occupation. Housing from the fund will be used to resettle internally displaced persons (IDPs) to the reclaimed territories and will later be transferred to them as private property.

The legislation also clarifies the grounds on which a person may lose IDP status. This applies to those who refuse housing offered by the state, as well as to those who are provided with alternative housing that meets the officially established housing standard for the relevant region instead of accommodation in their previous place of residence. At the same time, social protection measures will remain in place for three years after a person loses or voluntarily relinquishes their IDP status.

The changes are intended to strengthen the legal framework for the Great Return programme. In practice, however, they could significantly affect the lives of hundreds of thousands of people who have spent decades building their lives in Baku and other parts of Azerbaijan.

The purpose of the law and the benefits linked to IDP status

Under the previous legislation, internally displaced person (IDP) status entitled holders to a range of social benefits, including a monthly allowance of 60 manats (about $35) for each family member, state-funded tuition at fee-paying departments of public universities, and exemptions from certain government fees and utility payments.

For people forced to flee their homes in the early 1990s and who had spent decades living in dormitories, temporary housing units or other makeshift accommodation, these benefits represented a basic form of social support. The status also carried legal significance, as it formally recognised that they had been displaced against their will.

Under the new rules, the state is deemed to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers an internally displaced person permanent housing. If the person accepts the apartment, ownership is transferred to them, but they simultaneously lose their IDP status. Those who refuse the offer also lose their status and may forfeit the temporary accommodation provided to them in Baku or another city.

During a three-year transition period, only social support measures, including financial assistance and education benefits, will remain in place. The legal status itself, along with the other rights and guarantees associated with it, will cease to apply.

Freedom of choice and the problem of “any available housing”

The law refers to “alternative housing that complies with the standards established for the region of residence”. In practice, this means that internally displaced people are not necessarily offered housing in their native village or on their ancestral land.

For example, a person who owned several hectares of farmland before being displaced may now be offered a house in a newly built settlement with a plot of only 100–200 square metres. Ownership of their original land is not restored, as the state provides housing only. As a result, the concept of “returning home” is significantly narrowed.

According to dozens of families whose accounts have been shared on social media and in public appeals, many of the homes offered to them suffer from poor construction. They report leaking roofs during rainfall, flooded yards, and repeated disruptions to gas, water and electricity supplies. In some cases, applicants say they have been told verbally: “You’ve been given a house — be grateful, or you’ll lose that too.”

Similar complaints have also been submitted through official grievance mechanisms, although the issue has yet to generate wider public debate.

Life in Baku after three decades of integration

A large proportion of Azerbaijan’s internally displaced people have spent more than 30 years living in Baku and other major economic centres. Over that time, they have found employment, received an education, gained access to healthcare and established stable social networks. After losing their homes in the early 1990s, they were provided with temporary accommodation by the state, including places in dormitories, unfinished buildings and container settlements, as well as apartments in purpose-built residential complexes.

Under the new rules, however, this housing may be reclaimed once a person loses IDP status. As a result, many people face a difficult choice: accept an apartment in Karabakh and leave behind the life they have built in Baku, or lose both their IDP status and the accommodation provided to them by the state.

International human rights standards, including the UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement, require that return be voluntary, safe and carried out in dignity. These principles are based on freedom of choice, the provision of adequate housing and, wherever possible, the restoration of rights to former property. Under Azerbaijan’s new legislation, however, the state is considered to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers housing, while refusing that offer results in the loss of IDP status. This weakens the principle that return should be voluntary.

Official position and expert assessments

Pro-government media outlets, including Milli.az, Report.az and APA, have presented the amendments in a positive light, using phrases such as “restoring property rights”, “sustainable social support” and “providing a legal framework for the Great Return programme”.

MP Vugar Bayramov has also argued that the three-year transition period demonstrates the state’s continued commitment to social support. Official statements emphasise that the new housing is transferred into private ownership rather than provided on a rental basis, which the authorities say will encourage people to settle permanently in the region.

At the same time, independent observers and some human rights advocates argue that the changes restrict freedom of choice, fail to fully restore land rights and raise other concerns. They also point to the contrast between the urban lifestyles that many IDPs have built over the past three decades and the newly established rural settlements, as well as the risks of unemployment and inadequate infrastructure.

The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

World.title: EU’s 21st sanctions package targets Kulevi oil terminal and cryptocurrency platforms in Georgia
World.content:
Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

The European Union’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia includes an oil refinery in the Georgian town of Kulevi and several cryptocurrency platforms.

The sanctions against the Kulevi refinery, which processes and sells Russian oil, include a six-month grace period. The ban on transactions will take effect after six months unless the refinery changes its business practices.

The Kulevi refinery had previously been considered for inclusion in the EU’s 20th package of sanctions against Russia, but was ultimately removed from the sanctions list.

At the time, the EU said that “the Georgian authorities and the port operator had made positive commitments.” This was stated in a letter from the EU’s Special Envoy, David O’Sullivan, to Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili.

What does the new sanctions package include?

The EU’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia, which is expected to take effect shortly, was formally approved by the permanent representatives of the EU member states on 23 July 2026.

The sanctions are expected to enter into force on 23 July following approval by EU leaders and their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

The measures target sectors of the Russian economy that generate significant revenue for Moscow’s war in Ukraine, including energy, financial services and the cryptocurrency sector.

The package also imposes sanctions on more than 50 companies and organisations involved in supplying military goods and weapons to Russia.

It includes the EU’s largest-ever round of individual sanctions, targeting a total of 218 entities — 48 individuals and 170 legal entities.

It is one of the most significant expansions of the EU’s sanctions regime in the past four years.

Sanctions against the Kulevi refinery

“The package introduces the possibility of banning transactions with oil refineries listed in Russia and third countries that process Russian crude oil and petroleum products. Under these measures, the EU is imposing a ban on transactions with the Georgian oil refinery in Kulevi, which processes and trades Russian oil. The ban will take effect in six months,” the EU said in a statement.

According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, citing a source familiar with the matter, the introduction of a six-month deadline is unprecedented in EU sanctions policy.

The same source said the decision reflected Tbilisi’s willingness to meet the EU’s requirements, which became apparent during discussions over sanctions related to the port.

This means that if the Kulevi refinery continues processing Russian oil over the next six months, it will become subject to EU sanctions. The refinery’s owner, Black Sea Petroleum, announced on 1 July 2026 that it would begin full-scale processing of non-Russian crude from August or September.

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, domestic exports rose sharply in January 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, driven largely by exports of petroleum products.

Petroleum and petroleum products ranked as Georgia’s second-largest export category in January 2026, with exports worth $58.7 million, accounting for 12.2% of the country’s total exports.

Cryptocurrency platforms added to the sanctions list

The EU has imposed transaction bans on 14 cryptocurrency platforms based in Georgia, Panama, the United Arab Emirates, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus and the Marshall Islands.

For the first time, the EU has introduced a mechanism allowing it to impose a complete ban on transactions between EU companies and cryptocurrency platforms that help Russia circumvent sanctions.

The measure also applies to crypto service providers operating in third countries if they facilitate activities that serve Russian interests.

What does the inclusion of Georgian companies in the sanctions package mean for Georgia?

The inclusion of the Kulevi refinery in the EU’s 21st sanctions package has already sparked debate in Georgia.

“The EU’s 21st sanctions package is a national disgrace: Georgian assets are being used as cannon fodder for Russia’s war machine. By allowing the Kremlin to circumvent sanctions, those in power are betraying our sovereignty. Georgia’s place is in Europe — we will never become a loophole for Russian aggression,” Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zourabichvili, wrote on X.

Analyst Lela Djedjelava said sanctions against such an important economic asset would have an impact on the Georgian economy.

“The consequences will become increasingly visible over time. The reality is that the Kulevi refinery is probably not the only facility that could be exposed for cooperating with Russia. If other businesses in Georgia are also hit by sanctions, it will naturally have a very negative impact on the country.”

Gedevan Popkhadze, one of the leaders of the opposition Coalition for Change, said the EU sanctions against the Kulevi refinery were the result of the Georgian government’s inaction.

“If you are not helping Ukraine, why are you helping Russia? If you do not want war, why are you acting in favour of one of the parties to the conflict? We must clearly understand that these sanctions are not a message to the Kulevi refinery itself — they are a message to Georgia’s de facto government. It should realise that claiming to be neutral is hypocrisy.”

Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

World.title: Opinion: ‘There is no longer peace in Georgia’
World.content:
Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

Professor at Ilia State University and literary critic Zaal Andronikashvili comments on the events that unfolded in Georgia on 22 July 2026, including the arrest of a journalist, a shooting in central Tbilisi, and an attack on an opposition stand-up comedian.

He writes that there is no longer peace in Georgia and blames Bidzina Ivanishvili and his Georgian Dream party.

Journalist Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 14 days of administrative detention over satirical social media posts about members of the Georgian Dream party. A shooting took place in central Tbilisi on 22 July, leaving four people injured, including two minors. One of the minors later died in hospital. Comedian Onise Okriashvili, a critic of the government, was brutally beaten at his home. Before the attack, he had been the target of a disinformation campaign on pro-government television channels.

Zaal Andronikashvili: “It is important to find the right name for what is happening in Georgia. The situation is new, and historical parallels apply only in part.

Since at least 2019, during the ‘Gavrilov Night’ protests, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have done everything possible to prevent a peaceful transfer of power. Some scholars describe this as a ‘coup from above’.”

This “coup from above” is not peaceful.

Anyone who believes that Georgia is at peace today is deeply mistaken. Beyond dragging Georgia into a geopolitical confrontation on Russia’s side — at an enormous cost to the country — Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are waging an asymmetric, hybrid civil war against the overwhelming majority of the Georgian population.

Part of this hybrid civil war consists of unlawful restrictive legislation enforced only against certain groups of citizens and against civil society as a whole.

There is also financial repression aimed at depriving opponents of the regime of their livelihoods, as well as the deliberate destruction of education and culture. Alongside this come aggression, hopelessness, and an absence of love and empathy elevated to the level of state policy.

There is micro-level violence — encouraging crime and fostering a culture of impunity that ultimately erodes trust in the law, the justice system, and the very idea of justice. There is macro-level violence carried out by the police and special forces, along with many other elements.

“I repeat: this is not peace.

It is a hybrid civil war waged by a regime that controls the police, the legislature and the country’s financial resources against the majority of Georgia’s population, especially its most active citizens. Its goal is to suppress, subjugate and ultimately enslave them.

The other side has nothing but the truth and peaceful resistance. But the truth is a powerful, almost invincible weapon — and it can never truly be defeated.

Despite this asymmetric civil war, whose domestic objective is to cement the regime permanently in power and make the current government irreplaceable, while its foreign policy goal is to sever Georgia once and for all from the European values-based community and turn it into a banana republic under a quasi-colonial regime, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have failed to win this unequal conflict.

Peaceful resistance is alive. The people have not been broken. They have not been intimidated.

Those who support the regime today, or choose silent complicity, should look at Russia.

People there also believed that if they kept quiet and buried their heads in a bowl of caviar, none of it would affect them. Other people’s children would die, someone else would go to prison, someone else’s life would be ruined. Perhaps someone would stop greeting them, but they could live with that.

In reality, supporting injustice always comes at a price. Injustice and lawlessness may begin by targeting only selected groups, but they very quickly spread to everyone.

By supporting injustice, you create an environment in which that injustice will inevitably reach you in one form or another.

But people are willing to ignore it until it affects them personally. There is a powerful metaphor in the Gospel of Matthew (26:52): ‘All who draw the sword will die by the sword.’ This is not really about the sword itself, but more broadly about the laws of social reality and their universal nature.

There is no peace in Georgia. Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are responsible for that.”

Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

World.title: Diamonds on the board, Tonga on the map in Glasgow
World.content:
The game was never going to be close between the Diamonds and Tonga, but as Uneeq Palavi hit the Griddy on her way onto court, it was clear the result was only part of the story.

One was the undisputed number-one team in the world and defending champions, the other was on Games debut.

"[Before the game] we were pretty much telling ourselves 'oh, we're gonna beat the diamonds' but it's just a hype up to get around," Palavi said.

Tonga's Uneeq Palavi (right) had plenty of support in the stands at the Hydro. ( Getty Images: Morgan Harlow)

"It's just another step closer to putting our little country on the map and that's all that matters."

As is so often the case, especially at the Commonwealth Games, the gulf in profile and quality meant every Australian goal was met with polite applause and each Tongan bucket led to cheers usually reserved for contests of significantly more consequence.

Only 36 hours earlier, the British King and Queen had elicited a similar reaction in the same venue, Glasgow's colosseum-like Hydro arena.

There was no shortage of physicality on display. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

On Saturday, there was more royalty in the house, with Tongan Princess Lātūfuipeka Tukuʻaho, albeit sitting with the plebs in the stands, rather than in the royal box populated by Charles, Camilla and other dignitaries at the opening ceremony.

"I didn't expect so many Tongans to be out there but that's the crazy thing, no matter where you are in the world there's always Tongans to support and I feel like that's the best thing to have behind us," Palavi said.

The crowd at the Hydro was firmly on Tonga's side. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

And it wasn't just Tongans.

Perched in the upper decks were Diamonds reserves Amy Parmenter and Jessie Grenvold.

Diamonds mid-courter Amy Parmenter was in the stands cheering for Tonga. (Instagram: Jessie Grenvold)

Rather than cheering for their girls in gold, they held a sign reading "Princess Pav", backing their Melbourne Mavericks teammate.

In the second half, Palavi clocked them and any time she managed to have a moment against the vice-like defence of Jo Weston, Courtney Bruce, Matilda Garrett or Sarah Klau, her eyes went straight up to them.

"It was good to see their faces to ground myself and remind myself that, although the loss was tough, it's great to have people around me like that," she said.

Unfortunately, there weren't many chances for those fans to get up and about.

Palavi and Lavinia Lavea got vanishingly few opportunities in the face of the locked-in, well-oiled defence of the Diamonds.

Uneeq Palavi scored 30 of Tonga's 38 goals. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Stacey Marinkovich rolled out her first-choice seven to start the match.

By half-time, Tonga had taken 22 shots for 19 goals. Australia was 52/55, with six intercepts.

In the second half, Marinkovich rattled through different line-ups en route to a 99-38 thumping in a bit of a test case for later group matches against England, South Africa, Malawi and Northern Ireland.

The Diamonds almost cracked 100 against Tonga. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

For Tonga, things should only get easier.

"It wasn't the best, but to come up against the world's best it's obviously gonna be something like that," Palavi said.

"We're not a new team but we're new in this environment. I feel like it's a lot to come up against the world's best and put out what we wanted to do, but I feel like we did good regardless."

World.title: Indian education minister resigns after Cockroach movement protests
World.content:
Indian Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan has resigned after nationwide protests over the country's education system.

The Cockroach Janta Party organisation has been calling for the minister's resignation for months, amid ongoing exam paper leaks.

Dharmandra Pradhan has resigned following youth-led protests. (AP)

The movement made international headlines this week after thousands took to the streets of New Delhi and tried to march on parliament in a rare show of force against the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government.

They were stopped by authorities using batons, tear gas and smoke bombs to break up crowds. More than 100 people were hospitalised, according to local media reports.

"We have done it," said Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, as the protesters at the Jantar Mantar site celebrated.

Abhijeet Dipke celebrates with supporters after the education minister's resignation. (Reuters: Francis Mascarenhas)

In a letter published on X on Saturday, Mr Pradhan said he "took responsibility" for the leaking of India's national medical entrance exam in May.

The leak led to the cancellation of results and the government ordering a retest, which affected two million young people across the nation.

"The situation that has emerged at Jantar Mantar and elsewhere in the country should not be exploited by anti national forces, that the unity of the country should remain, that not a single student's future should be entangled in legal complexities, and that our children should focus on their studies and careers, keeping these considerations in mind, I have sent my resignation to the Hon'ble Prime Minister," the letter said.

"I deeply respect the aspirations, feelings, and legitimate expectations of the country's youth."

Supporters of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) celebrate India’s Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. (Reuters: Anushree Fadnavis)

Upon hearing the news of Mr Pradhan's resignation, protesters shouted "Jai Hind" in the streets, a patriotic slogan meaning "Victory to India".

The national anthem was also played on loudspeakers throughout the area while hundreds of police officials stood on guard nearby.

"We feel very excited. You can see everybody is happy, and I believe this is just the start," one protester told the ABC.

"This feels like a festival for democracy. We are very excited about what happens next. We are hopeful that the education system will get better," another said.

After occupying Jantar Mantar — New Delhi's official protest site — for 36 days, CJP leaders have now officially ended the protest and asked demonstrators to go home.

"The CJP declares that we withdraw the agitation in good faith," spokesman Saurav Das said.

The CJP said the government had agreed to withdraw charges against protesters in Delhi and BJP-ruled states and ⁠⁠guarantee no legal action would be taken against protest organisers.

It also agreed to provide compensation to families of students who committed suicides in the wake of exam leaks earlier this year, and ⁠⁠consider a four-point plan to reform India's exam and education system.



From 'commendable efforts' to resignation

Mr Pradhan had been India's education minister for more than five years and is one of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's most senior cabinet ministers.

The 57-year-old previously served as the minister of petroleum and minister of steel.

The resignation is a significant shift from the government's initial response to the exam leak scandal, which saw Mr Modi praise Mr Pradhan for his "commendable efforts towards the implementation of the National Education Policy" in a social media post.

The BJP government has also announced a bill to amend the country's Public Examinations Act to increase the punishment for offences related to paper leaks.

According to local media, individuals involved in leaks will face a maximum of 10 years in prison and a fine of up to Rs 50 lakh ($74,050).

'A victory of patience'

Activist Sonam Wangchuk ended a hunger strike this week that lasted 26 days and saw the 59-year-old forcibly removed from the protest site by police after the Delhi High Court ruled the government was responsible for his welfare.

Mr Wangchuk began his strike when the CJP began its sit-in protest at Jantar Mantar to draw attention to and support the movement.

He said Mr Pradhan's resignation was "a victory of peace, patience and perseverance," in a post on social media.

Inside the 'Cockroach' party A student who started a youth uprising across India is fast becoming the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12-year reign.

The protests also reflect anger over job scarcity, corruption and government accountability.

The months-old Cockroach movement and the protest have been seen as the biggest public challenge Mr Modi has faced in his third term.

Mr Pradhan is the second minister to resign following a scandal since Mr Modi came to power in 2014.

MJ Akbar resigned from his position as junior foreign minister in October 2018 following sexual harassment allegations.

ABC/wires

World.title: Houthis and Saudi Arabia trade fire amid Red Sea blockade
World.content:
Yemen's Houthi rebels have claimed responsibility for missile attacks on the Saudi Arabia cities of Jazan and Yanbu, marking a widening of conflict in the Middle East.

The Iran-backed group's military spokesperson Yahya Sare said in a statement that the group carried out operations targeting Saudi Aramco facilities in Jazan and Yanbu.

Greek security sources said that air defence systems in Saudi Arabia had intercepted two ballistic missiles from Yemen on Saturday, which were targeting oil refineries in Yanbu.

Video posted to social media suggested the Aramco oil refinery in Jazan had been hit.

The Houthis had accused Saudi Arabia — a US ally — of a "dangerous escalation" after Riyadh struck military targets belonging to the Houthis on Friday, following the rebels announcing a maritime blockade of the top oil producer and hitting Riyadh's ships in the Red Sea.

The Iran-backed group claimed attacks on two Saudi ships earlier this week, with Saudi Arabia confirming one of the attacks in the Red Sea.

Riyadh did not immediately comment on the newest strikes, but its civil defence agency issued brief warnings to residents in the city, as well as Yanbu, earlier on Saturday.

The Saudi-backed Yemeni government air force also carried out air strikes on Houthi missile and drone launch sites and arms depots in the Marib and al-Jawf provinces, two military officials said.

The officials said the strikes were among the first offensive operations launched by the Yemeni government against the Houthis amid the latest conflict.

Talks 'most serious that we've seen them'

Donald Trump says talks with Iran are continuing. (AP: Rod Lamkey Jr)

This flare-up marks a new front in a war that has engulfed the Middle East region following US-Israeli strikes on Tehran in February, and comes on top of Iran's parallel blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia's only other maritime route.

The key waterway of the Strait of Hormuz, the entrance to the Gulf, has so far been the focus of a war that has killed thousands over almost five months, stoked global inflation and fanned fears of an economic downturn.

The escalation came after US President Donald Trump said he would hold off on a major operation because Iran was now getting "serious" in talks with Washington.

The US military broke its daily announcement of fresh strikes on the Islamic republic on Saturday, following 13 nights in a row hitting military targets there.

"We are talking to them," Mr Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday.

"I think they're being serious. I think … they are being by far the most serious that we've seen them, but that doesn't mean we get there."

Asked what the exit strategy was for the Iran war, Mr Trump said there was a "military exit where we just keep going just the way we are, and we can even make it a heavier dose, and it's knocking out everything they have. Or there's a smarter strategy that you make a deal".

He said Iran had a choice between making a deal or facing a "much higher level" of strikes after nearly two weeks of US attacks that left the ceasefire in tatters.

"We're locked and loaded. We're ready to go," Mr Trump said.

He added that he did not know what the "tipping point" would be for a decision, but reiterated that Iran being close to developing a nuclear weapon would be a red line.

Russia, China not arming Iran, Trump says

Mr Trump also insisted that Russia and China were not arming Iran, despite reports both were feeding Tehran intelligence to target US forces.

US and Iran trade strikes The strikes came after US President Donald Trump vowed "major military punishment" for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen over moves to block a second major international shipping route.

"President Xi [Jinping] said he will not partake, and President [Vladimir] Putin said the same thing … I trust them," Mr Trump told reporters.

"I don't think they'd want to have me disappointed."

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Kyrgyzstan, calling for a memorandum of understanding aimed at easing tensions in the Middle East and the Gulf region, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.

ABC/wires

World.title: Two people shot by police during altercation in Cairns
World.content:
Two people have been shot by police in far north Queensland.

Authorities were called to an address in Mount Sheridan, a suburb of Cairns, just after 5pm, after reports of a man armed with knives.

Police say they attempted to engage the man before he was shot by officers.

A woman was also shot during the altercation.

The Queensland Ambulance Service says they have both been taken to the Cairns Hospital.

They are both in a stable condition.

World.title: Live: Blow to host nation as Scottish star McColgan ruled out of Games
World.content:
Eilish McColgan's win four years ago made her a Scottish sporting heroine - sadly the distance runner won't be competing in Glasgow (Getty Images/SNS Group)

Four years ago in Birmingham, Eilish McColgan produced the run of her life to win the women's 10,000m at the Commonwealth Games.

On the final lap of the event, she burst around the last turn and outkicked Kenya's Irene Chepet Cheptai to set a new Games record of 30 minutes, 48.60 seconds.

In doing so she became a Scottish sporting heroine — and matched her mother Liz, who had won the same event in Edinburgh in 1986 — while breaking her mum's 32-year-old Games record.

Sadly for McColgan and Scottish sports fans, Eilish will not be able to defend her title in Glasgow, after aggravating a foot injury in the London Marathon - she has been ruled out with a stress fracture.

"Sadly, I won't be competing at Glasgow 2026," she said in a statement. "After almost 10 weeks out, it probably won't come as a huge surprise.

"The good news is I'm back running. The bad news is I've simply run out of time to get myself, and my toe, back into spikes.

"Having started the year stronger than ever, I know the fitness is there but having only taken my first run outdoors a couple of weeks ago, the clock was always against me.

"I'll be in Glasgow all week cheering on Team Scotland and wish everyone on the team the best of luck at the Games."

World.title: Drivers urged to play their part as five people die on WA roads in 24 hours
World.content:
Five people have died in separate crashes in Western Australia in less than 24 hours, as the state's road toll continues to soar.

The first fatality happened on Friday afternoon when a male driver died after his car crashed into a tree on George Road in Wuraming, near Boddington in the Peel region, at about 1.10pm.

Just five minutes later in WA's Mid West, a 46-year-old man suffered the same fate in Cape Burney, near Geraldton, after the vehicle he was driving left Brand Highway and hit a tree.

On Friday night in Martin in Perth's south-east, a female passenger was killed after two vehicles collided at the intersection of Mills Road West on Tonkin Highway at about 10:45pm.

A female passenger died after two vehicles collided on Tonkin Highway at the Mills Road West intersection in Martin on Friday night. (ABC News)

The 30-year-old woman was a passenger in a Toyota Hilux and was taken to Royal Perth Hospital where she later died.

The vehicle's 33-year-old male driver was taken to Armadale Hospital with serious injuries, while the 38-year-old male driver of the other vehicle was taken to Royal Perth Hospital.

As WA school holidays loom, fears mount for road safety With road deaths in WA on track to surpass their highest toll in almost two decades, first responders fear the upcoming school holidays will make things worse.

In the state's north west this morning, Major Crash investigators travelled to Mount Anketell in Karratha, where police said two people are believed to have died in a crash on the North West Coastal Highway.

Police said at about 5:30am, two vehicles collided head-on near the intersection of De Witt Road, with one vehicle catching fire.

The driver of the second vehicle was critically injured and taken to hospital.

Police urge any witnesses or people with video footage of the four crashes, to contact Crime Stoppers.

Surging road toll

So far this year, there have been 126 road fatalities, higher than the 121 deaths recorded in the same 2025 period and above the 101 deaths of 2024.

WA minister Simone McGurk said the government was committed to improving road safety across the state but urged the public to also play its part.

Simone McGurk has urged drivers to take more care on the roads after this latest spate of deaths. (ABC News, file photo: Keane Bourke)

"As a state government we've spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to improve our roads … but we also need the public to get on board," she said.

"I don't know the exact circumstances of these fatalities. I just urge people to think about fatigue, seatbelt, speed, distraction and also alcohol and other drugs.

"Please take care on our roads because the price of not being careful can be just too much."

Insurer RAC recently predicted the state's yearly road toll would exceed 200 deaths and said the fatalities had been at crisis levels for several years.

WA has the second highest road death toll of any state or territory in the nation, even though road deaths per capita have decreased over the last 10 years

World.title: Husic lashes Labor culture after push for Gaza debate fails
World.content:
A push to recognise claims of genocide in Gaza failed to gain enough support for a debate on the floor of Labor's national conference, sparking criticism of the party's internal culture.

Labor MP Ed Husic was unable to secure a seconder for his proposed resolution on Israel and Palestine in the final hours of the 50th ALP National Conference today.

The outspoken backbencher said he was "surprised" at the energy factional powerbrokers had applied to preventing open debate and declared he did not "give a shit" if senior colleagues put him in the freezer for speaking out on contentious issues.

Delegates at the conference instead voted to adopt positions on Israel, Palestine and Hamas that broadly aligned with the Albanese government's view, though have been criticised by the Israeli embassy.

MPs Josh Burns, who is Jewish, and Basem Abdo, the son of Palestinian refugees, both spoke in favour of the platform in what was intended as a show of unity.

Josh Burns and Basem Abdo both supported the party's platform. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

The conference concluded in Adelaide this afternoon without any major stoushes on the floor as the 400 elected delegates voted to adopt the party's 2026 National Platform.

Mr Husic had sought to amend the platform to acknowledge a United Nations inquiry that determined Israeli authorities had "deliberately targeted Palestinian children, resulting in genocide and atrocity crimes in the Gaza Strip and war crimes in the West Bank".

His resolution was initially seconded by the Maritime Union of Australia, but Mr Husic revealed the left-faction union had withdrawn support earlier in the morning.

"I have been surprised at the extraordinary amount of energy that has been applied to stop this, as opposed to talking about this, being able to have discussions and better set it out," Mr Husic said.

'Don't give a shit' if I'm put in the freezer: Husic

In the lead-up to the triennial conference, Mr Husic had spoken out on a range of issues, including Labor's support for the AUKUS submarine deal, a tax on gas and the Middle East.

Asked if it had been a "strategic" error to spread his focus, potentially at the expense of securing support for a debate on Israel and Palestine, Mr Husic said it was a "fair question".

"I've been consistent on the things I really care about and I've spoken up in that way," he said.

Ed Husic spoke out about the AUKUS submarine deal, a tax on gas and the Middle East ahead of the conference. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

When pressed on whether senior ministers, such as Defence Minister Richard Marles and Foreign Minister Penny Wong, had frozen him out from platform discussions about Israel and Palestine, Mr Husic replied: "If they put me in the freezer, I don't give a shit."

Senior Labor sources pushed back on the idea Mr Husic had been iced out, suggesting he had not sought to discuss the matter with the prime minister during the three-day conference.

Allowing disagreement a 'big test' for Labor

Mr Husic believed the "divisive" Rudd-Gillard era had led to a cooling effect on debate within the party.

"People are almost traumatised into a position that … anything that looks like a debate is a schism, a difference, a divide that means that the government might topple over," he said.

"I don't think that's the case at all.

" You've got to be able to find a way to disagree respectfully and try and work with people and have that discussion. "

Australia's 'monoculture' might be at the Labor conference The party's supreme policy-making machine has been busy honing a platform that's as tight and shiny as a button.

Mr Husic said there was a lesson for Labor to learn as One Nation gathered support from voters who believed the party would stand up for what they thought was "right" for the country.

"I think the big test for us, as one of the big parties, is to be able to show that we're willing to take [voters] with us and not jam the lines of the day in people's ears," he said.

Brandishing his ALP membership card, Mr Husic said when people signed up to the party they "didn't 

"The party of change — change sometimes involves conversations and you need to bring people together," he said.

Asked if Labor was still the "right fit" for him, Mr Husic said "yes".

Burns calls for 'empathy over outrage'

As Mr Husic was addressing the media, Mr Burns and Mr Abdo walked onto the conference stage together in a show of support between the Jewish and Palestinian communities.

"We stand here to demonstrate what is possible when people choose to work together, and that the Australian Labor Party has room for both of us and for the communities we love," Mr Burns said.

In a passionate speech, Mr Burns urged members to choose "empathy over outrage" as he rallied support of the party's platform on Israel and Palestine.

He acknowledged the document did "not represent everything either of us might wish to say, nor every aspect of government policy".

"But through hours of conversation and compromise and respect, we are both standing here together," he said.

Abdo says humanity 'universal'

Mr Abdo said the party's platform committed Labor to "stand by the foundations Australia has helped shape and long defended — a rules-based order".

"For generations of Palestinians living under occupation, so many of those things we take for granted remain out of reach," he said.

"Occupation reaches into homes, into schools, into workplaces, into communities, every single day."

Mr Abdo said human dignity was "universal" and should "never be determined by where you are born or who you are".

Pro-Palestinian protesters gathered outside the conference on Friday. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

He also thanked his colleague Mr Burns for "good faith in what is an uneasy process" leading up to the conference.

The procedural motion that allowed Mr Burns and Mr Abdo to speak had been proposed by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Mr Marles.

Speaking at the conference, Mr Marles thanked delegates who had "compromised" to reach consensus.

Labor stakes out positions on Israel and Palestine

Labor's platform, which is designed to guide the party for the next three years, opposes the "annexation of Palestinian territory" and calls for Israel to end "illegal settlement activity".

In July 2024, the International Criminal Court declared Israel's settlements in the Palestinian territories violated international law and ordered their dismantling.

Israel has rejected the illegality of the settlements, with senior far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, who are both sanctioned by Australia, advocating for their expansion.

Labor's platform also urges the government to implement "further action and sanctions as necessary" to address the issue.

Acknowledging Australia has "always stood against the death penalty as an inhumane and degrading form of punishment", the platform condemns "recent Knesset legislation and all other discriminatory laws which target Palestinians".

Australia sanctions two far-right Israeli ministers Foreign Minister Penny Wong says Australia hs joined the UK, Canada and New Zealand in sanctioning Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich for inciting violence against Palestinians.

This year the Israeli government passed laws that implement death by hanging for Palestinians convicted of terror-related killings in the West Bank.

That platform also states a belief that "Israelis and Palestinians deserve to live their lives free from terror and violence," backs the two-state solution and "unreservedly condemns" the terrorism and violent extremism, "including as perpetrated by Hamas".

The Israeli embassy last week released a lengthy statement criticising the then-draft platform, arguing it weakened Labor's position on Hamas and the Palestinian Authority.

"The embassy respectfully submits that several elements of the draft national platform risk placing responsibility for the conflict on one party," it said.

World.title: Liberty Bell Bay may have been insolvent for more than a year before closing
World.content:
The administrators of the Liberty Bell Bay manganese smelter believe the company had been insolvent since May last year, months before the Tasmanian government loaned it $20 million.

The smelter in northern Tasmania was placed into administration in March and officially closed last week, leaving about 200 workers without jobs.

Liberty Bell Bay was part of GFG Alliance, which is owned by Sanjeev Gupta.

In its voluntary administrators' report, EY Parthenon identified that Liberty Bell Bay may have been insolvent.

"The Administrators are of the view that the Company was insolvent from as early as 1 May 2025," it stated.

The company was given a $20 million loan from the state government in August 2025, $14 million of which was used to buy one 23,000-tonne shipment of ore.

The Tasmanian government provided a loan that enabled the smelter to buy a shipment of ore. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

The report estimated that Liberty Bell Bay owed creditors between $70 million and $300 million, including $27 million owed to employees:

$661,000 in superannuation

$2 million in annual leave

$2.5 million in long service leave

$22 million in redundancy and pay in lieu of notice

A company is deemed insolvent when its debt cannot be paid.

Some of the administrators' reasons for identifying the insolvency included:

Yearly revenue dropped from $172 million in the 2024-25 financial year, to $11 million in 2026

Consistent operating losses since 2022-23

Aged payables exceeding 60 days increased from 18 per cent of total payables in 2023-24, to 86 per cent in 2026

"Our preliminary estimate of a claim for insolvent trading is in the order of approximately $25 million, if proven," the report stated.

The report found that Liberty Bell Bay incurred net losses in 2022-23 of $21 million and in 2024-25 of $80 million.

Deputy Premier Guy Barnett said it was a concern that Liberty Bell Bay may have been insolvent before receiving the loan from the state government.

"The administrators have highlighted the absolute irresponsible behaviour of Sanjeev Gupta and GFG," Mr Barnett said.

"Our security is the ore … and that is why that due diligence was undertaken and that security was locked in on behalf of the tax payers.

"We put everything on the table that we possibly could."

Inter-company loans

The report also confirmed previous reports that GFG Alliance had moved about $200 million out of Liberty Bell Bay via inter-company loans.

The administrators found that the net inter-company loan balance was $191 million.

"Cash outflows to related parties … have meant that the Company has had very limited cash resources to withstand supply chain difficulties and commodity price fluctuations which have impacted profitability," the report stated.

A creditors meeting will be held on August 3 to resolve whether the company will be wound up, and if so, whether it wants to appoint a liquidator.

World.content:
England couldn’t match Australia’s opening day tally of 99 goals but they still completed a thumping win over Northern Ireland today to open their competition with an 83-34 win.

The Roses will take on the Diamonds on Sunday evening AEST in their second group game in a match that could well decide which nation will top Pool A although South Africa will also hope to disrupt those plans.

World.title: As Diamonds begin bid for gold, a pay dispute is brewing in netball – again
World.content:
SportNetballCommonwealth Games As Diamonds begin bid for gold, a pay dispute is brewing in netball – again Hannah Kennelly July 25, 2026 — 11:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: The Diamonds have pushed aside a pay dispute with Netball Australia to clinch a clinical and ruthless 61-goal win over Tonga in their opening match of the Commonwealth Games. The Diamonds’ win on Saturday was the first step in the defence of their 2022 gold medal from Birmingham, but once again they will have a campaign overshadowed by a battle with Netball Australia over pay. The Diamonds huddle up during the win over Tonga. Getty Images The current Super Netball collective player agreement expires on September 30, meaning all 88 players, including the Diamonds squad, will be off contract. The dispute between Netball Australia and the players’ union centres on the distribution of netball’s revenue and player frustration over pregnancy and parenting policies. It is a similar situation to the messy and extended pay negotiations that dominated headlines during the Diamonds’ World Cup campaign in 2023, as players battled for a revenue-sharing partnership and more financial transparency.



Related Article Super Netball Two years ago, Netball Australia was in trouble. Now they want to expand Super Netball The long and bitter dispute culminated in the resignation of chief executive Kelly Ryan. Diamonds and Melbourne Vixens star Kiera Austin said after the win over Tonga that the team was keeping its focus on the competition. She pointed out that the Commonwealth Games are one of two marquee events for netball, and therefore an opportunity that doesn’t come around often. But she acknowledged that player delegates were doing “lots of work to get that [deal] done”.



Diamonds coach Stacey Marinkovich dismissed suggestions the pay dispute would be a distraction for her players at the Games, saying the team was “fully focused on the job at hand”. Kiera Austin (centre) and Australian Diamonds teammates. Simon Schluter But the Australian Netball Players’ Association had previously confirmed that players rejected a “final offer” from Netball Australia at a recent full board meeting and at a player meeting. “The bottom line is that players were not prepared to take a real wage cut,” a union spokesperson said. “Especially without real improvements in conditions. “The ongoing CPA negotiations are causing the players a lot of stress.
